#5678. The EV Takeover Is Taking Shape, Despite Heroic Efforts To Stop It

Whelp, the AI boom has had one positive knock-on effect. It is creating new multi-millionaires by the bushel, any one of whom can afford to splurge on a pricey new electric vehicle. That aside, EV stakeholders in the US are springing back to life after a year-long slumber. Even General Motors is in play, stirring up long lost memories of its 1990’s-era EV1 debacle instead of hiding its head in shame. What’s up with that?

I’m just going to stick my neck out and say that the eponymous Aptera solar-powered autocycle from the US startup Aptera will attract enough AI-enriched drivers to make a go of it. The on-again, off-again, on-again automaker has been on this year, working towards volume production of a plug-in, three-wheeled two-seater EV that can travel up to 40 miles on its own solar-plus-storage system (see more Aptera news here).

Autocycles were once common here in the US and overseas markets, distinguished from motorcycles by their front-facing seats and steering wheels, rather than straddled seats and handlebars. They fell out of favor in the US by the middle of the 20th century, but 21st century hot-rodders have revived the form with a focus on eyebrow-raising, open-air, gas-guzzling showpieces. In particular, interest has spread in states that do not require autocycle drivers to invest in an additional motorcycle license.

The Aptera is showy in its own right, resembling a rocket ship with unique aerodynamic styling. Perhaps it may even show up in the next James Bond adventure with James Pattinson at the wheel. In the meantime, the company has just made good on its pledge to reward early investors in the world’s first solar-powered car with the first production models to role off the assembly line. Aptera #1 goes to the founder and CEO of GDP Venture, Martin Hartono, aka “Accelerator #1.”

Drivers can reserve an Aptera of their own for just $100, and they can expect to pay about $40,000 for the ride. Considering that the solar fuel is free, anyone in the mood for a head-turning ride will get quite a bargain for their $40,000 compared to other competitors in the zero emission two-seater field, such as the recently refreshed Tesla Roadster.

Speaking of refresh, General Motors has been weirdly lavishing attention on the EV1 sedan all this year, even though the automaker has been roundly criticized for the killing the short-lived car in its cradle. The automaker began producing EV1 electric sedans starting in 1996, following the unveiling of its Impact electric concept car in 1990. Unlike the Impact, EV1 was designed for use on the road. However, it was also designed mainly for the California market, and primarily for lease, not for sale. Production halted in 2003 at just about 1,000 vehicles, all to be recalled by GM and sent to the crusher as chronicled in Chris Paine’s 2006 documentary, “Who Killed The Electric Car?”

Or, maybe not so weird after all. GM’s electrification journey long predates the launch of Tesla Motors in 2003. The legacy automaker is now determined to stake out its claim on automotive history, with 2026 marking the 30th anniversary of the start of EV1 production.

GM has been celebrating the anniversary all this year with multiple long form articles about the Impact and EV1 on its website, eager to remind everybody that its industry-leading vehicle electrification efforts of the 1990’s continue to manifest decades later, in the form of heat pumps for climate control, by-wire technology, and regenerative braking among other elements.

GM’s latest love letter to the EV1 popped up on November 17, when the automaker officially celebrated the completed restoration of the EV1 “V212” alongside its a private owner, Billy Caruso. The rare survivor of GM’s the junkyard crusher was evidently hiding out in an impound lot in Georgia all these years, until Caruso acquired it at auction and enlisted Jared Pink of the popular show The Questionable Garage to fix it up. Considering TQG’s large following on YouTube, GM wisely lent its engineers to the effort, along with several donated parts from its own EV1.

US President Donald Trump and the Republican majority in Congress have made a heroic effort to dial down the vehicle electrification movement, but facts on the ground keep getting in their way. For starters, today’s advanced batteries apply across multiple energy resources, fossil and non-fossil alike. So, it’s no surprise to see the US Department of Energy continuing to throw taxpayer dollars at new energy storage projects (here’s one example), even though some of that activity will eventually ripple into the vehicle electrification field.

The US Department of Defense is also getting into the act. DoD’s electrification journey has been a tedious one, but in recent years it has begun creeping stealthily towards a vision of ground mobility enabled by electricity, providing the key tactical advantages of silent running and a low heat signature.

The latest news on that score involves a $1.4 billion loan commitment from DoD’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), enabling the silicon-based battery materials startup Sila to vault its signature product into commercial production. DoD’s primary interest in the company consists of applications in the electric drone and autonomous mobility fields, but Sila has long been eyeballing the EV market as well.

Sila secured the loan commitment in August, and it has not let the grass grow under its feet. On November 18 the company announced an off-take agreement with the well-known Tesla EV battery supplier Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America. “The multi-year agreement is part of a long-term commercial relationship with the potential for over $1 billion of offtake over time,” Sila explained in a press statement, further elaborating that Panasonic will deploy its proprietary Titan Silicon silicon-carbon anode material in battery cells.

“The partnership is also expected to support significant manufacturing and construction job creation in the United States. With Sila’s U.S.-based anode production underpinned by proprietary American technology and know-how, Panasonic and its OEM customers gain a clearer path toward a more secure, resilient, and sustainable domestic supply chain,” Sila emphasized.

That’s…interesting! Aside from Tesla as one of Sila’s OEM customers, keep an eye on another Panasonic offtaker, the up-and-comer US startup Harbinger Motors, which also has a foot in the DoD door.

Photo: The vehicle electrification movement is far from over in the US, with the startup Aptera among the stakeholders betting on an EV sales rebound in the coming years (cropped, courtesy of Aptera).

#5677. Is AI A Public Or A Private Asset?

Isabelle Ferreras is a professor and research director at the University of Louvain, an Accelerator fellow at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford, and a senior research associate at the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard University. It safe to say she knows a thing or two about computer technology and AI.

She told The Guardian this week that she has grave concerns about the way AI and the corporations promoting it are managing this brave new technology. Her concerns are spurred by the number of high profile computer engineers who have quit recently over fears that AI development is out of control.

Last month, a person responsible for overseeing safety reports at OpenAI left the company, claiming its culture was “broken.” He added that the entire AI industry was careless when it comes to developing AI technology. The month before that, a researcher at Anthropic — which went public yesterday at a valuation $1.8 trillion dollars — warned that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

“When the only way for a conscientious engineer to raise the alarm is to leave,” Ferreras said. “it is a clear sign that corporate governance in the industry is broken. Each departure takes with it the very knowledge needed to steer these systems safely. We cannot regulate AI safely from the outside if the companies building it remain autocracies on the inside.”

Ferreras warned that governments think of AI either as a “consumer product to be tested for defects or as a geopolitical race to be won by relaxing rules on business. Corporate lobbyists encourage this view as a trade-off between safety and innovation by arguing that legislation imposes too many burdens.

“This is a dangerous path. AI is not merely a software product. It is a technology of government. Yet inside frontier labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google, a handful of executives and capital investors decide which values are coded into models that shape millions of lives,” she said.

Interestingly, Michael Connolly, the award winning author of the Bosch and Lincoln Lawyer novels, published a book last year in which the family of a young woman, who was murdered by her boyfriend after he interacted with an AI agent, sues the company behind the AI agent. The essence of the lawsuit is that AI only does what it is programmed to do, and since the lead programmer of this particular AI agent was a misogynist in real life, it reflected his values when it interacted with humans. The book is called The Proving Ground and it is a fascinating read.

While Ferreras applauds those who warn of the malignancies built into AI, she pointed out that humans have short attention spans. “Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. As a society, we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle — and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal. As the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.”

In a democratic society, the exercise of governing power requires the consent of the governed, Ferreras told The Guardian. “Yet corporate law still treats firms as the property of shareholders, and the labor investors, who put their intellect, health and lives into the firm, as subordinates. To align AI with the public interest, we need a dual strategy: alongside solid public regulations on AI ‘from the outside,’ we need to enter the corporate black box and force corporate governance into alignment with democratic principles.”

An analogy can be made to the Federal Communications Commission, which licenses broadcasters and promotes the free flow of information to the public. The digital world thinks such controls are archaic, but the lack of them is a clear and present danger to a civil society.

Ferreras suggested that “governments must outlaw non-disclosure and non-disparagement clauses that silence staff on safety risks, and enact robust whistle blower protection. Tech workers also need a collective standing over corporate strategy, independent channels to report safety breaches, and formal representation inside frontier labs before models are deployed.”

In addition, she argued that “legislators must establish a binding right to co-decision over workplace AI. No algorithmic system that monitors, evaluates or disciplines workers should be deployed without prior negotiation. At national and EU level, we need to consider collective bargaining on AI deployment and veto rights for works councils or trade unions, backed by independent technical experts and a strict ban on automated firing.”

Lastly, she supported the democratization of boardrooms and rewarding firms that refuse to concentrate power at the top. “Legislators should mandate worker-elected directors on boards, moving towards dual-majority governance in which strategic decisions require the consent not only of capital but of labor.” Some, like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, would characterize her suggestions as liberal claptrap, and they would be correct. Ferreras would happily unravel the “tech bro” manosphere in order to promote a more open and just society.

She pointed to the research by Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson, the 2024 Nobel laureates in economics, which demonstrates that technological revolutions do not automatically produce shared prosperity. Instead, institutions decide who benefits and who pays.

“Extending democracy into the firm is not an old battle over power for its own sake, but a practical necessity for more ethical judgment. Aligning AI with the good of workers and society requires more wisdom than closed executive rooms can offer. It needs what the Yale political theorist Hélène Landemore calls ‘democratic reason’ — the collective intelligence of diverse, deliberating voices, brought to bear on corporate decision-making,” Ferreras wrote.

“Left to self-regulation and the occasional whistleblower, AI governance will entrench an unaccountable algorithmic oligarchy. Accountability and alignment begins with giving those who build these systems and those whose work they govern an enforceable voice, from the code floor to the boardroom.”

Ferreras’ point of view is decidedly liberal, and yet her arguments are clear and concise. How can we give so much power to digital agents and not take reasonable steps to ensure the needs of society as a whole are respected? The tech industry enjoys almost unfettered freedom of action today. It may be time to consider whether that is a good long term strategy.

#5676. The Metals Company Has a Seabed Mining Production Gap That Its Pilot Has Not Closed

In 2022, The Metals Company (TMC) and offshore contractor Allseas recovered 3,021 wet tons of nodules from the Pacific seabed. Their integrated test system moved material up a riser stretching more than four kilometres from the ocean floor to the Hidden Gem. During production runs, the collector achieved 86.4 wet tons per hour. Four years later, TMC is discussing a million tons a year from an upgraded system and eventually 12 million tons annually across four vessels.

What matters between those endpoints is the operating record: sustained collection rates, marine maintenance, vessel availability and delivered tons sufficient to carry fixed costs. TMC has yet to demonstrate those economics.

The November 12, 2026 corporate update describes a phased approach: begin with an upgraded pilot collector and limited modifications to Hidden Gem, then invest in larger systems as operations develop. Phasing reduces the initial capital commitment. It also pushes the demonstration of the projected commercial production rates into the future.

The annual arithmetic is straightforward. At 5,000 productive hours, about 57% of a calendar year, a system collecting 200 wet tons per hour delivers one million tons. The second-year target of 1.5 million tons requires 300 tons per hour. Three million tons from one production system requires 600 tons per hour. TMC’s 2022 production-run rate of 86.4 tons per hour would deliver 432,000 tons at that utilization.

The upgraded machines are expected to be different from the 2022 test collector. Their performance must be demonstrated, not assumed from the pilot. The operating gap is central to the project economics, and it grows with production ambitions.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing examines TMC’s production gap alongside Impossible Metals’ autonomous collection model and the investment consequences of underperforming equipment. The source assessment and fleet sensitivities are linked there.

A collector, a multi-kilometre hydraulic riser and a production vessel have to work together. The crawler encounters uneven ground and varying nodule coverage. The riser and pumps handle abrasive slurry. The vessel must remain on station while crews inspect, maintain and repair equipment. Offshore access and weather affect when those activities can occur.

A system can produce at its test rate and still lose the year on maintenance and interruptions. Fewer productive hours push the required hourly rate higher. Repeating a successful short production run does not establish a year’s availability, let alone multiple years of fleet productivity.

The difference matters because capital and offshore operating costs continue while production is interrupted. Ships, crews, marine maintenance equipment and financing cost money whether or not nodules are arriving on deck. Smaller annual production spreads fixed expenses over fewer tons and raises the cost of every ton recovered.

TMC’s August 2025 prefeasibility presentation estimated offshore collection and transport at $179 per dry ton, or about $129 per wet ton under its 28% moisture assumption. Those are projections for a future system. They are not an audited cost record from continuous industrial mining. The revised first-production configuration needs its own cost data.

The missing commercial evidence is a long enough operating record to estimate productive hours, rate degradation, planned and unplanned maintenance, retrieval time, replacement costs and the delivered cost per ton. Until then, moving from a pilot to a production forecast remains a major assumption.

Impossible Metals proposes to collect individual nodules with autonomous underwater vehicles rather than a tracked crawler and riser. A vehicle would descend, select nodules, fill its cargo compartment, return, undergo surface recovery, unload and prepare for another mission. Every trip must be repeated across an entire fleet.

Its September 2026 scientific trial, reported by Reuters, recovered approximately 450 grams of nodules from more than 4,000 metres depth. It demonstrated selective scientific collection. A commercial robot would have to carry vastly more material and sustain cycle times and availability that the experiment did not measure.

In the 2025 commercial concept examined by metallurgical specialist Lyle Trytten and me, each proposed vehicle carried 12 tons of nodules and had 18 collection arms. At one nodule every 1.5 seconds per arm and an average nodule mass of 100 grams, filling the cargo requires roughly 120,000 successful picks. With all arms continuously working, collection alone occupies approximately 2.8 hours.

The proposed complete mission cycle was four hours. Descent, ascent, searching, repositioning, failed picks, recovery, unloading, inspection and relaunch also consume time. The architecture has too many interdependent activities to fit those requirements into that cycle at the assumed performance.

Autonomous navigation and manipulator tests cannot substitute for evidence of an entire fleet repeatedly executing commercial missions. Increasing payload changes vehicle weight, buoyancy, energy use and recovery equipment. Faster picking leaves the surface operation and deepwater transit to be solved.

Our 2025 independent techno-economic assessment tested the financial effects of weaker-than-assumed robot productivity. At the illustrative $180 per dry ton nodule sales value, the model required approximately $2.52 billion in capital with the originally assumed robot throughput. Halving throughput while maintaining output increased required capital to approximately $4.51 billion.

At a 10% discount rate, the modeled net present value moved from positive $863 million to negative $769 million. Even at two-thirds of original productivity, NPV fell to about $15 million, a negligible margin for a multibillion-dollar first-of-a-kind industrial fleet.

These are scenario calculations, not actual bills or calibrated probabilities. They identify the key failure mode: more robots, recovery capacity, batteries, vessels and maintenance are needed to compensate for each production shortfall. A financial model based on high productivity can look attractive until realistic availability and turnaround times are included.

TMC is further along technologically than Impossible Metals, but its future-scale production economics are also unsupported by a sustained operating record. Neither company has demonstrated the productive hours, throughput and maintenance costs needed to support its advertised commercial proposition.

Policymakers and investors should ask for extended end-to-end offshore operating records and audited unit economics before treating future production targets as investable output. The technology risk exists before accounting for nodule processing, metals markets, permitting or environmental liabilities.

The complete TFIE Briefing and linked assessment show the fleet calculations, technical assumptions and capital sensitivities. The remaining articles in the five-part series address processing, metals markets and American Samoa’s exposure.

#5675. Electric Vans — Are They The Final EV Frontier? Kia PV5.

We took a trip to see the Kia PV5 electric van. Our brief takeaway: “Kool like a Kia.” Should keep the bean counters happy.

Inspired by a comment in the Electric Vehicle Council report about electric vans, Majella and I decided to have a short visit to a group of dealerships under the Norris Motors banner. We hoped to check out the LDV eDeliver 5 van, touted as selling for under AU$50,000. However, there was no stock to view and we ended up chatting to the dealer and then moving on to the MG U9 BEV ute. You can read about it here. And then we found the Kia PV5 delivery van.

Julie Delvecchio, the CEO of EVC, calls the lack of affordable electric vans in Australia “the single biggest unclaimed opportunity left.” We think that is about to change. Since its launch in May, 496 PV5 have sold in Australia.

The Kia PV5 reminded me a lot of the Renault Kangoo in both size and shape, and it is able to carry about the same payload. And the front looked like the BMW i3. The one we looked at had been sold and was awaiting a fitout as a camper van. The Norris Group Kia specialist was generous with his time and the information he shared. He has been selling the Kia EV5 for the past 5 months and delivered 5 of the vans. He sold his first one within a week of its arrival on the lot — to Ray, a driver working for Amazon.

Ray appreciated the 390 km range. My friendly sales rep tells me that this will be increased in 2027 models to 420 km. Ray was getting out of diesel and most of his questions were around charging and regen braking. Most of his trips were around the burbs and he was not intending to take the van on the highway. The Kia PV5 is a workhorse, with a passenger car feel and level of comfort. It even has electric lumbar support for the driver — great when you are spending so much time in the van delivering parcels in the lead-up to Christmas. It certainly has a lot more tech than the diesel he was trading in.

In fact, he was “blown away” by the standard features — the 360-degree camera, for example. “Vans are not known for their visibility.” On his return to the dealership for his first service, he commented on the smoothness of the torque: “It has no issues going uphill.” He reported that the van felt “well planted on the road.” Ray has gotten used to trickle charging at home and has lost his range anxiety. Like most new EV drivers, once he started living and working with the vehicle, his fears vanished. The PV5 supports fast charging also for when Ray needs a boost on the road.

But what about that all-important question of cost? Can we make the bean counters happy? The Kia PV5 retails for AU$56,000 (before on-road costs), which is about the same price as comparable diesel vans like the Ford Transit and the Toyota HiAce. Add to that the savings on fuel, the peace of mind from fuel security, and the reduced servicing and it is easy to build a business case for the Kia PV5 — cost per parcel delivery. The PV5 even comes with vehicle to load.

And it isn’t made in China! Can the PV5 replace Toyota’s HiAce? Find the answer in this video. The reviewer points out many features that make the PV5 an attractive option: the charge port is on the front. The van has lots of nooks and crannies for storage. She measures storage by capacity to fit in bottles of wine — for example, two in the glove box. There is a step provided to alight the van, aided by grab handles. More storage space is provided above the steering wheel, including a nifty phone slot. There are customizable buttons on the steering wheel to create shortcuts; for example, to the air conditioning settings. A wireless phone charger is nestled near the dash. The glovebox contains the V2L adaptor supplied with the van.

The fact that the van reverts to the lowest regen setting every time you restart the car is a little niggle. That, and there is no frunk — reducing the reviewer’s all-important need for wine storage. Full specs can be found here. Kia even gives you helpful advice on how to apply for electric vehicle subsidies (last page, bottom right). One of the pictures that caught my eye shows the PV5 as a flatbed truck.

The PV5 was recently named 2026 International Van of the Year. It measures 4695mm long, 2255mm wide, and 1899mm tall on a 2995mm wheelbase. Range is stated as 416 km, but will of course vary with driving style and load. The battery is a 71.2kWh nickel cobalt manganese (NCM) lithium-ion battery. Kia offers a 165,000 km warranty on the battery. The van is front-wheel drive.

The PV5 has over 4 cubic metres of cargo capacity, double both that of the ID Buzz and the Tesla Model Y. Space enough for two euro pallets. There are multiple access points, with sliding doors on both sides and barn doors in the rear. The rear barn doors open to 180 degrees, and a low 419mm load height improves accessibility.

Goods being shipped are protected by padding on the rear doors and insides of the back. The PV5 can carry up to 740 kg. Tiedowns on the floor of the rear of the van help to secure cargo. There is also a power point in the back of the van. Perhaps a tradie can recharge their tools on site. No frunk for wine.

From the spec sheet: “Standard driver assist features include blind-spot collision avoidance, navigation-based adaptive cruise control, lane-keep assist, lane centring with hands-on detection, and parking collision avoidance assist.”

A launch in the USA is financially difficult because of the 25% “chicken tax.” Kia builds the PV5 in South Korea and classifies it as a commercial vehicle, and it faces a 25% US import tariff on light trucks and commercial vans.

Sadly, the Kia PV5 doesn’t come in red, but only in white, grey and black. Most companies may take up the option of wrapping the van in their own livery. Overall, we were impressed with Kia PV5 and look forward to seeing more of them on the road throughout the suburbs as Australian delivery drivers move towards a bright electric future.

#5674. Cardiovascular Screening Test Called Into Question

— MedPage Today reporters offer further insights into recently covered topics

The following is a transcript of the podcast episode:

Rachael Robertson: Hey everybody! Welcome to MedPod Today, the podcast series where MedPage Today reporters take a deeper look into the week's biggest healthcare stories. I'm your host, Rachael Robertson.

Cheryl Clark is kicking off today's episode with her reporting on an ongoing debate on whether to test all adults for Lipoprotein(a). Then, Kristen Monaco will fill us in on major developments in the GLP-1 medication space. To close out, I'll give us a rundown on the latest measles numbers and what it means that the U.S. lost its measles elimination status after 26 years.

A March recommendation from the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and 10 other medical societies for the first time said all adults should have their blood tested for something called Lipoprotein(a), also called Lp(a) or "little a," which is a risk factor you may have never heard of. But many cardiologists and primary care doctors are strongly resisting doing this. Cheryl Clark is here to tell us more.

Cheryl Clark: Thanks, Rachael. Yeah, "little a" – this is a component in blood that is believed to be strongly associated with one's risk of getting an earlier cardiovascular event or aortic stenosis. A growing number of studies seem to show that. But it's genetically inherited, so the score you get basically stays the same throughout your whole life. Diet, exercise, lowering low-density lipoprotein (LDL), body mass index (BMI), they don't change it. So for a long time, doctors said there was really nothing they could do about it. So why measure it?

Scores, it turns out, that are higher than 125 nanomoles per liter might just scare people, especially those without established disease or symptoms. And some doctors are reporting otherwise healthy patients, some even in their 70s, with scores in the high 300s or even higher. So it seems like a high score is survivable, but it is scary.

Now, European cardiology associations in 2022 and again in 2025 began to rethink this. The idea was that if you knew your score, you could change other elements in your life that raise your risk, like trying harder to lose weight. I mean, like really try harder to lower LDL, blood pressure, improve your diet, exercise, do all of that stuff.

The American groups, including the ACC and the American Heart Association, in March joined in. They issued similar recommendations in a 134-page document, basically agreeing with the Europeans. So now this is a standard recommendation that everybody, all adults, should get this at least once in their lifetime.

It might be that their thinking was rooted in the fact that now pharmaceutical companies have been developing drugs that lower this "little a," but they needed clinical trials to prove it. They also needed to prove that it would prevent heart disease and strokes, which of course is the point. Why would we do this otherwise? There are at least three drugs in development, so now lots of smart people are pretty darn sure they'd be successful with this drug and save lots of lives. So a few weeks ago, the first drug trial for a drug called pelacarsen was released, but the results were shockingly disappointing.

Clark: Well, it was called the HORIZON study. It was a large placebo-controlled trial, and it found no reduced risk in these cardiovascular events. It tested pelacarsen, which did lower "little a," but participants were still getting diagnosed and dying. So there is something else clearly in play that's causing heart disease. Maybe Lp(a) is a marker for something else, or maybe something else is protecting some people. Who knows?

So I asked a lot of doctors, were they ordering these tests? Especially now that we have the HORIZON results, and several said they were. Some said they were just ordering these tests in people with established familial linkages, like genetic predisposition. But many said they vehemently opposed such a universal recommendation or aren't ordering it at all. My own doctor orders it, but said other doctors in her office practice are not.

One cardiologist said otherwise healthy patients are seeing their high scores online in their portals and are freaking out, crying, and thinking they're going to die tomorrow, and they have to spend time reassuring them. One physician told me the committee should have prioritized calcium CT scoring instead of "little a." He thinks CT scoring shows real disease that can be treated. And Rita Redberg, MD, MSc, a prominent cardiologist at UCSF – she's known for less is more approach – called "little a" a useless test.

And by the way, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has not joined the bandwagon on testing for "little a." It allows regional Medicare jurisdictions across the country to make case by case determinations about whether to cover the tests. So some beneficiaries are going to get stuck with paying for this out-of-pocket.

Robertson: It sounds like there's still a lot of confusion.

Clark: Yes, the bottom line seems to be: live a healthy life. If you get a high score, be thankful and adhere to strategies that we know reduce your LDL and your other risk factors. We'll see in a few years if any of these other three drugs now in clinical trials clarify this complicated issue.

Robertson: Well, thank you so much for your reporting here, Cheryl.

Robertson: Pediatric obesity took center stage at ObesityWeek in National Harbor, Maryland. There were two major phase III trials showing strong weight loss results for GLP-1 medications in kids and teens. This was just days after the FDA added a new vision-related safety warning across the entire drug class. Kristen Monaco is here to break down the latest developments.

So, Kristen, starting with the adolescent data from ObesityWeek, what did the SURMOUNT-ADOLESCENTS trial show for tirzepatide?

Kristen Monaco: SURMOUNT-ADOLESCENTS was a phase III trial simultaneously published in JAMA that looked at the very popular dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist tirzepatide, also known as Zepbound, in 160 adolescents ages 12 to 17 with overweight or obesity. All participants also received lifestyle intervention. At week 72, teens who were taking tirzepatide saw an average BMI reduction of 18.5%, compared with a 0.5% increase in those taking placebo. Nearly half on tirzepatide achieved at least a 20% reduction in BMI, and over half were no longer considered to have obesity by the end of the trial.

Notably, researchers also saw improvements in quality of life and physical comfort scores, with no signals of disruption to growth or pubertal maturation, which is a concern of using these agents in this age group. Tirzepatide is currently only approved for adults with obesity or kids 10 and older with type 2 diabetes. So these data lay the groundwork for potential obesity indication in teens. However, rival GLP drug semaglutide is already approved for teens with obesity.

Robertson: Those are really impressive results. Researchers also presented data looking at even younger children, those ages six to 11. What did the STEP Young trial find for semaglutide?

Monaco: STEP Young, which was published in the New England Journal of Medicine, looked at semaglutide, also known as Wegovy, in 167 children, ages 6 to 11, with obesity alongside lifestyle counseling. Right now, semaglutide is only approved for obesity in patients ages 12 and up. There are no GLP-1 therapies right now that are FDA approved for this very young age group. So treatment options are largely limited to lifestyle modifications.

In the trial at week 68, semaglutide reduced BMI by 13.5%, and nearly 40% of children on the injectable no longer had obesity by the end of the trial. Children on treatment also saw improvements in cardiometabolic markers like waist circumference, triglycerides, and blood pressure. Gastrointestinal side effects like vomiting, diarrhea, and nausea were more common, especially during the dose escalation phase, which is expected with GLP-1 drugs. Though they were mostly mild to moderate and transient, with no safety signals affecting growth or pubertal development. Drug maker Novo Nordisk hasn't announced yet whether it plans to submit these data to the FDA, so that will be something to look closely for.

Robertson: That's super interesting. So stepping back from your conference coverage, you also reported on a major regulatory update involving GLP-1 drugs and eye health. What is this FDA warning, and what led to it?

Monaco: Yes, so the FDA is now requiring manufacturers of all currently marketed GLP-1 medications to include a warning about the potential risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, also known as NAION, which is a rare but potentially blinding eye condition caused by reduced blood flow to the optic disc. This update follows a wave of observational studies, including a 2024 JAMA Ophthalmology study on semaglutide, that prompted this FDA review. The agency concluded from its review that there is indeed a rare but potentially increased risk of NAION events in patients taking GLP-1 drugs. Cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 products.

So the FDA told healthcare providers to tell their patients to report any sudden, painless vision loss or visual field changes in one eye immediately, and then to refer them promptly to an ophthalmologist. They should also consider discontinuing the GLP-1 drug unless the treatment benefits clearly outweigh the risks.

Robertson: Well, thank you so much for this important context as these medications continue to expand into younger populations. Thanks for being here, Kristen.

Robertson: The U.S. has officially lost its measles elimination status after 26 years. It's no surprise, considering there have been at least 830 hospitalizations and 13 measles-associated deaths in the past 2 years.

Losing this status is a big deal. Our editor-in-chief, Jeremy Faust, MD, sat down with pediatric infectious disease expert Paul Offit, MD, of Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, and public health researcher Noel Brewer, PhD, of the University of North Carolina in Chapel Hill. They talked about the resurgence of measles outbreaks, declining vaccination rates, timing of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, the influence of vaccine misinformation, and the challenges facing public health officials as they work to restore confidence in vaccination and prevent further transmission. It's a lot, but I really recommend you listen to the full conversation. We've linked it here.

Last week, there were 334 cases of measles, and there were 319 the week before that. Pennsylvania is still really struggling with more than 100 cases in the last 2 weeks, but things are also really heating up in Wisconsin, which had more than 200 cases in that same time period. The other states that we're keeping an extra close eye on are New York, Indiana, and Minnesota. With holiday travel coming up, we'll see in the coming weeks how that influences the spread of measles.

As always, check out our interactive measles map, which is updated at the top of each week, and we've linked it right here.

This episode was hosted and produced by me, Rachael Robertson. Sound engineering by Greg Laub. Theme music by Palomar. Our guests were MedPage Today reporters Cheryl Clark and Kristen Monaco. Links to their stories are in the show notes.

MedPod Today is a production of MedPage Today. For more information about our show, check out medpagetoday.com/podcasts.

#5673. Why Warming Up Your Car Unattended Is Illegal In Some States And Cities

As a seasoned driver, you may be aware that some states' roads are more dangerous in winter. Did you also know that four out of five of these states, as well as 27 others, have laws against puffing? No, not that puffing. Puffing, or "car puffing," is a slang term for the ritual of letting your car get warm and toasty before driving off. This is usually accomplished by starting your car and then heading back inside for a bit. The term comes from the telltale puffs of smoke that can be seen coming out of the tail pipe.

The reason behind the laws is rather simple: Those puffs of smoke in the chilly air indicate a running, usually unlocked, vehicle. This makes it an easy target for crime. Someone can jump in and take off in your vehicle in a matter of seconds — not good for anyone involved.

All is not lost for the dedicated puffer, though, as there is an exception to the rule. Vehicles equipped with a remote starter are often exempt from these rules, as a remote start system allows you to keep your vehicle locked and your keys in your pocket.

We get it — getting into a cold car sucks. But having your car stolen sucks even more. Even beyond your own personal grief, stolen vehicles are often used in subsequent crimes. Also, items left in your vehicle, such as registration information, can be used for identity theft, and a garage door opener can become easy access into your home. According to the National Insurance Crime Bureau, "By the end of 2021, just over 100,000 thefts facilitated by keys or key fobs were reported nationally. This total accounts for 11% of vehicle thefts of all types reported in the U.S. in 2021."

Outside of the crime aspect, there are other reasons to avoid puffing and other forms of idling. Cold weather already hurts your gas mileage, and burning gas while you're not moving is only going to make that worse, costing you money in the long term. On the environmental side, according to the U.S. Department of Energy, "It is estimated that idling personal vehicles generate around 30 million tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) every year," which is roughly the equivalent of adding an additional 5 million vehicles to the roads.

Back in the olden times — sometime after the last horse and buggy but before the first DeLorean — it was common knowledge that you had to let your car warm up before driving it. So, a little puff session before work was thought to be good. That is an outdated notion today, and, in fact, experts such as AAA declare that a modern vehicle only needs a few seconds to warm up. Excessive idle time can stress the engine, as it isn't running at its preferred temperature.

Laws against puffing are clear that leaving a running car unattended is a no-no. One pro tip based on this definition is to warm up your car while you are shoveling snow out of the driveway, scraping ice off of the windows, or performing any of the other tasks that make up the unbreakable laws of winter driving. That way, you have an eye on the vehicle and are taking care of your pre-driving chores.

Puffing-specific laws are on the books in the following states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, West Virginia, and Wisconsin. If you live in one of these states, check your local statutes to see how the law may affect you. One final note to all the EV owners out there: It is recommended that you warm up your vehicles while they're still plugged in, preventing you from burning too much energy.

#5672. Mazda Miata Engine Swaps Ranked Best To Worst (For Your Budget And Your Patience)

Jalopnik has long maintained that the Mazda Miata is the answer to every question. What's the best affordable convertible? Miata. What if you want a fun commuter that's reliable and sips fuel? You should consider a Miata. What if you want a car to take off-road? Surprisingly, the Miata is the answer again. Emme Hall won her class in a Baja race with her off-road modified Miata. It's an excellent sports car, relatively cheap, abundant, and just plain fun. Over four generations, the only only real critique of the venerable roadster is that it's never been particularly quick in a straight line.

But Miata enthusiasts are a crafty bunch, and over the nameplate's 37-year history, their quest for more power has driven the development of camshafts, turbochargers, and, of course, engine swaps. Swaps are not for the faint of heart – they often consume a lot of time and capital — but they are a great way to add power without the complexities of a forced induction setup on the factory engine.

Not all swaps are created equal, though. For example, transplanting an engine from a newer Miata will be easier and cheaper than shoehorning a V8 into the engine bay. However, the V8 will net you way more power for the extra effort and money. There are so many Miata swaps out there — from Honda K24 four-cylinders to Toyota V12s — so we have compiled a helpful a list of engines that go in Miatas, organized from the cheapest and easiest to the most difficult and expensive.

The easiest Miata swaps involve upgrading to a larger Mazda motor within the same engine family. Early first-generation Miatas (1990 to 1993) were equipped with a 1.6-liter four-cylinder. Its output was a tepid 116 horsepower. Luckily, later first-generation cars (1994 to 1997) and all second-generation cars (1999 to 2005) came with a more powerful 1.8-liter four-cylinder that will bolt up to the factory transmission. Flyin' Miata sells an affordable kit that makes the swap to the 1994-to-1997 engine essentially plug-and-play. The later engines make more power, but they still require some effort to work in the 1.6 cars. To get the most power for your money and effort, look for a 2001-to-2005 Miata engine donor. They have variable valve timing and provide 142 horsepower .

Similarly, third-generation Miatas (2006 to 2015) have an easy path to more displacement and power. A 2.5-liter Duratec four-cylinder engine from a Ford Fusion, Mazda3, Mazda6, or Mercury Milan fits in place of the Miata's 2.0-liter four-cylinder with minimal effort. The larger engine is plentiful in junkyards and can be had for as cheap as $350. The swap isn't completely plug-and-play — the Miata's lower intake manifold needs to be modified to fit the 2.5 — but most of the 2.0-liter's accessories fit the larger engine without issue. A stock 2.5 makes about 10 more horsepower and 35 more pound-feet of torque over the factory Miata engine. But with upgraded cams and a freer-flowing exhaust, Grassroots Motorsports made 196 hp at the wheels with its 2.5 swap.

Under the hood, the Miata has never had much more than an economy-car four-cylinder turned sideways. By contrast, when Honda decided to make a roadster of its own, the automaker equipped it with the F20C four-cylinder — an engine with a 9,000-rpm redline that held the title for the most naturally aspirated horsepower per liter until the Ferrari 458 came along. Intrepid engine swappers may think a Miata with an F20C could be a good way to create a low-buck, bootleg S2000. But S2000 engines aren't exactly affordable or easy to come by.

However, there is another Honda option that can rev almost as high as the F20C and makes similar power. Enter the K24, the budget friendly and readily available alternative. The K24, like its name might suggest, is a 2.4-liter four-cylinder with dual-overhead camshafts and Honda's i-VTEC system. The high performance variants of the engine found in the Acura TSX and Honda Civic Si make around 200 horsepower in factory trim. But the aftermarket for the engine is immense, and with the right combination of parts, the K24 has the potential to make nearly 300 hp without boost.

Although it was only available in front- and all-wheel-drive cars, tuners like KPower Industries recognized the engine's potential for rear-wheel-drive applications. As such, KPower Industries makes kits to swap a K24 into all four generations of Miatas. It's not a simple or cheap swap. Bits like a transmission adapter plate and a standalone ECU are needed to make it all work, and the most comprehensive kits start at around $6,000. But for a powerful, lightweight engine that doesn't mess with the balance of the Miata chassis, the juice is worth the squeeze.

The next rung on the Miata-swap ladder is the V6. A V6 swap is an exercise in more — more cylinders, more power, more effort, and more money. There are three V6 engines that have readily available Miata swap kits: the 3.5-liter Honda J35 found in the Odyssey and various Acuras, the direct-injected 3.6-liter GM LFX found in the Chevy Camaro and Cadillac CTS, and the 3.0-liter Jaguar AJ30 V6 found in the S-type and XJ. Each option has an aluminum block and heads, and depending on the variant, outputs roughly 40 to 100 more horsepower than a stock K24.

No matter what engine you choose, the kits are not cheap. Luckily, with a kit, you don't have to fabricate your own front subframe, motor mounts, and other swap-related parts. The Honda J35 kit from Mini Tec is the most affordable at $3,350, and it utilizes the factory Miata transmission and differential. But that doesn't include any provisions for the cooling, power steering, and fueling systems. The next kit on the list is the $7,260 GM LFX V6 conversion from V8Roadsters, which requires a Camaro transmission and other GM donor parts. This adds more complexity to the swap, but the GM parts are more durable than the factory Miata stuff. Rocketeer Cars takes the most comprehensive approach to V6 swaps. It will sell you everything you need for the conversion, including a refreshed Jaguar AJ30 V6. But that will set you back roughly $22,040. If you are going to spend all of that money on a V6, you might as well go for the gusto and consider our next swap option.

If the Miata is the universal answer to any sports car question, the Chevy LS is the the answer for any engine swap inquiry. The V8 LS-series engines are still such a popular swap for a reason. They're compact, powerful, readily available in junkyards, and have massive aftermarket support. The LS engine is available in many configurations, from 4.8-liter truck engines to 7.0-liter sports car screamers. Even the wimpiest 4.8-liter LS can make 400 horsepower without much effort. That type of power is a tantalizing prospect for those looking to make a modern version of a Shelby Cobra with a Miata. Fortunately, for those with enough capital and bravery, the big V8 can be stuffed into every generation of Miata. Although Colorado-based tuner Flyin' Miata stopped doing V8 swaps years ago, other manufactures like Monster Miata and V8Roadsters will sell you the parts to roll your own.

There are many tradeoffs involved in putting an LS in a Miata, first of which is the car's balance. Monster Miata says the weight distribution moves from a perfect 50/50 to a nose-heavy 53/47 with a big V8 under the hood.  Also, the rest of the Miata's driveline can't hold up to V8 power, so it needs to be swapped as well. You'll need parts like a T-56 six-speed transmission, new driveshaft, and a differential from a fith-gen Camaro. Costs are highly variable depending on which engine you choose, but they generally fall somewhere around $20,000 for the average completed swap.

A Miata with more than eight cylinders is like an automotive cryptid. There's evidence that it exists, but it can only be found in the murky depths of internet forums and YouTube. During our dive into the internet swamps, we found a Miata with a Viper V10, one with a Jaguar V12, and another with a Toyota 1GZFE V12 from a Toyota Century.

The efficacy of these swaps is questionable, as there are no off-the-shelf kits for them. And more cylinders means more weight over the nose of the Miata, even further messing up the roadster's weight distribution compared to an LS. Plus, an LS can make just as much power or more power than the engines above. The LS also fits in the engine bay a whole lot better. The guy who did the Jaguar V12 swap said he had to cut the firewall and move it 6 inches back. But if you're crazy enough to try one of these swaps, you'll certainly have the only Miata at the Cars and Coffee with more than eight cylinders.

#5671. RISE St. James, Sierra Club Sue LDEQ to Vacate Hyundai Steel Air Permit

LDEQ issued air permit to the facility despite serious flaws in permit.

Donaldsonville, Louisiana — Today, RISE St. James Louisiana and Sierra Club filed a lawsuit challenging Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality’s decision to issue an air permit to Hyundai-POSCO for its proposed steelmaking facility. The groups claim that the air permit must be vacated because LDEQ did not conduct an environmental justice analysis, nor did the agency give full and careful consideration to mitigation measures like electrified components and green hydrogen, or to the environmental costs of Hyundai’s added pollution in an already overburdened area, as is required by the Louisiana state constitution and the Clean Air Act.

Throughout 2026, Sierra Club, working with other experts and local groups, submitted a series of comments to LDEQ in an effort to bring to light the errors, miscalculations, and omissions in the permit application. Despite some improvements to the permit application, made by Hyundai Steel following public pressure, the final air permit issued by LDEQ authorizes the facility to emit substantial quantities of greenhouse gases, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, carbon monoxide, lead, mercury, ammonia, and other pollutants. Many of these pollutants cause significant and irreversible damage to human health even at low levels.

The area around the planned facility already bears a toxic air pollution burden greater than 96% of the rest of the country, and ranks high across a range of environmental and socioeconomic indicators. The Hyundai Steel Plant is one of multiple polluting facilities planned as part of the 17,000-acre Riverplex MegaPark in an area known as Cancer Alley in Ascension Parish, Louisiana.

In response, the petitioners issued the following statements:

Andrea Issod, Sierra Club Senior Attorney, said: “LDEQ must ensure the Hyundai Steel Plant permit complies with the legal requirements to reduce harmful pollution impacts as much as possible on the surrounding community, which already bears a 96% percentile burden of toxic releases as compared to the national average. By refusing to conduct an environmental justice analysis, consider cleaner technologies like electrifying components and replacing dirty gas with green hydrogen, or consider any environmental costs of Hyundai’s pollution, LDEQ has failed to perform the most basic function of its role and deprived the community of a transparent, thorough, and accurate assessment of the facility’s potential negative impacts. For that reason, we are asking the Court to reverse LDEQ’s final decision and vacate the permit for Hyundai Steel’s proposed facility.”

Mekaylyn Lavigne, Modeste Coordinator for RISE St. James, said: “I was born and raised in the small and peaceful community of Modeste. Although this region is now known as Cancer Alley because many chemical plants have polluted our air and water, my family and neighbors still enjoy sitting on our porches, watching birds and wildlife, and fishing. Now, LDEQ is allowing a steel mill to move in next door to my home, and tells us the air quality is fine and this massive iron and steel making facility will not have any negative impacts. Modeste residents deserve the truth. The court should make LDEQ go back to the drawing board on this permit to disclose all the impacts and use the cleanest technologies to reduce pollution.”

Additional information about the petition:

Rise St. James and Sierra Club note in their petition that Hyundai Steel’s air permit was issued despite LDEQ missing or critically lacking key elements of a public-trust analysis, including:

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. In addition to protecting every person's right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action. For more information, visit www.sierraclub.org.

#5670. Every Car Brand That's Put Rotary Engines In Production Cars (There Aren't Many)

Beyond the realms of car enthusiasm, most normies wouldn't have actually heard of a rotary engine – also known as a Wankel engine (after Felix Wankel, the man who patented the design in the first place). These are fondly called "spinning Doritos" because at their heart is a triangular rotor that whizzes around a central shaft and makes power in a similar way to how a regular piston engine does. There are many pros and cons to rotary engines, and the cons are why they have seldom been used in automobiles.

When it comes to street cars, the most coveted example is Mazda's famous RX-7. The same brand was also responsible for arguably the most mythical race car ever created: the quad-rotor 787B. It won the 1991 edition of the famed 24 Hours of Le Mans and leaves a lasting impression on anyone who hears it, thanks to the orgasmic, high-pitched wail it generates as it climbs toward 9,000 rpm.

But Mazda isn't the only car brand to have ever used a rotary engine in its production cars. The very first instance came from a German company called NSU (which eventually became part of Audi), and there were also examples from Citroën and the Russian brand Lada. Maxton, a low-volume sports car maker from the U.S., also briefly used rotary engines in the Rollerskate. But since it used Mazda engines and was built in such small numbers, it is often discounted.

In fact, the famed Japanese brand is estimated to have built around two million rotaries between 1967 and 2012, starting with the much-loved Cosmo sports car and ending with the equally adored RX-8 coupe. It has since resurrected the rotary, but only as a generator that forms part of a hybrid package in the MX-30 electric SUV, so it hardly counts.

Mazda really did try it all at the height of its rotary days, even building the now highly collectible Rotary Pickup. It was — and is — humanity's sole rotary-powered pickup truck, equipped with a 110-horsepower 1.3-liter Wankel unit, and made purely for the U.S. and Canadian markets. The company built around 15,000 examples, and well-maintained, low-mileage trucks still go for close to $30,000. Further afield, ardent enthusiasts will also remember the Mazda Furai concept, which is among the weirdest one-off cars ever built.

Before Mazda's love affair with Wankels, NSU rolled out the very first rotary-powered production car, the Spider, at the 1963 Frankfurt Auto Show. Its single-rotor, 500cc engine wasn't hugely powerful: it produced just 50 hp when it debuted, and maxed out at 54 hp in its most powerful guise. Despite getting positive reviews from the automotive press, the Spider never really took off. Just 2,400 units are estimated to have been built before production ended in 1967.

NSU replaced it with the Ro 80, which was a sleek, four-door sedan with a 115-hp twin-rotor motor and a fancy independent suspension. It was so good that European Car of the Year jurors voted it as their winning candidate for 1968 – making it the first German vehicle to ever win the coveted prize. It enjoyed a 10-year run rolling off the production lines, with NSU building around 37,000 examples before retiring it in 1977.

It was in 1964 that Citroën struck up a partnership with NSU to develop rotary engines. While NSU went on to join the VW Group, Citroën stayed the course and eventually unveiled the M35 in the late '60s — its first true rotary-powered car, built in a limited run of 267 examples. Based on an Ami 8 – the same model James May used during the "Top Gear" classic time trial rally challenge in Mallorca – the M35 even had Citroën's super-soft hydropneumatic suspension, with 49 rampant French horses under the hood.

Then came the GS Birotor in 1973, whose twin-rotor setup produced an even mightier 106 hp and allowed for a top speed of 109 mph. Citroën eventually dropped its rotary experiment by the late '70s, in part due to low sales volumes, but also because of the world's oil crisis. The latter is significant here because rotary engines, by nature, guzzle fuel. They burn a lot of oil, too.

Yes, who'd have thought it? Little about these cars ever made it past the Iron Curtain, but Lada started its Wankel journey in 1978 with the VAZ-21018. Though it may have shared model codes with a fax machine of some kind, the 21018 did have a pretty prominent place in society. The four-door sedan used a 71-hp rotary engine that was basically reverse-engineered from either an NSU or a Mazda engine, depending on who you ask, and proved horribly unreliable. Some accounts say these engines couldn't manage more than 12,000 miles before succumbing to issues such as seal and bearing failures.

Lada took another crack at it in 1982 and created a twin-rotor engine with two outputs: 115 and 140 hp. These were fitted to the VAZ-21019 sedan, and provided a notable step up in performance from "regular" Ladas. They proved slightly more reliable too, at the cost of poorer fuel economy. Lada did stick by its rotary engines all the way until the early 2000s, albeit on an increasingly small scale, before wrapping up production entirely.

Citroën, Mazda, Lada, and NSU aren't the only manufacturers to have dabbled with rotary cars. General Motors was at the height of its power in the '70s, and saw an opportunity to reinvent how vehicles were engineered by placing rotaries at the heart of its plans. It had intended to offer its then-new Vega compact car with a Wankel engine, and committed $50 million just to license the technology. There was even the Aerovette: the best-looking Corvette of all time that never made it out of the concept stage and had a rotary engine. Unfortunately, as would soon happen with Citroën and the GS Birotor, the global oil crisis forced GM to ditch its rotary plans by the end of 1974.

Mercedes-Benz also got in on the act with its jaw-dropping C 111 experimental vehicle, first previewed at the 1969 Frankfurt Auto Show. It seemingly had everything a discerning celebrity would've wanted back then: a funky wedge-shaped body, a striking orange metallic paint job, and gullwing doors. Whereas the very first experiment had a three-rotor configuration, the second cranked it up to four rotors and was claimed to have a top speed of 186 mph. It all sounds super exciting, right? Well, Mercedes chose not to put it into production. Sorry to burst your several-second dream of owning one. But of the rotary-powered cars that did make production, which would you most like to own?

#5668. Alzheimer's Light and Sound Stimulation Therapy Misses Main Goal in Pivotal Trial

— But gamma wave approach hints at slower decline in mild Alzheimer's disease

A novel Alzheimer's therapy platform that delivered 40 Hz light and sound stimulation to engage gamma-frequency brain activity did not meet its primary endpoint, the HOPE pivotal study showed.

In the primary analysis population of 663 people with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's, the change from baseline on a composite measure of Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study-Activities of Daily Living (ADCS-ADL) scores did not differ between those who used the Spectris stimulation goggles or sham at 12 months, reported Marwan Sabbagh, MD, of the Barrow Neurological Institute in Phoenix.

Secondary endpoints in the overall study population also showed no significant differences. However, a prespecified subgroup analysis of 395 people with mild Alzheimer's disease (MMSE scores of 21-28 on the 30-point scale) showed favorable results for the device on some measures, Sabbagh said at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in Boston.

In the mild subgroup, the device was associated with a 55.8% slowing of decline in ADCS-ADL scores (nominal P=0.016) and a 46.8% slowing of decline in Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores (nominal P=0.004), Sabbagh noted.

Results in the moderate subgroup (MMSE scores of 15-20) did not favor the device, and some outcomes nominally favored sham.

The difference in outcomes between mild and moderate disease suggests that earlier intervention may be key to clinical benefit, observed Laura Nisenbaum, PhD, interim chief science officer at the Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation in New York City, which provided funding for the trial.

"While the HOPE study did not meet its primary endpoint, the signal in the mild Alzheimer's subgroup raises important questions that are worth exploring further," Nisenbaum said. "Daily function is what patients and families tell us matters most, so it will be important to see whether the early signs of slower decline on that measure in people with mild Alzheimer's hold up as more data become available."

The device delivers audiovisual stimulation intended to evoke steady-state gamma oscillations across broad cortical regions, Sabbagh explained. "Spectris was developed as a non-invasive, home-use investigational medical device that delivers daily 1-hour treatment sessions," he said.

Earlier research showed that sensory-evoked 40 Hz neural activity engages brain mechanisms essential for cognition and daily function, he added.

The HOPE trial evaluated the device in participants who had baseline MMSE scores of 15-28 and Alzheimer's biomarker confirmation. Participants were randomized within stratified mild and moderate disease subgroups.

The primary outcome was the integrated Alzheimer's Disease MMSE and ADCS-ADL Rating Scale, an equally weighted composite of global cognition (MMSE) and daily function (ADCS-ADL) scores, Sabbagh said.

In the overall study population, adverse device effects were reported in 18.3% of participants who received active treatment and 15.5% who received sham. The most common were headache, tinnitus, fatigue, dizziness, and ear pain. Seizures occurred in 0.9% of the active treatment group.

The gamma wave approach to treating Alzheimer's disease was first discovered in 2014 at the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). Executives at Cognito Therapeutics, an MIT spin-off, said they will pursue FDA approval for the 40 Hz light and sound stimulation device based on the nominally significant benefits seen in the mild Alzheimer's population.

An open-label extension of the HOPE trial is ongoing.

#5667. Charles Lindbergh Flew 3,610 Miles Despite The Disadvantage Of Not Having A Windshield

First off, let's keep in mind that Charles Lindbergh wasn't the first person to fly across the Atlantic Ocean. Some 66 to 80 people had already made the trip before him. Lindbergh, though, became the first person to fly solo and nonstop, from New York to Paris, in 1927.

Naturally, that achievement took a special kind of plane, so LIndbergh's Spirit of St. Louis had been modified for the attempt. And perhaps most importantly, that meant making room for enough fuel to cover his route of more than 3,600 miles. In the end, the plane carried 450 gallons of the stuff, an amount that weighed 2,750 pounds, representing more than half the craft's gross vehicle weight. Yep, that GVWR is as important for pilots as for RV and truck owners.

Of course, the engineers had to find a place to put all that fuel. The result was that the Spirit of St. Louis featured a main gas tank in front of Lindbergh's seat and extra tanks in the wings. Now, carrying all that fuel made sense, given the flight's nonstop nature. But Lindbergh had requested that the forward tank should fit between the engine and the cockpit for safety reasons in case of a crash. That may seem counter-intuitive, but Lindbergh was apparently worried about being crushed between the engine and fuel tank if the latter was mounted behind the cabin.

You can probably see where this is going, but Lindbergh certainly couldn't. With a large gas tank directly ahead of him, he had no way to look out the front of the plane. So it wasn't like the Spirit of St. Louis lost its windshield in flight, exposing Lindbergh to the elements. It didn't have a windshield in the first place.

Lindbergh had a few tricks up his sleeve when it came time to fly the Spirit of St. Louis, starting with one he picked up in his days as an airmail pilot. Packed into relatively small planes crowded with bags of mail, he developed the skill of looking out his side windows to fly the craft. In fact, modern pilots are still taught how to use the so-called "Lindbergh Reference" method when something blocks their forward vision. It's basically a way of learning to use just the view from the left-hand corner of a windshield to understand a plane's roll, pitch, and yaw.

Helping matters — at least somewhat — was a retractable periscope Lindbergh could extend from the left-side window. The scope wasn't exactly easy to use, however. Lindbergh had to rely on a small mirror mounted to the instrument panel to get a view. Still, it's too bad that modern cars with terrible visibility don't have something similar.

Some modern pilots may wonder what the big deal is about Lindbergh not seeing what was in front of him, since flying, taking off, and landing can all be accomplished today in zero visibility. Well, the Spirit of St. Louis lacked the kind of sophisticated technology that makes that sort of feat possible. Heck, Lindbergh's plane didn't even have a radio or gas gauges — he kept track of fuel by penciling marks directly on the instrument panel. It all seems to have worked out, though. After taking off from New York's Roosevelt field on the morning of May 27, 1927, he touched down at the Le Bourget Aerodrome in Paris 33½ hours later.

Logically enough, Lindbergh was sharply focused on the airplane's range — which explains why he carried so much fuel and so little else. Not only did he ditch the radio, he said goodbye to the parachute, navigation lights, and even a traditional pilot's seat. He sat on a wicker chair instead, designed his own lightweight flying boots , and skipped unnecessary maps.

The work paid off, as the unladen Spirit of St. Louis weighed only 2,150 pounds. Built for Lindbergh's transatlantic flight, it was based on a Ryan M-2 mail plane and adapted to meet the challenge. For example, its wings were stretched to a span of 46 feet, which required a longer tail, too. Meanwhile, the forward-mounted fuel tank extended the fuselage. The outcome was an overall length of more than 27 feet.

Providing motivation for the aircraft was a Wright J-5C Whirlwind engine. The air-cooled nine-cylinder mill delivered 220 horses and was known for its durability. Experts at the time claimed the motor could run for 9,000 hours, giving Lindbergh a cushion of roughly 8,965 hours in the Spirit of St. Louis. FYI: The plane was named for the city that hosted the first real gas station in the nation; it in St. Louis that Lindbergh found a group of businessmen to sponsor the flight.

Also, in an odd bit of foreshadowing, Lindbergh had a "Native American swastika" painted in the plane's nosecone for good luck. Just nine years later, he discovered a different use for that symbol at the 1936 Olympics in Berlin, where he and his wife were special guests of Nazi leader Hermann Goering. Lindbergh must have liked what he saw, as he became a full-on Nazi sympathizer and antisemite.
