#5665. 7 Long Distance-Focused EV SUVs Ranked From Best To Worst Range

Both average new-car prices and fuel prices are hitting record highs left and right. The state of things would be enough to get any car enthusiast down, if it weren't for the fact that electric cars are rad as hell. Fast, stylish, and fuel-efficient, EVs seem to get better with each new model that is released and each new generation that refines an already good vehicle into something great (we're looking at you, Toyota bZ).

However, despite some highly competitive offerings, EVs haven't quite popped off yet. The Trump administration's brutal murder of the EV tax credit and subsequent loosening of CAFE standards didn't help. The technology is still relatively new, so EVs are generally more expensive upfront than gas-powered cars, and there's also the question of range, one of the major specters haunting EV adoption at larger scales.

Concerns about the range of EVs may have once been well-founded, but that's not so much the case anymore. Tons of electric vehicles, SUVs included, can now breach 300 miles on a charge, and several are pushing past the 400-mile boundary, too. With ranges like that, road tripping is more than feasible, say nothing of the 34 miles the average American drives per day.

To illustrate the point, we've gathered a list of seven electric SUVs with excellent ranges — all over 300 miles on a full charge. This isn't a comprehensive list, but rather a sampling of the field, from awe-inspiring Lucids to affordable-ish Fords. To make the list, the cars needed an official fuel economy estimate published by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Perhaps unsurprisingly, more range is typically more expensive, and the longest-range SUVs out there are luxury vehicles, but a few more accessible rides made the list, too.

Debuting for the 2027 model year, the BMW iX5 is a shakeup to the luxury EV SUV world in a couple of big ways. For starters, this is the German automaker's first electric iteration of the popular (but once-controversial) X5. Iterating on a beloved idea is always sure to ruffle some feathers, but actually driving the iX5 might just unruffle those feathers right back down. The iX5 is also one of the exceedingly few EV SUVs that come close to matching the range of the Lucid Gravity. However, the iX5 actually dethrones the Gravity and takes the top spot among long-distance-focused EV SUVs. The icing on the iX5 cake is that it somehow manages to be even cheaper than its Lucid rival.

There's only one version of the BMW iX5 for its inaugural year, known as the iX5 60 xDrive, and it MSRPs at $81,250 with the destination fee included. This leaves the iX5 around $20,000 cheaper than the Lucid Gravity with the longest range. That's an impressive accomplishment, even if the iX5 doesn't quite stack up in other ways. To get the full 456 miles of range, you'll need to opt for BMW's 21-inch M Aero Polygon 1116 M wheels or the 21-inch Aero Double-Spoke Bicolor 1113 wheels with summer tires that can be chosen for no additional cost. Other available wheels result in a range from 418 miles to 447 miles. Still not bad.

When it comes to performance and style, the iX5 feels distinctly X5-like, though it reportedly doesn't handle quite as well. BMW advertises a 0-60 mph time of 4.4 seconds, which is slower than some rivals, and the iX5 also has less cargo space than the Gravity. Features abound, and the interior is comfortable and stylish.

Lucid Motors flipped the American EV world on its head when it debuted the Lucid Air, which had a maximum range of up to 517 miles. Then the mad lads did it again with the Lucid Gravity, which held the record for the longest-range SUV until the BMW iX5 came onto the scene. Still, the Gravity is a lot more than just an exceptionally long-range SUV that, admittedly, looks like a cooler minivan.

In our test, we found that the Gravity is just hands-down exceptional. The SUV has also earned astounding 10/10 ratings from both Car and Driver and U.S. News & World Report, and it consistently lands among the top two or three entries in its class in other major publications. It's lauded for its alacrity off the line, generous cargo area, and its refined interior.

To get the most range possible, you'll need to get your hands on the mid-tier Grand Touring trim and keep the standard wheels, which are 20 inches in the front and 21 inches in the back. Other wheel options are available but reduce your overall range. This setup will run you $98,900 plus the $1,600 destination fee, which puts the Lucid Gravity GT just within the six-figure range before tax. In return, you get a screaming-fast 3.4-second 0-60 mph time, 828 horsepower, and the ability to charge up to 200 miles in under 11 minutes. And you get to drive one of the coolest cars on the road today.

Standard features on the Gravity GT include PerLuxe leather upholstery, 12-way power-adjustable front seats, a power liftgate, a 34-inch cockpit display, a 12.6-inch landscape pilot display, a wireless charging pad, a 10-speaker stereo, and tons of safety and driver assistance features. All-wheel drive is standard, but the optional third row reduces the range to 437 miles.

The final 400-mile top dog on this list is the illustrious Rivian R1S. While Rivian has just recently dropped the smaller and better-than-we-ever-hoped-for 2027 R2 and has some of us biting our nails in anticipation of the smaller-yet R3, enthusiasts would be remiss to forget that the R1S is still a wildly impressive machine with monstrous off-road capabilities and up to a delicious 410 miles of maximum range. And on top of that, the R1S was one of just two large SUVs to earn the IIHS Top Safety Pick+ designation in 2026.

Another aspect that sets the R1S apart from its long-range competition is its status as a default seven-seater. While the Lucid Gravity offers an optional third row, the R1S is designed for it natively, and it's all the better for it. All three rows have adult-friendly legroom, even if getting all the way back takes some squeezing. The 2027 R1S starts at $85,885 for the base Premium trim with destination, and unlocking the full range requires upgrading to the long-range battery, which costs an extra $7,000. The setup produces 533 horsepower and can hustle from 0-60 mph in 4.5 seconds.

The interior is spacious and comfortable, offering abundant head- and legroom in the first two rows and well-cushioned seats. The design aesthetic is modern and distinctly premium, featuring metal and wood accents and soft plastics. It's the electro-minimalism we're used to by now but done superbly. The R1S can tow up to 7,700 pounds when properly equipped and also has off-road chops for days, thanks to its high torque rating, good ground clearance and standard surround-view camera system. Like many EVs, it's screen-forward, almost obnoxiously so, but that's a small price to pay for greatness.

Say what you will about Tesla — from dodging hundreds of millions of dollars in taxes probably being a bad thing to the company's vehicles' being inextricably linked to Elon Musk's questionable politics — but the fallen automaker did help pave the way for some of the truly exceptional EVs we have today, and the Tesla Model Y was no small part of that. You can yet see some of that luster in the Model Y's still-impressive range of up to 355 miles — 3 miles more than the larger Model X's 352-mile maximum.

The Model Y's range is a steep drop from the other luxury EV SUVs on this list, but it's important to remember that the above entries are the crème de la crème – the boundary-pushing pinnacle of EV design and the culmination of years and billions of dollars of R&D. They are, simply put, outliers among electric SUVs. Meanwhile, 355 miles of range is still far more than the majority of the field. And while the Model Y loses 55 miles of range compared to the R1S and its ilk, this Tesla is drastically less expensive up front. For the full 355-mile range, you'll need the standard-wheelbase Model Y Premium with rear-wheel drive, which runs a mere $47,630 with destination.

The downside, of course, is that you own a Tesla in a reality where the CEO appeared to have publicly thrown up a Sieg Heil. While the Model Y was once the world's best-selling car, it's been surpassed by many rivals in recent years. It has been knocked for its cumbersome touch controls, a stiff ride, and lots of cheap-feeling plastics. Sure, even the Long-Range Model Y Premium can sprint from 0-60 mph in 5.4 seconds (4.3 seconds with AWD), and has a spacious interior, but that's not particularly special anymore.

Hyundai has been killing it in the electrification game recently, and the Ioniq 9's introduction for the 2026 model year took the company's cred even higher. Made stateside, the Ioniq 9 is the most expensive Hyundai ever, with a starting price of $60,655 after destination fees. And while that's pretty pricey, you sure do get what you pay for. There's tons of space for both passengers and cargo, and the interior design is sleek and modern. It's also a three-row ride with room for six or seven, depending on the configuration, and the third row is largely adult-friendly. I'm a serial third-row hater, and I adored my time spent in the way back on the Ioniq 9. It's even easy to access, which earns it big points in my book.

The lineup's best range of 335 miles is found on the base S trim, which uses a single-motor rear-wheel-drive setup that produces 215 hp and 258 lb-ft of torque. That's a lot less power than what you'll find above, meaning the Ioniq 9 is one of the slowest SUVs on this list, but a decent torque rating means it won't feel sluggish from a stop. Somewhat surprisingly, upgrading to a dual-motor trim with all-wheel drive only reduces the range by 15 miles while bumping the power output up to 303 hp, and it costs just $3,810 extra, which might just be worth it depending on how badly you need the extra range.

Standard features on the base S trim include cloth upholstery, heated seats, an eight-way power-adjustable driver's seat, a 12.3-inch touch screen, a wireless charging pad, and a whole seven USB-C ports. Factor in the Ioniq 9's long list of ADAS features, like Hyundai's Highway Driving Assist 2, pedestrian and cyclist detection, and traffic-sign recognition, and the price starts to feel justified.

While you might balk at seeing the beloved Mustang name slapped on an electric SUV of all things (an SUV Mustang? Make it make sense!), this Ford actually is the real deal. When we talk about well-rounded cars, this is what we mean. Heck, the 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E even has a soft-roader trim. The Mustang Mach-E is screaming fast, super charismatic, fun to drive, spacious, relatively affordable, and long-ranged. Finding something to dislike about this SUV involves a level of nitpicking that isn't worth getting into here. If you haven't found yourself inside a Mustang Mach-E, reserve all judgment until you do, and get in one as soon as possible.

To get the most out of the Mustang Mach-E's range, you'll need to get the rear-wheel-drive Premium model with the extended battery pack, which unlocks the full 320-mile range. The Premium trim starts at $41,090 and carries a $2,045 destination fee, while the battery upgrade costs an extra $4,750. This version of the Mustang Mach-E sports 272 hp and 387 lb-ft of torque, which is more than enough to make this crossover feel truly fun.

The interior is upholstered with synthetic leather, and it's known to be comfortable and spacious in both rows, though you may want to stick to a maximum capacity of four due to the center column eating some of the rear middle legroom. The cabin design is centered around the Ford's 15.5-inch touch screen, which is vertically mounted and controls many car functions in addition to infotainment. Other standard features on the Premium trim include dual-zone automatic climate control, power-adjustable front seats with heating and ventilation, and ambient interior lighting. Despite the Mustang Mach-E not having seen a refresh in a few years, it still feels stylish and modern.

Coming in just shy of the Mustang Mach-E's 320-mile range is the 2027 Chevrolet Equinox EV at a very respectable 319 miles. The Chevy Equinox EV is what you might call the people's car. It's the least expensive SUV on this list by a few thousand bucks and a somewhat modest offering compared to the rest of the entries here, but it's by no measure a poor choice for EV shoppers.

The base LT 1 trim starts at $37,195 with destination. It's one of very few EVs under $40,000 that gets over 300 miles on a single charge, and you can get that mileage on any trim with front-wheel drive. Models with all-wheel drive lose about 12 miles of range, leaving them still solidly above the crucial 300-mile mark.

The best way to describe the Equinox EV is perhaps to call it familiar and predictable. There's not much flashy about it, and it's not particularly sprightly with its 220 horsepower. Testers report the Equinox EV rides smoothly with engaging handling, but notably heavy understeer takes some joy out of taking the SUV through corners. However, as a practical car used for commuting, city driving, and the occasional road trip, there's not much to actively dislike. The interior is spacious, albeit not exactly beautiful, and even tall passengers will have space in the back row. The Equinox EV also dodged Chevy's recent EV recall involving faulty brakes, which is a big point in its favor.

On the base LT 1 trim, you'll get features like cloth upholstery, manually adjustable front seats, a couple USB ports, and a 17.7-inch touch screen. Safety features include forward collision alert, rear park assist, and Teen Driver mode.

#5664. Novel Oral HAE Drug Measures Up to Injectable Options

— Randomized trial hits the mark for reducing hereditary angioedema attack rates

Prophylactic use of the novel oral bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist deucrictibant substantially reduced hereditary angioedema (HAE) attacks, a pivotal phase III trial showed.

For the primary endpoint, extended-release deucrictibant lowered the attack rate by a relative 83%, to 0.35 events per month compared with 2.06 in the placebo group (P<0.0001), reported Marc A. Riedl, MD, of the University of California San Diego, at the American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology annual meeting.

During the 24-week treatment period in the CHAPTER-3 trial, 45% of study drug-treated patients were attack free, compared with 3% of the placebo group (P=0.0018).

"We don't have head-to-head studies, but it is in the same ballpark of what the subcutaneous long-term prophylactic drugs have shown," Riedl told MedPage Today. "This is what we were hoping to see as investigators -- this high level of efficacy in a once-daily pill."

That's meaningful given what's been seen with the only approved targeted oral HAE prophylactic medication, berotralstat (Orladeyo), Riedl noted.

"The overall efficacy, at least in the pivotal trial for berotralstat, didn't measure up quite as well compared to some of the subcutaneous treatment options for long-term prophylaxis," he said. "So this is an effort to try to look at another oral agent that might be more effective across the population, just given that we know some patients really prefer oral medication for convenience and less burden of treatment and so forth."

Of the 85 patients in the trial, five had genetically confirmed HAE with normal C1 inhibitor levels. While two of three of these patients on deucrictibant had good results with the drug -- one had a greater than 80% reduction and the other had 100% reduction in HAE attacks -- the third patient had only a very small reduction in attack rate.

A post-hoc analysis looking at only patients with deficiency or dysfunction of C1 inhibitor levels showed an 87% reduction in attack rate with deucrictibant, a rate that Riedl said "reflects the type 1 and type 2 HAE population that every other study has reported when they report out their efficacy data for prophylaxis."

The international trial enrolled patients ages 12 years and older (mean age 39) who had at least three attacks within 3 months before screening and at least two attacks during the up to 8-week run-in period. Participants were randomly assigned 2:1 to 24 weeks of double-blind treatment with extended-release deucrictibant (40 mg once a day) or placebo.

Baseline HAE attack rate was 3.8 per month in the study drug group and 3.5 per month in the placebo group. Attack rates dropped within the first week with deucrictibant and remained lower than in the placebo group through week 24.

The relative reductions in events that required rescue medication and in moderate-to-severe HAE attacks were 83% and 77%, respectively (both P<0.0001). Nearly all patients on deucrictibant had their attack rate reduced by at least 70% (96% vs 23% on placebo, P<0.0001). The drug increased the proportion of patients who had at least a 90% reduction in attack frequency as well (65% vs 10%, P<0.0001). Deucrictibant also resulted in significantly greater improvements in mean Angioedema Quality of Life questionnaire total score and all domain scores as compared with placebo.

Riedl called the safety profile favorable overall. One treatment-emergent serious adverse event occurred in the deucrictibant group, a case of laryngeal dyskinesia that resulted in a stay in the intensive care unit for evaluation but was deemed not related to the study drug.

The sole discontinuation in the active treatment group was due to asymptomatic elevation in liver function tests. Riedl noted that this is in line with what has been seen in most of the long-term prophylactic studies with HAE medications. "These patients do sometimes have a history of fatty liver. They've been on androgens, which we know can affect their liver function," he said.

Gastrointestinal side effects seen with berotralstat were not observed with deucrictibant (1.8% vs 6.7% on placebo).

An immediate-release version of deucrictibant is also being developed for on-demand treatment of acute HAE attacks and is under review by the FDA for that indication. Riedl suggested that if the extended-release formulation were to be approved as an additional prophylactic treatment option, it could be appealing for patients who prefer oral medications over injections.

"This would potentially be an oral treatment that gives very similar efficacy in terms of preventing attacks compared to what we've seen with the subcutaneous drugs, and we don't actually have that at the moment," he said.

He pointed to the increasing options for HAE management as good for patients. "Trying to make that preventative treatment as easy, as least burdensome as we can is part of the goal," Riedl noted. "And I think this is one way to potentially do that for people -- just a once-daily medication that's portable, easy to travel with, and makes their lives easier."

#5663. Laid-Off Textile Workers Ran Their Bosses' Hidden Exotics As A Museum For Two Years

What's the coolest automotive museum you've ever seen? What about the most mind-blowing piece of automotive history you've ever beheld with your own eyes? I live right down the street from the National Automotive Museum in Reno, NV, which is a great time, but it doesn't quite take the cake. There are some real gems out there, like the Gilmore Car Museum, which lets you drive a Model T, or the Studebaker National Museum, where you can watch footage from 1932 of grown men throwing cars down a hill for safety testing. But if I had a time machine and could visit any car museum anywhere in time and space, there's one in particular that I'd just love to see.

That would be the Schlumpf collection in Mulhouse, France, specifically during the two-year period in the mid-to-late-70s when it was run by laid-off textile workers after their bosses shut their factories down and fled the country. Yes, the story is as wild as it sounds.

Now housed in the Musée National de l'Automobile in Mulhouse, the Schlumpf collection is an astounding piece of both car collecting and labor history. It began as the personal (and, sure, slightly obsessive) collection of Fritz Schlumpf, a long-time Bugatti driver who, along with his brother Hans, ran a textile business with factories in Mulhouse. Born around 1906, Fritz Schlumpf began collecting Bugattis intentionally in the 1960s. He hunted them down with the help of the British Bugatti Owners Club, who helped him locate around 50 individual cars, plus a stash of 30 vintage Bugattis owned by John W. Shakespeare of Hoffman, Illinois. Over two years, Schlumpf and Shakespeare negotiated a purchase price, bringing Schlumpf's personal Bugatti collection up to 80. Then he bought 18 more off Ettore Bugatti himself. Schlumpf was only getting started.

Eventually, Fritz Schlumpf owned an estimated 105 Bugattis, which might've comprised as much as 20% of the Bugattis in existence at the time. Who can blame Schlumpf for apparently wanting them all? After all, Bugattis do drive like a dream, even the old ones. But Schlumpf hadn't just been buying up cars of his favorite French brand. He'd actually been amassing a mind-bogglingly large stable of rare cars, both vintage and contemporary.

By the 1970s, Schlumpf had over 400 cars stashed in an unused factory in Mulhouse that was being fitted into a museum. But in order to acquire them all during a worsening economy, he'd spent money from a government grant intended to keep his factories in operation. When his transgression was discovered, he promptly shut down all his businesses and fled to Switzerland, putting about 1,800 workers out of business.

In response, the workers decided they didn't need a boss and could keep things running without Schlumpf's oversight, so they formed a workers' co-op to keep themselves employed. When members of the co-op traveled to the supposedly unused factory in Mulhouse, what they discovered was a building packed to the gills with exotic cars. A collection the likes of which had never been seen. The workers collectively decided to run the museum while using it to spread the message of their cooperative to the wider world.

The museum was open for two years, with public access to the vehicles for a few hours a day, and it contained some real stunners, including gems like two Bugatti Type 52s, which were electric race cars sized for children. You can still see the collection today, though not exactly as Schlumpf originally had it. The collection was seized by officials and eventually reopened in 1982.

#5662. How Can Energy Improve Lives? Why Counting Connections Isn’t Enough

Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.

Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.

But access is only the first step. A health clinic can’t perform surgery if frequent power cuts make its equipment unreliable. An electric irrigation pump is unlikely to raise a farmer’s income if crops can’t reach buyers. And a small business may gain little from electricity if it lacks financing to buy the equipment it needs to expand.

For energy to improve people’s lives, it must be affordable, sufficient, and reliable—and people and businesses must be able to put it to productive use.

The United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7) calls for “universal access to affordable, reliable, and modern energy services” by 2030. But the two indicators used to track its universal-access target focus only on whether people have access to electricity and whether they primarily rely on clean fuels and technologies. They do not address reliability, affordability, or economic impacts.

Other approaches already offer a fuller picture. The World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program developed the Multi-Tier Framework to measure electricity access beyond connections, including whether electricity is available when needed, adequate for the equipment people want to use, reliable and affordable. While the framework is used by some countries to assess these broader dimensions of energy access, such measures are not the default, as many countries rely on the U.N.’s official global indicators.

As governments consider what should follow the SDGs after 2030, they should make multidimensional energy-access measures a regular part of national surveys and use the results to track progress globally. Since access alone does not necessarily deliver better livelihoods, improved measures of access could also be paired with indicators of whether energy is delivering the development outcomes it is intended to support. These could include whether clinics and schools can function as intended, farmers can increase yields and incomes and businesses can grow revenues and employment.

Together, these measures could shift energy planning from the largely supply-side question of how many people have access toward the demand-side questions of what people and institutions need energy for and whether the energy system enables them to meet these needs.

The examples below show why looking beyond connections matters in practice.

National electrification rates can mask large differences in where electricity is available within a country. Addressing those gaps requires looking beyond national averages to identify the households, businesses, and public facilities that lack access.

In 2023, WRI, working closely with Uganda’s Ministry of Health, used WRI’s Energy Access Explorer (EAE)—an online mapping tool that combines energy data with information on infrastructure, public services, and economic activity—to assess the electricity needs of health facilities. The analysis found that 675 facilities serving more than 3 million people had no electricity, either grid or off-grid, yet all were in areas with significant solar energy potential. The analysis helped identify places where solar power could fill the energy gap.

In Ethiopia, the Ministry of Water and Energy and the World Bank used EAE to help design a financing program for off-grid electricity. The analysis identified 145 priority woredas, or districts, where investments could reach more than 19 million people. Having this location-based data helped translate national energy-access goals into decisions about where public financing should be directed.

Ethiopia also illustrates why simple access figures can overstate the level of service people receive. A 2025 national energy-access survey found that 65% of households had access to at least one source of electricity. However, just 44% of the population received at least a basic level of electricity service, enough for uses such as lighting and charging a phone for at least four hours a day.

Simply having an electricity connection is not enough if the supply lacks the capacity or voltage stability to operate the equipment people need.

In the Gumla district in Jharkhand, India, villages that had gained household grid connections still lacked enough power for many businesses to function. WRI found that the single-phase electricity supplied was insufficient for productive uses such as milling and oil pressing. Beginning in 2015, Mlinda Charitable Trust, a nonprofit, installed solar mini-grids that supplied three-phase electricity, allowing local enterprises to run equipment, including rice and wheat hullers, oil expellers, flour mills, and pulverizers.

Governments should assess not only whether communities are connected but also whether the electricity supplied can meet the capacity and power-quality requirements of the services and equipment people need—and plan grid upgrades or complementary systems accordingly.

A connection provides limited benefit if households, businesses, or public facilities cannot pay for enough energy to meet their needs. Measuring meaningful access therefore also means asking whether the energy is affordable for the people and institutions expected to use it.

In Ethiopia’s Berbere district, farmers initially used petrol-powered pumps to irrigate their fields, but high fuel and maintenance costs meant these were too expensive for many to keep using. Petrol cost $91 to $203 per hectare a year, while repairs and the cost of transporting fuel added further expenses.

WRI and the Danish nonprofit DanChurchAid later installed two solar-powered pumps serving 48 farming households. The solar systems have no fuel costs, while maintenance costs are less than $10 a year, compared with more than $1,300 for petrol pumps. But the two pumps’ combined $19,200 upfront cost was beyond what most farmers could afford out of pocket. Governments and funders should therefore assess both the ongoing cost of using energy and the upfront cost of the technologies needed to use it, and provide financing or targeted support where high initial costs remain a barrier.

Being connected to the grid does not mean electricity will be available whenever it is needed. WRI researchers documented power cuts lasting three to 12 hours a day at two health facilities in Jharkhand, with outages worsening during the monsoon season. The facilities relied on diesel generators and small battery backups during outages.

In 2017, after solar photovoltaic systems and larger batteries were installed, the facilities were able to keep wards and offices running and power other essential equipment during grid outages, reducing their reliance on grid electricity.

Tracking the frequency and duration of outages would give a clearer picture of whether electricity is dependable enough to support essential services.

Even when energy is available, adequate, affordable, and reliable, it may not translate into better livelihoods. People also need equipment, financing, and access to markets to put energy to productive use.

In Uganda, WRI Africa and partners used EAE to identify $15 million in potential investments in renewable energy technologies, including solar-powered irrigation systems and equipment for cooling and milling, that could benefit more than 28,000 farmers. Some organizations identified through that work have since secured funding for related projects. Masaka District Farmers Association, for example, received an IKI Small Grants award for an irrigation project that equipped 150 hectares of coffee-growing land with drip irrigation and worked with 1,500 smallholder farmers.

In Berbere, solar-powered irrigation has enabled farmers to harvest three to four times a year and grow higher-value crops. In their first season, many farmers earned four to 10 times as much from onion, pepper, and cabbage sales as they had previously earned in a year from staple crops.

Tracking these outcomes alongside measures of energy access can help show whether investments are translating into higher productivity and incomes.

Making greater use of existing multidimensional measures, alongside complementary indicators of development outcomes, could change not just how governments report progress but also how they plan and direct investment.

Rather than starting with how many new connections a project can deliver, governments and funders would ask what people and institutions need energy for, what prevents them from using it effectively, and which investments could remove those barriers. In some places, that may mean extending electricity supply. In others, it could mean improving reliability, lowering costs, or helping farmers and businesses obtain the equipment and financing needed to use energy productively.

Energy is essential to improving human well-being, but it is only one part of what drives development. Like water, health care or education and energy is necessary but not sufficient. Treating access as a starting point rather than an end goal—and measuring whether people can use, afford, and rely on the energy they receive—would give governments a clearer picture of whether energy investments are improving people’s lives.

Courtesy of WRI. Experts: Dimitris Mentis, Harsha Meenawat

WRI is a global research organization that spans more than 50 countries, with offices in Brazil, China, Europe, India, Indonesia, and the United States. Our more than 450 experts and staff work closely with leaders to turn big ideas into action to sustain our natural resources—the foundation of economic opportunity and human well-being. Find out more at www.wri.org

#5661. Why Toyota Land Cruisers Have A Reputation For Being Nearly Indestructible

In 1971, Toyota put out an ad for the Land Cruiser. The picture was of a 12-year-old FJ25, and the headline read, "We'll know how long it lasts when the first one wears out." In the ad Toyota touts how the Land Cruiser is designed and built to last. From its steel bumper to its heavy-duty suspension to the straight-six 155-horsepower engine, everything was engineered for durability.

Even back then, the Land Cruiser was already establishing a reputation for being hard to kill. Indestructible, some might even say. Earning this title was no accident. Toyota built it from tough stock — the Land Cruiser literally used commercial-grade parts the first go-around. Once it was released into the wild, it was soon being used around the world in all sorts of harsh conditions, completing jobs that tested its mettle. Land Cruisers became known as being reliable and tough.

So where did that legacy for toughness begin? Let's look at the very first step in the Land Cruiser lineage, a prototype for the Japanese National Police Reserve. Back in 1950, Toyota needed a Jeep-sized ¼-ton four-wheel-drive vehicle built with parts local to Japan. Toyota used the chassis from the one-ton SB truck, which came with a ladder-style frame, solid front and rear axles, and leaf springs. The Type B engine came from the four-ton BM truck. Let's do some quick math here–a one-ton chassis plus a four-ton engine divided by a ¼-ton truck equals a chassis that was overkill and an engine that was understressed. Thankfully, that turned out to be a great equation and became the template for Land Cruisers to come.

To see how that reputation evolved, let's next take a look at the legendary Land Cruiser 40 Series, which included the iconic FJ40. Launched in 1960, the FJ40 rode on a heavy-duty ladder-style frame to tackle high-stress and twisting forces. This was the second generation powered by the F-series engine, an inline-6 with a cast-iron block. It was built to have high torque at low rpms, keeping it understressed and reliable. That engine, incidentally, was in production 43 years before being retired, which meant it had the longest run of any Toyota engine. It became known worldwide as a reliable, durable all-terrain vehicle over its 24-year production run.

Toyota engineered the Land Cruiser to be tougher than its environment. The chassis and suspension were overbuilt for the vehicle, and the engine was designed to keep on going. Travel to just about any remote part of the planet, and you will still see a Land Cruiser variant being put to work. Land Cruisers have been used worldwide as farm trucks, fire trucks, and even combat platforms. They also deliver mail in the Outback in Australia, save lives as ambulances in Costa Rica, and are the vehicle of choice for aid organizations and the United Nations and the Red Cross. Land Cruisers are trusted around the world to handle these tough tasks for one reason — they consistently get the job done.

That ethos was passed down through the generation of trucks that followed. Yes, they got more comfortable, but they didn't compromise on the core promise. The understressed (and still thirsty) engines changed over the years, but the stout cast-iron block stuck around in the North American market until the 200-series arrival in 2008. The frame got boxed in 1967 and body-on-frame construction is still in place today. Solid front axles were standard until 1998 with the 100-series.

Throughout these measured changes over the Land Cruiser's 75-year history, there has been one other constant — the passion of Land Cruiser owners. These enthusiasts have arguably done more to contribute to building the reputation than anything else. Ask any Land Cruiser owner about their truck, and will gladly tell you how 200,000 miles is just getting broken in. As an owner of two — one at 240,000 miles and another at 284,000 miles — I can confirm. Claims of 400,000 and 500,000 miles are not unheard. This trust in their vehicles and reluctance to part with them is a good part of why Land Cruisers have such good resale value.

Those looking to get into a new Land Cruiser are in luck. In 2024, after a two-year absence, Toyota gave us the revival of the off-road icon in the form of a brand-new Land Cruiser. It comes from the Prado line of Land Cruiser, which has been upholding the Land Cruiser name and reputation worldwide since 1990. Will it be another legend?  Time will tell.

#5660. New ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept: This Electric GTI Is Ready For The Racetrack

270 kW (367 PS), top speed of 240 km/h and 4.7 seconds from 0 to 100 km/h: With the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, Volkswagen is marking the 50th anniversary of the GTI by showing how uncompromising an electric GTI with motorsport ambitions can be. The concept car will be presented to the public next week at the Essen Motor Show (27 November to 6 December 2026). Its performance figures meet a two-door silhouette and flared wings as well as a large front splitter, diffuser and rear wing. The result: a powerful appearance and maximum downforce for fast laps. At the same time, the concept vehicle provides a preview of how the GTI idea can be further developed in the electric age.

Kai Grünitz, Member of the Board of Management for Technical Development, Volkswagen Brand and Brand Group Core: “The GTI has been one of Volkswagen’s great success stories for 50 years. This year, we launched our GTI as an electric vehicle in series production for the first time. With the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, we are showing how much more potential there is in the electric GTI world. Our platform strategy and MEB+ give us the technological freedom to make even extreme concepts possible.”

Designed for performance. The design of the new ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is based on the production model, the 166 kW (226 PS) ID. Polo GTI. In both models, the drive power is transmitted to the front axle. In the 270 kW (367 PS) ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, this power delivery is controlled – thanks in part to an electronically regulated front differential lock (VAQ) – so that the model reaches 100 km/h from a standstill in just 4.7 seconds with Launch Control. Like the drive system, the electrical infrastructure has also been adapted to the high performance of the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept. The 52 kWh high-voltage battery can provide up to 290 kW at short notice, enabling a top speed of 240 km/h. The DCC (adaptive chassis control) has also been tuned for use on the racetrack and ensures precise handling and high traction in conjunction with the front differential lock. The new ceramic brakes of the one-box brake system are also designed for high performance.

Dynamics are visible in the design. On the exterior, the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept follows the powerful clarity of the ID. Polo GTI production model, while at the same time incorporating design elements that underline the motorsport characteristics. Particularly striking features are the two-door instead of four-door silhouette, pronounced flaring of the wings by 50 millimetres in each case, a large motorsport splitter at the front, a wider rear end, a new diffuser and a rear wing in carbon fibre that protrudes above the roof line.

Two-seater. Reduced to racing. The interior is also tailored to the racetrack, and only the basic layout of the overall cockpit has been adopted from the production model. This means there is no infotainment system, for example. The focus is solely on ergonomics and driving. The driver and front passenger sit on Recaro racing bucket seats with red 5-point harnesses. The rear and luggage compartment have been completely cleared. Instead of a rear seat system, a rollover bar painted in the GTI colour Tornado Red is integrated above and behind the front seats. The dash panel, side trims and many other details are covered in dark ArtVelours microfibre fabric with red topstitching – work that has been carried out with great precision by Volkswagen trainees. In many areas – in keeping with Volkswagen tradition – the young employees were directly involved in realisation of the concept vehicle by the Development department and designers.

550 instead of 290 newton-metres. The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept features the high-torque APP550 motor. The special technical challenge here: this motor is actually intended for the rear of large models such as the ID. Tiguan or ID.7. It therefore had to be fitted into the smaller ID. Polo as front-wheel drive and additionally combined with an electronic front differential lock. Thomas Schmall, Member of the Board of Management Volkswagen AG for Technology, and CEO of Volkswagen Group Components: “The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept shows just how emotive electric mobility can be: This is made possible by our APP550, one of the most efficient electric drives in its class. Manufactured over one million times at the Group Components plant in Kassel, this drive was actually developed for larger vehicle classes. Integrating it into the Polo required millimetre precision and is a powerful example of engineering skill and teamwork at Volkswagen, from Development and Design through to our trainees who worked on the project.”

GTI from the master of modular platforms. The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is based on the modular electric drive (MEB+) platform with front-wheel drive. Volkswagen has used the basic technical layout of the production model and taken it to a new level of performance with a 104 kW (141 PS) more powerful electric drive. The result is the most dynamic interpretation of a front-wheel drive ID. model to date. At the other end of the scale is the Mission Efficiency, which is also based on the ID. Polo and set four world records as a particularly efficient near-production electric vehicle. Both concept vehicles show the large bandwidth offered by electric drive systems from maximum sportiness to outstanding efficiency.

2026 is the year of the GTI. Following the Golf GTI EDITION 50, the new ID.3 GTI (sales start early 2027) and the new ID. Polo GTI (available to order since October), the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is making its debut this year as the fourth new model under the umbrella of the iconic GTI product brand. No other compact sports car family has been as successful worldwide for half a century now – with more than 2.5 million units sold – as the GTI models.
