#5655. Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027

Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Federal health officials are focused on rebuilding trust with the public and working across the aisle with the new Congress.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., spoke at the Milken Institute’s Future of Health Summit last week in Washington, D.C. Over 1,200 attendees gathered at the event, the theme of which was “better health within reach.”

In a fireside chat, a chipper Schwartz tried to answer a tough line of questioning about Americans’ loss of trust in her agency, controversial vaccine changes, measles and other public health issues.

When asked about her potential disagreements with Kennedy, Schwartz said, “I disagree all the time. He’s a lawyer, I’m a lawyer. […] What I love about the secretary is that he listens to those disagreements. He's not someone who just says, ‘No, I don't have room for that.’ He really does value differing opinions.”

The U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, global health officials announced just this week. On that issue, Schwartz stressed the importance of supporting CDC’s state partners on awareness, prevention and surveillance efforts.

“MMR is the number one way to prevent measles,” Schwartz said. Today’s outbreaks “happen in communities that are very close-knit communities … that typically do not and have not vaccinated their children,” she said. Most cases are currently among kids over the age of five and adults, according to Schwartz.

Under Schwartz’s leadership, the CDC changed its method of reporting measles deaths from real-time reporting by state public health departments to death certificate data, which can face multi-month lags. Schwartz is being investigated by Energy & Commerce Committee Democrats who, during a briefing on CDC’s alleged suppression of the total number of national measles deaths on its dashboard, have called her unresponsive and misleading.

“As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of measles deaths that CDC reports to the public, concealing the fact that 10 people have died of measles-related deaths this year alone,” the Committee leaders wrote (PDF) in a letter on Tuesday. “We are expanding our investigation to examine the threat your actions pose to Americans’ health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required.”

During her fireside chat, Schwartz acknowledged that "we've lost trust not only externally with the American public, but also internally with the team that works at the CDC,” she said. To address this, Schwartz wants the public to understand that CDC follows the science, is being transparent and “leading with humility.” She pointed to COVID-era “arrogance” from institutions, directing at instead of conversing with the public.

“I want to be a CDC director that really has a conversation with the American public,” Schwartz said.

Internally, the first priority is to add stability to the body, including hiring leaders within the agency so they have a permanent leadership role. The CDC has also created a strategic hiring plan for 2027 with the input of staff and is looking to its “force extenders” like epidemic intelligence officers and its Public Health Associate Program.

On how she’s planning to work with the new majority-Democratic Congress, Schwartz noted she was encouraged to see more Congress members coming in with a healthcare background, “who understand how these policies will impact patients.” She said is eager to work with the Congressional Doctors Caucus and to work with both sides of the aisle.

“I know that we may not agree on every issue, but I do think there's a common ground where we can actually focus on really trying to make Americans healthy again,” she said.

One of her priorities for 2027 is having a “21st-century CDC” by bringing innovation into the public health sphere. She called out the Biothreat Radar, a proposed wastewater surveillance program about which she recently spoke with Sen. Andy Kim (D-New Jersey). The program’s proposed (PDF) budget is $52 million. The CDC has also tentatively put out a call for new Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) members, which will depend on a final ruling from the appellate court in the agency’s favor.

At the Summit, Schwartz’s comments did not necessarily satisfy some of the attendees. When asked by Fierce Healthcare for his impressions of the interview, a public health worker in the room who did not wish to be named called her a “traitor."

In his fireside chat closing out the Summit, Secretary Kennedy primarily spoke about food and obesity.

One of HHS' most consequential accomplishments during his tenure, Kennedy said, has been changing the dietary guidelines to be “science-based.” Earlier this year, the White House released new federal dietary guidelines, calling for prioritizing quality protein, healthy fats, fruits, vegetables and whole grains, while avoiding highly processed foods and refined carbs.

The agency is focused on transforming food across a number of sectors, including in Head Start programs—free federal early childhood programs—which have received about $151 million in supplemental HHS awards to strengthen nutrition services. HHS is also focused on rolling out healthy food options in the military, Kennedy said, and within SNAP by allowing states to request waivers to restrict what SNAP dollars are spent on. As of this summer, HHS has launched a Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge, challenging hospitals to put nutrition at the center of patient care. HHS has also encouraged medical schools to increase their number of education hours on nutrition from an average of two to 40 hours, Kennedy said.

“Real” food sales in grocery stores, Kennedy claimed, went up 8% this year, while obesity rates have dropped by 7%. He acknowledged that the drop in obesity rates is more likely due to GLP-1 access rather than healthier eating. “If we can reduce obesity, we can reduce our healthcare costs,” he said, praising Trump’s Most Favored Nation negotiations for lowering the price of drugs like Ozempic.

“We reward people at every level—the hospitals, the providers, other providers, doctors, insurance companies, pharmaceutical companies—we reward them financially for keeping people sick. And as long as those financial incentives are in place, we are going to be operating a sick-care system rather than a healthcare system,” Kennedy said. HHS has started to change that by shifting more to value-based care, he added, so stakeholders get paid to keep patients healthy “rather than being paid to keep them sick.”

When asked what he wants his legacy as Health Secretary to be, Kennedy echoed Schwartz on the idea of following science. “What I want to do is to end corporate capture and the politicization of science … that Americans once again trust the regulatory agencies, they trust the science that’s coming from them,” he said.

He referred to newer guidelines meant to encourage extra transparency from researchers. In 2026, the HHS Scientific Integrity Policy was updated (PDF) to support publishing raw data and code in publicly accessible repositories, preregistering study protocols and transparently reporting all results.

He said he wants "to make sure that we’re not kowtowing to the food industry, the pharmaceutical industry, all these people who are at the trough taking on the $2.3 trillion that my agency gives out every year. And that instead, that Americans believe that this agency is devoted to their health, that they trust it, and that we are doing the science that we need to find out what is making them sick so that we can all eliminate it as a society.”

Kennedy's interview at the event did not touch on measles or vaccine policy, where the secretary's policies and communications have garnered broader criticism and controversy than his views on nutrition. Tuesday's announcement that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination status garnered a fresh call for Kennedy's resignation among his critics, including the Democratic Doctors Caucus.

Also coinciding with Milken's event was the announcement of the inaugural 2027 cohort of the Elevate Investment Initiative. The effort, part of the Milken Institute’s Women Health Network, aims to mobilize $1 billion in net-new capital for women’s health innovation. The 10 fund managers and companies include Borski Fund, Cross-Border Impact Ventures, Foreground Capital, Meridian Health Ventures, How Women Invest and more. [cut this or move?]

#5654. What Car-Related Books Are You Reading Right Now?

'Tis the season when Americans drown the last few months of hardship, like the doubled cost of car repairs and record new car price highs, in gravy and egg nog and go gung-ho on buying gifts for friends and family. I tend not to partake in the yearly ritual, but if I do participate, one of my favorite gifts to give or receive is a book. Sometimes the people in your life surprise you with titles you would have never come across on your own.

The act of book-giving is actually a common practice for the Christmas Eve holiday in Iceland. "Jólabókaflóð, which translates to "Christmas Book Flood" is the practice of gifting your loved ones books on Christmas Eve. In this ever-present digital world, it's nice to be given something tangible that can be enjoyed and shared with others.

Lucky for automotive enthusiasts, there's an endless bounty of books on everything from cars to planes, to race cars and sinking ships. You name it — there's probably a book about it. So, tell us, what car-related books are you reading right now?

Thanks to my ADHD and tendency to "mood read," I have a terrible habit of starting a book, setting it down, and finishing another book instead, therefore leaving a trail of unfinished, to-be-read-later books behind. In that collection sits "Life After Cars" which I started months ago, and appear to have only finished the introduction. If you want to know more on it, Jalop Collin Woodard wrote this insightful review earlier this year. The other I truly need to finish is "Bruce McLaren, The Man and His Racing team" by Eoin S. Young. It's just shy of 200 pages of reading, so it's a light read. So far it comes off much like a parallel accompaniment to the McLaren documentary.

If I had to list the books I'm eyeing to eventually read in the near distant future, there's the coffee table book I purchased earlier this year on the Porsche 718 and 804, and also I picked up a book called "Carmageddon" which looks like it runs along similar messaging to "Life After Cars."

Now, take a look at your bookshelf, end table, desk, or whatever odd place you find yourself leaving your books and tell us about the car-related books you've been reading. Our own magnificent fearless leader, Erin Marquis, is reading "Terror in the City of Champions: Murder, Baseball, and the Secret Society That Shocked Depression-Era Detroit." She says it's a gripping read about the heyday of Detroit covering sport, city, political, labor and automotive history.

If you're not reading something that hits the spot via car, racing or anything transportation-related, is there a book you've finished recently you'd like to share with your friends here? Or is there something you purchased that calls out to you every time you pass it in the room, and you can't help but go "man, I really need to read that soon?" Bring on the book recommendations!

#5653. Medicare for All Has Capitol Hill Abuzz, but It's Unlikely to Pass Soon, Experts Say

— Instead, gradual additions like lowering the eligibility age are seen as a better bet

The idea of expanding Medicare to cover the entire population -- otherwise known as "Medicare for All" (MFA) or "single-payer" -- has been a popular catch phrase among the incoming Democratic members of Congress.

"In the richest, most powerful country in the world, you should not have to suffer for your healthcare," Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, MD, DPhil (D-Mich.), an MFA supporter, told a roomful of nurses last month, The Guardian reported.

"Medicare for All is at the top of my list," Rep.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) told the Minnesota Women's Press last month.

But is that a realistic possibility, especially when Democrats -- although they gained large numbers of seats in the midterms -- don't have enough votes for a veto-proof Senate majority? Probably not at this point, Katie Keith, JD, MPH, director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown University, in Washington, said in a phone interview. "There is a lot of talk ... that there's a need to improve traditional Medicare before you get to open it up and transition to a single-payer system," she said.

This is best illustrated by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) -- a long-time champion of single-payer -- who recently came out with a plan to get to MFA, but incrementally. "It doesn't seem to be an abandonment of MFA itself but that's what Sanders came out with -- lowering the Medicare eligibility age; focusing on [adding] dental, vision, and hearing coverage; and covering kids," Keith said. "These are all significant changes."

An incremental approach also appeared in a memo sent in September to House Majority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) -- widely expected to be elected Speaker of the House in the incoming Congress. The memo from the Democrats' Cost-of-Living Healthcare Working Group called for capping Medicare beneficiaries' annual out-of-pocket costs at $5,000 as well as adding dental, vision, and hearing coverage -- all part of the group's "First 100 Hours" plan. Then, during the first year in office, the proposal calls for Democrats to "commit to achieving universal coverage" through "comprehensive examination of various single-payer and public option models."

But aspirations alone won't determine the fate of incoming Democrats' legislation, Keith added. "Who knows what committees these new members will be on? Sure they'll be committed to their campaign pledges, but where will they each be in the Senate or the House to push on policy positions of their choice? If El-Sayed is on the [Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee], that gives him a platform, but he might have other priorities. On the House side, there will be a change in leadership at the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee -- what new members will be joining that? It will be interesting to see who lands where and what their priorities are."

Mark Weller, JD, shareholder at the Polsinelli law firm in Washington, doubts that MFA will make it across the finish line any time soon. "The most ambitious healthcare proposals have little chance of becoming law," he said in an email. "In the Senate, Democrats will have 56 [votes], but it's not 60, and it's certainly not the 67 needed to override a veto. President Trump still has the veto pen, and Republicans can still block things in the Senate."

In addition, "there are competing factions in the Democratic caucus," he said. "The challenge is for Democrats to deliver on the affordability mandate. The alternative is spending the next 2 years explaining why divided government prevented them from doing so. If voters feel the economy is not working for them, hearings on Medicare for All aren't going to make their life better. The trick will be to find some opportunities for bipartisan progress."

MFA also has plenty of influential detractors inside and outside of Congress. "MFA is grabbing lots of attention while keeping candidates from discussing much more important issues like our $40 trillion public debt, how to reduce our $2 trillion-per-year federal budget deficits, solvency of Social Security and Medicare, child and elderly poverty, and climate change," Wendell Primus, PhD, visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution's Center on Health Policy, wrote prior to Election Day in an unpublished opinion article, which he shared with MedPage Today. "Let me explain why it should never be enacted."

First of all, compared to the Affordable Care Act (ACA), "MFA is an even more mammoth undertaking because the 10-year cost of $32 trillion is impossible to finance," wrote Primus, who, as the senior health adviser to former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), was the lead House staffer for getting the ACA passed in 2010. "While the health plan is generous and would provide more coverage than most health plans today, there will be many employers and individual voters who would consider themselves losers when they compare their tax bill to their out-of-pocket health costs. Those who lose because of MFA will stand in the way of enactment."

"In addition, many key stakeholders will balk at the initiatives to lower healthcare costs that will necessarily result," he added. "Specifically, it will be extremely difficult to get hospitals, doctors, insurance companies, and all other care providers to be convinced that MFA would be better than the status quo. And the fear of the unknown will also be a powerful force against enactment."

#5652. JA Energy Storage Launches an Internal Battery Passport Platform to Facilitate Compliance with EU Standards

JJA ESS has launched its own battery passport data platform to support lifecycle information management and help companies prepare for upcoming EU regulations. The platform is hosted in the company’s own cloud environment, giving the team direct responsibility for data policies, access permissions, and future updates.

According to the EU Battery Regulation, from February 18, 2027, battery passports are mandatory for batteries used in light vehicles (LMTs), electric vehicles, and industrial batteries with a capacity exceeding 2 kWh that are placed on the market or put into service. Further requirements will follow.

A battery passport is a digital data record linked to a single physical battery. A QR code and a unique identifier based on the ISO/IEC 15459 series connect the data record to the battery, enabling access to information throughout its entire lifecycle. This can include product identity, material composition, CO₂ footprint, recycled content, performance and durability, condition, supply chain due diligence, and end-of-life disposal. Taken together, these data points support consistent information management from product identification to the end of the product lifecycle.

For manufacturers, the challenge lies not simply in creating a QR code. The data must be traceable back to its source, up-to-date, and accessible in accordance with regulatory and business requirements. Companies must also manage access to sensitive information and comply with regulations governing cross-border data transfers and trade secrets. This balance is particularly relevant for companies operating in multiple markets. When companies utilize a third-party platform, its functionality, access to data fields, and interoperability can be determined by the provider’s configuration and service model.

JA ESS developed the platform internally and hosts it in its own cloud environment. Data policies, access permissions, and future platform updates are managed by the JA ESS internal team. This team ensures compliance with EU regulations regarding data access, presentation, and updates, while also giving JA ESS greater control over data management. The platform can also evolve as regulatory requirements change and real-world applications provide further insights.

JA ESS is the energy storage business unit under the JA brand. As a central component of JA’s energy storage strategy, JA ESS offers a wide range of FTM and BTM applications with safe, efficient, intelligent, and customized solutions for the large-scale, commercial, and industrial sectors as well as the residential market.

#5651. Every Car Brand Has To Install Seat Belts, But Wearing Them Still Isn't Universally Mandated

Buckling a seat belt is second nature, or it should be. Once the car door is closed, next comes that click of confirmation. But safety belts were introduced long, long, long after 1769, when the first car ever made came into existence. Not that seat belts were an afterthought; they simply weren't thought of at all. Not for cars, anyway.

Early iterations of the seat belt were developed in the 19th century and intended for aircraft. Seat belts weren't added to consumer cars until 1949, when Wisconsin-based Nash Motors Company introduced them. Still, not until 1968 were seat belts federally mandated for every seating position in passenger cars. This standard was later amended to include buses and trucks; however, this was merely a manufacturing requirement. Actual seat belt usage and enforcement were left to the states. Because of this, there remains one state that doesn't require adults to wear a seat belt: New Hampshire.

In 1984, New York became the first state to make seat belt use mandatory. The exceptions were children who, depending on age and weight, are to be secured either in a child safety seat or booster. Keep in mind that Volvo, the maven of automotive safety, introduced the three-point seat belt in 1959. Despite evidence showing seat belts not only minimize injuries but also save lives, automotive safety systems receive plenty of pushback, at least initially.

Following New York's lead, other states enacted seat belt laws throughout the '80s and '90s. Maine was the last state to make seat belt use required, putting its law into effect in late 1995. In the decades since, New Hampshire has remained a holdout, though its nonchalance toward seat belts is strictly an adult matter, to be fair.

All other states and the District of Columbia require front-seat occupants to buckle up. For backseat passengers, only 34 states and D.C. say it's a must. And kids being kids have different rules entirely. Some states necessitate seat belt use for front occupants only. Others require that each person be clicked in, regardless of seat location. For children, because standard seat belts cannot properly restrain them during a crash, we've got car seats, booster seats, and other safety equipment to consider.

The rules in New Hampshire do account for minors, requiring occupants younger than 18, including teen drivers, to be properly fastened. There are exceptions, though. Children don't need to be buckled if they're riding in a vehicle built before 1968 (or in a bus or taxi), have a physical condition that prevents seat belt use, or fall under certain special-education conditions. Everyone else? They take the state's motto of "Live Free or Die" to heart.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, seat belts reduce serious injuries and deaths by about 50%, and saved nearly 15,000 lives in 2017. Before seat belt use became law, only 14% of people wore them. Usage increased to 59% within a decade. In 2025, 92% of drivers and 90% of front-seat passengers buckled up, according to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety. But in New Hampshire, less than 80% of travelers bother to buckle.

New Hampshire authorities are aware of this less-than-stellar safety record. The New Hampshire Office of Highway Safety (NHOHS) promotes "Join the NH Clique," which coincides with NHTSA's nationwide Click It or Ticket seat belt enforcement campaign. Law enforcement takes a no-excuses approach during the program, but they might as well be yelling at clouds from their front porch because it achieves the same effect. After all, police can't write tickets when a law hasn't been broken.

The state legislature has tried multiple times to introduce bills requiring seat belts for all, but every effort failed. A 2023 attempt was even soft-pitched as a secondary offense. Had the bill passed, actual usage would have depended on whether seat belt violations were treated as primary or secondary offenses. As of November 2026, just 35 states and D.C. have primary enforcement laws, and numbers support that reasoning. Nevertheless, whether old-timey lap belts or innovative multi-adaptive safety belts (another Volvo invention), no amount of safety tech matters unless people are compelled to wear them.

The National Safety Council (NSC) compiled NHTSA data from 2024 that showed seat belt usage at 91.2%, yet unbuckled occupants accounted for 48.4% of passenger vehicle deaths. Among 21- to 34-year-olds, about 60% of occupants killed weren't buckled. The NSC notes that in California — where seat belt use is a primary-enforced law for everyone aged 16 and up – observed usage in the front seats was 97.5% and unrestrained occupants accounted for 43% of occupant deaths. North Dakota, which only switched to primary enforcement in 2023, saw 79.8% usage while unbelted occupants accounted for 53% of deaths. The statistics from New Hampshire are more somber, showing only 78.2% wear their belts, while unbelted occupants accounted for 59% of deaths.

#5647. The Legendary 1987 RUF CTR 'Yellowbird' Looks Like A Porsche, But It Isn't

Take a quick look at that yellow beast in our top photo, with its bulging muscular fenders, curved profile, and massive whale tail spoiler. Now, you could easily be forgiven for thinking it was a Porsche — perhaps a late-1980s 911 Carrera 3.2. You'd be wrong, however. That machine is actually a Ruf CTR, which was nicknamed the Yellowbird for its striking exterior finish.

There are a couple of dead giveaways, too, including the fact that the Yellowbird could outrun any real production Porsches of the time. In fact, a Ruf CTR beat all challengers at a famed 1987 Road & Track comparison of the fastest cars in the world: Its 211-mph top speed was 10 mph faster than the second-place car, which was a modified Porsche, while entries like the AMG Hammer, Ferrari Testarossa, Lamborghini Countach, and Porsche 959 all failed to reach 200 mph. Unsurprisingly, the CTR was also named one of our readers' favorite yellow cars of all time.

Of course, peeking under the skin of the Yellowbird tells the tale. Keep in mind that Ruf is much more than just a tuning shop or an in-house performance brand, like Mercedes' AMG was and now is. Ruf uses so many proprietary components — and so few from production Porsche models — that it was certified as a full-on automaker back in 1981. Ruf cars even have different W09 VINs from Porsche's WP0 vehicle identification numbers. The genesis, though, actually does start with a Mercedes-Benz — well, that and a Porsche 356.

The company now known as Ruf — pronounced roof – began when Alois Ruf Sr. opened his first repair shop in Pfaffenhausen, Germany, in 1939. Ruf and the shop would both survive World War II, and in the 1950s, he expanded into building his own tour bus — on a chassis originally sourced from Mercedes-Benz.

It was in 1963, when Ruf was at the wheel of his bus, that he happened to see a driver lose control of his Porsche 356 and run off the road. Ruf then played a key role in bringing both back to health: He drove the Porsche's owner to the hospital and — after buying it off of the insurer — took the car itself back to his shop to fix. That began a lifelong romance between the Rufs and rear-engined Porsches, and one that carried over to the launch of the 911. Today, 911s like the Carrera GTS T-Hybrid are still out there making the haters look real dumb.

We're going to skip a lot of steps in a pretty fascinating story, but Alois Jr. took over for his father in 1974 after the latter died. Under Alois Jr.'s direction, and in response to rumors Porsche would kill off the 911 after introducing the front-engine 928, the company committed itself to supporting the 911 even if Porsche didn't. The first Ruf-tuned 911, the Turbo 3.3, premiered in 1977 with a Ruf-built 5-speed manual transmission. However, legal worries soon reared their ugly heads. Porsche, naturally, wasn't too keen on being liable for what Ruf did to its cars, so Ruf would go on to officially become an independent automaker in 1981.

Yet, the car that really put Ruf on the map was the 1987 CTR, with a name derived from "Group C Turbo Ruf." The car started life as a 930-series 911 Carrera with a 3.2-liter flat-six engine, which was already one of the lightest models on the Porsche roster — it just wasn't light enough for Ruf. The company swapped out the production doors, engine cover, and bumpers to save more poundage. The car even has just one sideview mirror. The rear fenders also were reworked, with flares to handle its upsized tire/wheel package and NACA ducts for engine cooling.

Ruf increased the bore of the Carrera's donor engine as well, boosting displacement to 3.4 liters. Remember, bore and stroke are the two specs that decide an engine's power. Next up were twin-turbochargers custom made for the Yellowbird and Bosch fuel injectors to slake the motor's thirst. The result was 469 horsepower and 408 pound-feet of torque. The 1987 Porsche 959, for some perspective, came out with a twin-turbo 2.8-liter flat-six factory rated for 444 horsepower and 369 pound-feet of torque.

The differences were even more noticeable on the track, as mentioned above. We'll also add that while the 959 was a tenth quicker to 60, at 3.6 seconds, the CTR could keep on going to reach 100 mph in 7.3 seconds. That's 1.5 seconds quicker than the 959. But if you really want to get a feel for what the Yellowbird was all about, be sure to check out Weissach Group's video of Ruf driver Stefan Roser running one at Nürburgring in 1989. It's downright fascinating.

#5646. Is There Any Point In Upgrading Exhaust Tips Beyond Appearance?

Exhaust tips are the most visible parts of a car's exhaust system, making them a worthwhile option if you want to personalize your ride without spending a big chunk of cash on a complete aftermarket exhaust setup — especially if you don't want to risk voiding your warranty and ruining the mental peace of your neighbors. Available in different shapes, sizes, materials, and finishes, aftermarket exhaust tips can lend a sportier or more premium appearance to the car they're fitted to.

That said, some believe that in addition to the aesthetic uplift, aftermarket tips can produce a deeper or louder exhaust note, help direct hot exhaust gases away from the rear bumper, and even improve your car's performance by reducing backpressure. What's fact, what's fiction, and do these benefits justify upgrading your car's factory exhaust tips?

The short answer is that aftermarket exhaust tips can offer some practical advantages, but they have next to no impact on performance and only a subtle effect on sound, at best. To understand what you gain from replacing them, it is important to distinguish between the exhaust tip and the components that actually determine how an exhaust system works.

Unlike the muffler, resonator, or catalytic converter, the exhaust tip doesn't really play a big role in controlling exhaust noise, emissions, or gas flow through your car's exhaust system. Its primary purpose is to finish the exhaust outlet, which is why aftermarket tips are available in several designs. These include straight-cut, angle-cut, rolled-edge, dual-exit, turndown, resonated, and dual-wall tips. Owners can also choose between finishes like polished stainless steel, chrome, matte black, and carbonfiber-like materials. Most aftermarket exhaust tips are pretty straightforward to install, with clamp-on and slip-on designs that directly attach to the existing tailpipe.

There can be a minor change in exhaust sound, depending on the tip's diameter, length, shape, and the material used. A larger outlet may produce a somewhat deeper tone, while a longer tip can make your exhaust sound a little bit softer. A turndown tip directs exhaust gases and sound toward the ground, whereas a resonated tip can help reduce raspiness. To sum up, don't expect an aftermarket exhaust tip to make your daily-driver Toyota Camry sound like a V8-powered Lexus RC F.

One possible practical upside to an aftermarket exhaust tip is that it can help direct hot exhaust gases away from the bumper and surrounding body panels, and reduce soot accumulation around the outlet (particularly if you drive a diesel car), provided it is correctly sized and positioned. Stainless steel tips can additionally offer better rust resistance than some factory exhaust tips.

Despite what the marketing for some aftermarket exhaust tips may suggest, using them does not deliver a noticeable increase in power, torque, or overall performance. A common misconception is that a larger-diameter tip reduces exhaust backpressure, reducing the strain on the engine and thereby producing more power. However, since the tip is only the final outlet of the exhaust system, it has no effect on the system's overall flow characteristics. The diameter, length, and layout of the exhaust pipes, along with the design of the catalytic converter, muffler, and resonator, have a much greater impact.

If you're looking for more noticeable changes in sound or performance, your best bet is to upgrade other components of the exhaust system. A performance muffler can deliver a more aggressive exhaust note and reduce backpressure, while an aftermarket resonator can give you finer control over sound. A cat-back exhaust system replaces the components from the catalytic converter to the tailpipe and can also offer a substantial change in sound and performance by dialing up the exhaust flow. Upgraded headers and high-flow catalytic converters are a couple more viable options to get a more aggressive exhaust note and boost performance.

That said, these modifications are considerably more expensive than an aftermarket exhaust tip, and may affect emissions compliance and noise levels, possibly even put you in trouble with the law. On the other hand, an exhaust tip is relatively cheap (prices start at around $20) and easy to install, and worth the effort if you want a better-looking rear end, a more durable exhaust outlet, or a minor change in sound. Just don't expect it to deliver the performance and aural benefits of a proper aftermarket exhaust system.

#5644. Payer mix, non-labor expenses dragged hospital margins in September

Payer mix, non-labor expenses dragged hospital margins in September" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hospitals’ operations took another dip in September amid a slew of ongoing headwinds including weakened payer mix and rising costs, healthcare advisory firm Kaufman Hall reported alongside warnings of a “historically large portion” of the nation’s hospitals running on negative or near-zero operating margins.

The firm’s latest monthly benchmark report, released Tuesday, showed a calendar year-to-date operating margin index of 1.4% and a single-month operating margin index of 2.4% in September, the latter of which was a decline from August’s 3.0% operating margin (all including health system allocations for shared services costs).

The performance decline wasn’t for want of patients. Daily discharges and adjusted discharges both rose 3% from August to September, and are generally above the numbers from last year. Operating room minutes per calendar day also rose 6% from August—an encouraging sign for hospitals whose surgical slowdowns had hamstrung acuity—but remain 1% below September of last year.

The increased foot traffic also grew revenues, with daily net operating revenue rising 4% from August and 6% year over year while gross operating revenue rose 4% month to month and 8% year over year. Much of the increase came on the outpatient side, where daily revenue increased 5% from August and 10% compared to September 2025. Net patient service revenue per adjusted discharge was more mixed, rising 2% from August but remaining 1% below September 2025.

However, hospitals’ margins are being challenged by persistent bad debt and charity care burdens, Kaufman Hall’s data show. Daily bad debt and charity care may have remained flat from August, but is 17% higher than September 2025 and 16% higher when comparing both years’ first nine months. As a percentage of gross operating revenue, they’re 6% higher than Sept. 2025 and 8% higher year to date.

On the spending side, daily total expense rose 3% from August and is 5% higher than September 2025, primarily reflecting the heightened volumes even as hospitals held their average length of stay flat month over month or 1% shorter year over year. The expenses were more pronounced on the non-labor side, where increases on a per adjusted discharge basis were higher than labor’s per adjusted discharge decline.

"Hospitals continue to operate in an environment marked by significant financial variability," Erik Swanson, managing director and Data and Analytics group leader at Kaufman Hall, said in a release. “Many organizations continue to face mounting pressure from uncompensated care and rising expenses, underscoring the importance of proactive operational and financial strategies that build long-term resilience."

Another amplifying market trend is the “bifurcation of hospital performance” often highlighted by the firm and others that monitor multi-organization financial trends, such as credit rating agencies.

"The margin gap between higher and lower-performing hospitals has widened to 19 percentage points, with a historically large portion of hospitals operating at negative or very thin margins,” the report reads. “Even slight revenue reductions threaten organizations, which face increasingly difficult decisions on future operations, care delivery, and expense control.”

The firm encouraged hospitals to take “deliberate, proactive steps” to strengthen their financial situations, particularly as macro reimbursement trends stiffen and the site of care delivery shifts from the hospital to outpatient settings.

Kaufman Hall’s hospital reports pull data from more than 1,300 nationwide hospitals as collected by parent company Strata Decision Technology.

Accompanying the monthly hospital benchmark was also Kaufman Hall’s quarterly numbers on more than 200,000 employed physicians and advanced practice providers, which painted a much rosier picture for health system and hospital employers.

It showed, for the first time in five years of data collection, that healthcare employers’ investment/subsidy per provider and per physician has declined year over year (by 1%), and “across every cohort, including primary care, medical specialty, surgical specialty and hospital-based specialty.”

Kaufman Hall attributed the rare turnaround to revenue growth and sustained productivity increases that together outpaced expenses.

"Medical groups made meaningful performance improvements this quarter, achieving gains in revenue, productivity and thoughtful workforce management," Matthew Bates, managing director and Physician Enterprise Service Line leader at Kaufman Hall, said in a release. "The growing utilization of [advanced practice providers] and ongoing focus on operational and team effectiveness are helping organizations manage financial pressures while increasing access to care.”

#5642. 'Grand Slam' Pancreatic Cancer Drug Shows Promise as First-Line Treatment

— Response rate with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy was 61% in early-stage trial

The first-in-class RAS inhibitor daraxonrasib (Rasonque) in combination with chemotherapy showed promise as a first-line treatment for patients with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC), according to results from an early-stage trial.

Among 61 patients, the confirmed objective response rate with daraxonrasib plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel (Abraxane) was 61% (including 8.2% with a complete response), with a median duration of response of 11.1 months, reported Wungki Park, MD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City.

Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 12.8 months, with a 12-month PFS rate of 51.7%. The overall survival (OS) rate at 12 months was 76.6%.

"This represents a potentially transformative advance in first-line treatment for patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer, already outpacing the high end for the historical overall survival of 8.5 to 11.1 months with conventional chemotherapy," Park said in a press release.

He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain.

"These are very encouraging results in a disease where progress has historically been difficult to achieve," said Shivan Sivakumar, PhD, of the University of Birmingham in England, in comments posted to the Science Media Centre website.

"What is particularly exciting is the potential to move beyond chemotherapy as the mainstay of treatment for pancreatic cancer," he added. "By targeting RAS, a fundamental driver of the vast majority of pancreatic cancers, we may be entering an era where molecularly targeted therapies can meaningfully improve outcomes for patients."

However, the findings should be interpreted "carefully" considering this is a relatively small early-stage study without a randomized control group, Sivakumar cautioned. He suggested that if the findings are confirmed in the phase III RASolute 303 trial, "this could represent one of the most significant advances in the first-line treatment of metastatic pancreatic cancer in recent years."

Daraxonrasib, an oral RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibitor targeting GTP-bound mutant and wild-type RAS, doubled OS and PFS in patients with previously treated metastatic PDAC in the phase III RASolute 302 trial. Based on those results, the FDA in August approved the drug for patients who have received at least one prior systemic therapy or who are ineligible for multi-agent systemic therapy, after giving the green light to an expanded access program earlier in the year.

In his presentation, Park noted that current standard-of-care chemotherapy options for the first-line treatment of metastatic PDAC provide limited benefit, with less than half of patients receiving subsequent second-line therapy, "underscoring the need for more effective first-line treatment options."

The RMC-GI-102 platform study is an ongoing phase I/II multicenter trial of patients with RAS-mutant gastrointestinal tumors. The analysis presented here evaluated daraxonrasib and gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel among patients in the metastatic PDAC cohort.

Patients had a median age of 67, and 59% were men. Just over half (54%) had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1, 70% had liver metastases at enrollment, and 57% had stage IV disease at diagnosis.

The patients received 200-mg daraxonrasib, taken orally once a day, plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel given by intravenous injection on days 1 and 15 in 28-day cycles.

Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were observed in 75% of patients, the most common of which were anemia (33%), fatigue (16%), neutrophil count decreases (16%), rash (13%), and diarrhea (11%). Serious TRAEs occurred in 23% of patients.

Dose modifications due to daraxonrasib-related adverse events occurred in 66% of patients (most frequently due to rash), while treatment discontinuation due to daraxonrasib-related adverse events was infrequent, occurring in just 5% of patients.

As Every Electric puts it: “Get paid to plug in.” Alternatively, a customer can buy the batteries for a discounted price through the program of $650 and receive a higher payback per year, up to $250 per battery. Over the 11-year rated lifespan, purchasing the battery could increase the total net payback, although the upfront cost would be a little higher.

It seems almost too simple and convenient for the customer. However, a lot of complex work and coordination is happening behind the scenes. The Jackery battery is in communication with Every Electric, who automates power management to charge when electricity demand is low and discharge to run the air conditioner when electricity demand is high. This kind of active demand response can go far beyond the typical TOU plan to directly mitigate utility demand shifts. Every Electric monitors data for each battery. The demand response of the combined storage across thousands of individual batteries is aggregated and sold to the utility, in this case Con Edison. Then the benefits are divided up and distributed to customers based on their contributions. Over 2000 batteries were in the initial trial phase, with a larger scale rollout planned next year. I am already on the waitlist, along with over 15,000 other NYC households.

Because it does not feed electricity back into the grid, implementation is much simpler. No electrician needed. The system monitors the amount of energy being stored and deployed at the point of use with no need for user intervention. Unlike traditional demand response that turns off appliances, there is no inconvenience to the user. Thermostats do not need to be adjusted. Smart appliances are not needed. The battery simply provides power when grid demand is high, shaving off the peaks.

You may still be asking “what’s the catch?” Currently, the system needs to coordinate a large number of relatively small batteries under the same utility to have enough combined capacity to sell to the utility. To start, it is only being offered in New York City, which sets the blueprint. In the initial application, the batteries will be used with 120V air conditioners, up to around 12,000 BTU. This is a common size for NYC apartments, letting one battery size serve a wide range of customers, simplifying initial rollout. It also offers clear return on investment based on how much electricity is used, when that electricity is used and when demand peaks for the utility. However, I wouldn’t expect it to stop there.

The batteries being used are led by the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. This battery has 2042 Wh of capacity and up to 2200 W of output with 4400 W of surge power. A total of three outlets are on the front panel, as well as two USB-C and a USB-A port. Due to the UPS function, the portable power station adds protection and would be ideal to plug in a computer or sensitive electronics, in addition to the air conditioner. Although the VPP is based on air conditioner use, using all the outlets can potentially add to the amount of load shifted by the VPP and, as a result, increase the amount of payback for the customer. Plugging in other forms of energy consumption could also extend the benefit beyond the times of year when the air conditioner is being used.

At 40% smaller and 34% lighter than the previous generation model, the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 weighs 39.5 lb. That’s less than a 5-gallon water cooler bottle but less bulky to carry. Due to the plug and play nature, people changing apartments within the city can easily take it with them at 13.2” x 10.4” x 11.5”. Multiple levels of safety protections and a ruggedized portable design using automotive-grade LFP batteries ensure safe operation even if apartment occupants bump into it.

That portability also contributes to the emergency preparedness capability of the battery. For the months of the year when the air conditioning isn’t running, the battery could provide backup power for a refrigerator in a power outage, for example. Of course, Jackery also offers batteries specifically for refrigerators. Those batteries are not a part of the initial program… yet.

This also gets to a limitation of the current program. To keep the program manageable as it scales up, only one size of battery in one use case is initially being offered. Right now, the biggest challenge is scaling up. Making it too complicated at the start would make scaling up more difficult. However, once the program reaches scale, more options can become available. Jackery also offers batteries with greater aesthetic appeal, like the slim FridgeGuard, which may be a better fit for the homes of some customers. As the program scales up, the applications have the potential to diversify.

Much of RE+ focused on supplying power and storage for data centers. While residential clean energy tax credits (25D) have been cut, data centers can still benefit from the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit that can add up with bonuses to cover half the cost of the project. With additional state and federal incentives piled on top, the majority of the cost of data center ESS can be covered by subsidies. With the heavily subsidized storage and large-scale contracts with the utility, data centers can access benefits not typically available to residential customers.

However, the plug-in VPP changes the energy storage dynamic. People get credit for energy storage deployment at the point of use. AI technology, rather than just being a consumer of resources, is being used to automate the VPP system and let the benefits flow to more families. By starting with small window air conditioners, the system also tends to provide relief to people living in typically older apartments, rather than the sleek new high rises with multi-million-dollar apartments.

There is no need for home electrical upgrades. In fact, by taking some of the load off the circuit, the potential for my wife to trip the breaker from ironing in the living room while the TV and air conditioner are running on the same breaker is reduced. As the energy monitoring comes directly from the battery, it also isn’t dependent on smart meters.

For the system to have enough total capacity to sell to the utility, the plug-in VPP needs to connect thousands of batteries to provide multiple MWh of storage. This scale can easily be accomplished in urban areas. In addition, the value of the system will heavily depend on the local price of electricity and the variability in price. In NYC, electricity is significantly more expensive than in most of the US.

New York City apartments are a perfect starting place. While apartments tend to be far more energy efficient than detached houses and have lower net emissions overall, many of us living in apartments have traditionally felt a bit left out on clean tech. We don’t have roofs for rooftop panels. We typically do not have attached garages to place large permanent batteries or access to modify the electrical panel. If we do have the ability to make electrical modifications to the apartment, they can be prohibitively expensive in NYC. As such, a plug-in VPP is an exciting development for those of us living in apartments.

A plug-in VPP also makes the benefits of battery energy storage more accessible to urban areas. Often, there is not room for container-sized batteries. In places like New York City, the fire regulations are so strict, and the permitting is so complicated that large-scale BESS becomes exceedingly difficult to execute. Large-scale BESS, if approved, could take years to deploy.

According to NREL, the national average full installed price of utility scale BESS was $334/kWh of capacity in 2024, with hardware making up roughly two thirds of the total. However, the cost would undoubtedly be higher in NYC. For comparison, the discounted Explorer 2000 v2 in this program (which avoids retail markup) comes in at $318.32/kWh, with no added permitting or installation cost. That is also significantly less than the installed cost of many home batteries used in traditional VPPs, like Tesla Powerwall. Once delivered, it can be online within minutes.

Currently, plug-in VPP is the fastest, easiest and least expensive way to add battery capacity that shaves peak demand on urban grids in the US.

As high draw usage like air conditioning increases, more stress is placed on the grid. Transformer and other electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure upgrades can be expensive. Having storage at the point of use reduces the amount of electricity that needs to flow through the grid during peak periods. As plug-in VPP is deployed more broadly, the benefits will be experienced more broadly. And CO2 emissions can drop in the process.

While the benefits of the program are already attractive, the initial program may just be the tip of the iceberg. In New York City, buildings over 25,000 square feet must reduce their greenhouse gas emissions under Local Law 97 (LL97). This includes many apartment complexes and offices. The deployment of batteries at the point of use has the potential to reduce emissions.

While the current batteries and air conditioners in the program are 120V, Jackery also makes batteries that are 240V. For appliances that have intermittent use but high draw, like heat pumps, hot water heaters, ranges, etc., 240V connections are often needed to provide the necessary power. The electrification of applications that were previously run on gas or fuel oil can greatly reduce building emissions. But many apartment buildings do not have 240V outlets available. However, larger Jackery models can charge on 120V, accumulate charge and discharge at 240V for intermittent use. There is potential for batteries to support the higher voltage electrification without expensive electrical upgrades while also providing VPP benefit. The math would have to work out and it hasn’t happened yet. But the potential is clearly there.

Overall, the potential applications for this approach are massive. Already, I can see the potential to transform energy storage in NYC. In talking with Jackery and Every Electric, I started thinking about where the technology could go from here. Plug-in VPP could apply far beyond just New York City. However, that is for a follow-up article.

Larry lives in Queens, NY, with his wife and cats. While he has spent much of his professional career leading global marketing efforts, his passions focus on clean technology and the automotive industry. He believes in Green Free Trade and the potential for the application of engineering talent to create solutions to the world’s most challenging problems.

#5640. HLTH 2026 Daily Tracker: F1 mania takes over HLTH; Why DJ Steve Aoki is investing in innovative science

HLTH 2026 Daily Tracker: F1 mania takes over HLTH; Why DJ Steve Aoki is investing in innovative science" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Fierce Healthcare team is on the ground at HLTH 2026. Stick with this news tracker to catch all the highlights from the show floor, and click here for additional coverage from the conference.

DJ and music producer Steve Aoki told the HLTH audience that his father's passing was the catalyst for his interest in healthcare.

Learning more about what caused his death, and if it could have been prevented, drew him to the impacts of dementia and cancer. And in exploring that, he said he decided he wanted to invest in the people who are pursuing the "science fiction concepts" in healthcare, and support cutting edge innovation.

Aoki said that his celebrity status made it easier to get into a room with people leading the charge on innovation, and learn as much as he could.

"I was just as intrigued as working with a big artist in the studio or playing a big show," he said.

It was with that learning that he established Aoki Foundation, an organization he said is dedicated to bringing back the science and investing in what's next.

"People are excited about science fiction, about the possibility of doing things that are impossible," Aoki said. "And I feel like the superheroes of our time are like right right in our midst, and it's about it's about highlighting their journey and giving them a spotlight."

It’s been several weeks since Doximity integrated Wolters Kluwer Health’s UpToDate into its AI clinical decision support tool.

Doximity VP of Clinical AI Partnerships Kamal Menghrajani, M.D., told Fierce Healthcare at HLTH said the integration gives her “a little bit more confidence” in her own practice.

“Now I can use UpToDate to supplement and feel like what I'm doing at the point of care really is the best thing for the patient,” she said.

Menghrajani, who previously served as assistant director for cancer innovation and public health at the White House, took on the role with Doximity approximately four months ago.

“[I get to] be the physician voice and represent the interests of doctors within the company,” she said. “And think about what it looks like to actually take the tools we're building and serve doctors better.”

Menghrajani said the rapid expansion of the company’s AI suite has been a key takeaway, adding that a focus for the company is what physicians want out of AI. “I've seen Doximity evolve to meet all of those needs,” Menghrajani said.

As a range of AI tools saturate the industry, Menghrajani said the biggest use she has seen amongst clinicians is ambient scribes. “I think that has been a real game changer in terms of actual practice,” she said.

On the HLTH show floor, you may have noticed a theme.

Las Vegas is abuzz with the upcoming Formula 1 race, which is taking place on Saturday, Nov. 21. The city has been preparing for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, which is on the Strip, for weeks, and HLTH is taking place at one of the hubs for F1 excitement, The Venetian.

So at this year's conference, each of the stages is themed around racing: the Velocity Stage, the Ferrari Stage, the Monacco Stage. And each breakout track is referred to as a "circuit." In the conference livery, HLTH mascot Petunia is show driving a race car.

Activations on the show floor also play into the F1 theme. A racing simulation game is set up for attendees near the Pharma Force stage, and swag giveaways allude to the race.

Panelists at a HLTH session discussing the uptake of ICHRA — scratch that, CHOICE — faced a challenge around the nomenclature.

Individual coverage health reimbursement arrangements, or ICHRAs, represent a growing area of interest for employers and insurers participating in the individual market. But on Sept. 3, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that it would instead refer to these models as CHOICE, which stands for Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense.

In these models, an employer offers enrollees a stipend to purchase coverage on the individual market rather than securing a traditional employer-sponsored plan. ICHRA (or CHOICE) has gained traction with employers that may otherwise struggle to offer health coverage.

Moderator Joseph Mercer, senior managing director at Marwood Group, joked that the panelists had all agreed to call these plans CHOICE rather than ICHRA. But throughout the session, slip-ups drew a chuckle.

Even the panel's title made reference to the evolution of the name: "The ICHRA (CHOICE) Debate."

Healthcare platform Simple HealthKit announced Tuesday a partnership with Waters Corporation to expand access to at-home cervical cancer screening.

The collaboration aims to expand access to BD’s Onclarity HPV Self-Collection Kit, which is tested with the BD Onclarity HPV Assay  and Simple HealthKit's artificial intelligence-powered direct-to-patient-provider platform.

"We envision a future where personalized, world-class healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of where they live,” said Sheena Menezes, Ph.D, Simple HealthKit CEO and co-founder, in a statement. “Our AI-powered direct-to-patient and provider platform brings that vision to life by connecting people with the right education, intelligent personalized engagement, and clinical care at every step.”

Menezes continued, “Through partnerships with innovators like Waters Corporation, we are empowering individuals to take charge of their health while making seamless, personalized care accessible at scale.”

Oura CEO joined Counsel Health CEO and founder Muthu Alagappan Tuesday morning to discuss the wearable company’s recently announced $625 million acquisition of the virtual primary care company.

Hale said Oura selected Counsel as a partner after reviewing the landscape, and “uptake” from customers was “very positive.”

“We started talking seriously about taking that partnership,” Hale said. “And while we had been dating for a while, we thought maybe it was time to get married.”

Hale said the agreement was “really driven” by Oura customers using Counsel in “really novel and interesting ways.”

Alagappan said one of the most exciting aspects of the partnership is the potential impact of AI-fueled access to physicians on preventive care, adding the daily engagement of wearing Oura rings struck him.

“The buy-in from almost all users is tremendous, and so you enable primary care with the thing that has always been missing, which is engagement,” he said. “And now we have a way to incentivize, motivate patients to make the changes that actually prevent disease, alongside the screenings and lab tests that are also very important.”

During a Monday fireside chat, CMS Deputy Administrator and Chief Product Officer Amy Gleason said HHS and OCR colleagues “have done an amazing job” at looking at the issue to “remove friction from the patient experience.”

Gleason said there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a “personal health app,” identity verification and speed. “It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also says that this information is free to the patient,” she said.

Throughout the session with Zus Health CEO and co-founder Jonathan Bush, Gleason also touted the agency’s voluntary CMS Health Tech Ecosystem initiative.

“The idea of this was to stop waiting on regulation, like healthcare does for some reason, and to just charge forward and get the technology and people that are willing to go faster to work on it,” Gleason said. “And we set up a bunch of different technology working groups that are really about taking the friction out of the system.”

Evvy CEO and co-founder Priyanka Jain spoke with Fierce Healthcare Monday about research gaps in women’s health and how her company looks to bridge them through vaginal microbiome testing.

Jain said women were excluded from medical research from 1977 to 1993 after a drug being prescribed off-label for morning sickness was causing birth defects, adding the ramifications ar still being seen today.

“Women to this day are diagnosed on average four years later than men across over 700 diseases,” Jain said. “And it's hard to not point right back to the fact that we didn't study women until 1993.”

To bridge these gaps, Evvy offers an at-home vaginal health test with clinician-reviewed results and personalized treatment plans. “If we've essentially never studied women, then there must be so many biomarkers in the female body that we under leverage in our definition of health and disease, and so that's our focus,” Jain said.

Jain added Evvy uses AI and precision medicine to “actually predict the right treatment programs” for each patient using the biomarkers.

And, Jain said women’s health needs attention, awareness and funding when asked about recent Trump administration initiatives to focus on women’s health.

“I’m really excited to see the attention and awareness that has been happening,” Jain said. “But now we need to actually move dollars.”

Department of Health and Human Services Chief Counselor Chris Klomp said the administration is focused on bringing in top tech talent as it looks to make the massive, but aging, government insurance system work better.

Klomp spoke on a panel Monday morning at HLTH, where he discussed the challenges in harvesting the data necessary to transform Medicare, Medicaid and other key government programs. Klomp was recently nominated to serve as Deputy Secretary at HHS and is a rising star in the White House.

He said that technology can play a critical role in accelerate processes that have been historically inefficient and time consuming. At the Food and Drug Administration, for example, tech is hastening the process of developing drugs and making approvals, a timeline that previously taken a decade or more.

But embracing technology in this way isn't compromising safety for these medications, Klomp said.

In addition, he said the administration is leaning on the personal nature of healthcare to bring in workers with the tech know-how necessary to drive critical advancements and change.

"Most people don't care about healthcare unless you work in it," he said. "People also start to care about healthcare when you lose your health, or someone you love loses their health. And than it quickly becomes the most important thing to you."

"We're using that as an opportunity to drive requirement, drive amazing talent," Klomp said.

Houston Methodist announced Monday it has expanded its advanced inpatient monitoring care to include rural hospitals throughout Kansas.

Participating hospitals will provide patients with Medtronic’s BioButton, which continuously monitors vital signs, while the Houston Methodist remote monitoring team will review the data and work with bedside nurses.

The vital monitoring devices are used at all eight acute-care hospitals in the Houston Methodist system, across more than 2,500 inpatient beds, according to the Nov. 11 announcement.

“Innovation is most meaningful when we identify patient needs, take what works or doesn't work and find new ways to extend the positive impact,” said Sara Loewy, Houston Methodist virtual care vice president, in a statement. “What we’ve built in Houston has the potential to reach much further. By thoughtfully extending this model into new care settings, our goal with this program is to demonstrate how our system’s existing technology and clinical expertise can strengthen access and improve outcomes in rural communities.”

Loewy added the expansion is an opportunity to “explore how the capabilities of a major health system can be shared across geographic boundaries.”

While 72% of health tech startups lead with “AI-powered” in their descriptors, zero surveyed venture capitalists in a new report from HLTH and SolComms said the phrase increased their confidence.

Independently surveyed health tech reporters also ranked “AI-powered” as one of the most overused phrases in pitching–in addition to “revolutionizing/transforming” and “disrupting.”

Alongside these survey responses, researchers compared–and scored–the messaging of 72 U.S.-based, venture-backed health tech startups at series A to series C for the “Healthtech Attention Economy Report.” Startups’ messaging across their website and social media was scored on four main dimensions: clarity, differentiation, proof and policy awareness.

SolComms Vice President of HealthTech Isabella Morreale said in a statement the companies that will get attention within the next year “are leading with proof, not adjectives.”

“That means speaking to clinical data, measurable outcomes, and validation from third parties,” Morreale said. “Founder-led storytelling will also continue to stand out. Among the data, one common through-thread for investor and reporter interest was founders with a real point of view on the industry.”

Morreale continued, “Reporters don't need another company description; they need a source who can help them explain what's happening in healthcare.”

Less than half (42.2%) of patients say communications from healthcare providers “often” or “always” feel relevant to their needs, a new report from Lirio found.

Analysts at the behavioral science and AI-powered behavioral intelligence platform polled 1,500 adults across the U.S. for the survey. While 58% of respondents report communications not consistently feeling relevant to their needs, 55.6% rate overall communication experiences with healthcare organizations as “good” or “excellent.”

When asked why healthcare communications are ignored altogether, respondents report generic or irrelevant content (24.4%), too many similar messages (21.8%) and confusing, jargon-filled messages (18.8%) as top reasons.

Nearly half of respondents (47.9%) report the potential value of more personalized, better-timed messages as an “8, 9 or 10” for how much it could help them make better care decisions and stay engaged.

Lirio Chief Behavioral Officer Amy Bucher, Ph.D., said in a statement patients “are not rejecting healthcare communications outright.”

“They are telling us, in specific and measurable terms, that the system is talking at them instead of to them,” Bucher said. "The instinct in healthcare has long been to solve engagement with more outreach - more emails, more reminders, more portals. This data shows that volume is not the problem. What is missing is relevance — content and timing designed for where a specific patient is in their own health journey, rather than a single message broadcast to an entire population.”

Bucher added the healthcare organizations that close the communication gap will be “the ones that use behavioral data to determine the right message, the right channel, and the right moment for each individual patient, which is the model Lirio was built to deliver."

Community-based specialty palliative care provider Vynca is expanding its reach into four more states.

Patients will now be able to access Vynca’s services in Georgia, Hawaii, New Jersey and Texas. Vynca is one of the first practices approved to provide services under New Jersey’s Community-Based Palliative Care Medicaid benefit, launched in April, according to the Nov. 16 announcement.

Founded in 2013, the company’s hybrid care model combines in-home visits with virtual clinical support and predictive technology, and executives say it has shown 43% fewer emergency department visits and 52% less hospital stays within six months of enrollment.

“Health plan and government program leaders understand the value of community-based palliative care for people with serious illness,” said Darren Schulte, M.D., Vynca CEO, in a statement. “Our expansion in four key states reflects growing momentum to expand specialty outpatient palliative care outside of hospices. The key is to broaden access and convenience for the entire eligible population by offering home-based options. Too often, patients are limited to seeking palliative care when available in the community, at hospital-based clinics and facilities.”

#5639. The French Made This Adorably Practical EV, Available In An Array Of Vibrant Colors

As the average new car price hits unrealistic highs, it only furthers the case for affordable vehicles. To provide some respite for desperate consumers, the Slate Truck no one can seem to stop talking about is coming soon in the U.S., and Italy's friendly but limited Fiat Topolino is breaching America's shores as well. The French, too, have come up with their own little practical, affordable utility EV, although this one is not coming to America. It's called La Bagnole. Points to the brand, Kilow, for the name, which translated to English is actually "the car."

At first glance the little EV looks as if a Jeep and kei truck had a dependable, indestructible love child — indestructible simply because it's French. With the unrealistic expectations established in the "Carnage A Trois" episode of "The Grand Tour," where the trio tested the resilience of French cars in the "French way," by association these cars could be impossible to destroy, no?

The beauty of it is, if La Bagnole is a little destructible and breaks, Kilow has designed repairs to be simple. And even the batteries can be fixed, as they house individually replaceable cells.

The tiny tank of an EV truck is built on a steel chassis, with a customizable body. Customers can opt to have a removable roof color-matched to the body or go one further and also add transparent doors. Either choice allows the addition of optional roofbars for extra hauling ability. At the rear, flooring and tailgate can be Kilow's resinated wood fiber, which doesn't require any extra maintenance, while the Okoumé wood option does require the occasional varnishing. It also comes in at an extra 990 euros (about $1,100). If you prefer a more van-like delivery car look, there's a covered tailgate option as well.

Kilow markets La Bagnole as a simple vehicle. There are not a lot of parts to it, including no heating or cooling controls. What you can get is a minimalist dashboard made of the same resinated wood fiber or the Okoumé wood as well, fitted with a screen for battery updates, as well as toggle switches for the horn, wipers, washer fluid, and lights. You can really go all out and get a phone holder so you have your own navigation and tunes at the ready. No need to 3D-print it like you would have to for a Slate Truck.

The vehicle's less simple side comes down to the color choices, of which there are 24. Twelve are solid colors, including quite the array across the rainbow, except for red and purple. Six gradient choices transition between two colors, and then there are the flecked colors reminiscent of a granite countertop, showing up as "Memories" on a page translated from French to English. Match those to steel or alloy rims, and mud guards for a polished look.

Power for La Bagnole is available in three battery capacities and ranges. Unlicensed drivers in France, likely more in city regions, can purchase two kinds of 28 mph batteries. The smaller of them is 6 kWh with a range of 43.5 miles, and the Long Range is a 12 kWh battery good for 102 miles. Licensed drivers can buy a 12 kWh battery with that same 102-mile range, but with a top speed of 50 mph. Charging can be done from a 220V household outlet, which Kilow says will take about three to five hours for a full charge, depending on the size of the battery.

The accessories are fun as well. Avid campers can order a rooftop tent made by Decathlon, as long as you select a hardtop option. And if you about double the price of the tent, you can also get the camping kit complete with essential items like mugs, a coffee maker, stove and cooking pots, with the most attractive additions of the kit being the pressurized cooler, and pressurized shower. For the business-minded folks, you can also get your company logo added to the side panels, tailgate, and even the hardtop.

Each build takes about three months to complete, with prices ranging from 10,800 to 13,690 euros, which also includes the value-added tax (VAT). That's approximately $11,913 to $15,101 in the U.S. Yet as is the case for many fun vehicles made abroad, Americans will not be getting these little trucks as Kilow focuses sales on France and Europe. If we were to ever land these in the future, though, there could certainly be a case for using these utilitarian cuties across a good part of the country.
