#5638. Europe’s Modelled €5.70/kg Hydrogen Faces Industrial Buyers Who Can Afford Far Less

Europe’s industrial hydrogen plans have a buyer problem. A factory cannot make its products competitive by paying whatever a new hydrogen plant needs to recover its investment. Its maximum hydrogen price is set by the cost of making the same product, or delivering the same useful heat, another way.

The central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg. That starts with electricity at €60/MWh and 53 kWh of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen, so the electricity alone costs €3.18/kg. Electrolysers, capital recovery, maintenance, stack replacements, water and other plant costs bring the total to €5.70. Getting hydrogen to a customer can cost more.

At a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel. With 94% heating efficiency, delivering one MWh of useful heat requires roughly 31.9 kg of hydrogen. The fuel bill reaches €182/MWh before the burner, maintenance and other equipment costs. In the model’s central 2050 comparison, suitable direct-electric heating sets a hydrogen price ceiling of €2.07/kg. At that ceiling the same hydrogen heat costs about €66/MWh. The hydrogen production case overshoots the customer’s competitive input price by €3.63/kg.

The mismatch is not a prediction that hydrogen makers will never lower costs. It is the actual commercial test investors should apply before financing supply. Reducing the cost of production from €7 to €5 a kilogram achieves little if the relevant industrial customer can pay €2. Production-cost targets are meaningless without a corresponding market price ceiling.

The International Energy Agency’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 has made customer cost acceptability part of its assessment. Across most sector and region comparisons, the IEA finds maximum acceptable hydrogen prices below US$2/kg without policy support. Some incumbent-steel comparisons yield negative acceptable prices. The IEA examines a 2035 horizon and a different set of competitors; the same buyer-side arithmetic exposes the problem.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment calculates the maximum hydrogen input price for industrial heat, ammonia and ironmaking and compares it with distinct European supply cases. It also links to the underlying European hydrogen research and interactive model.

European ammonia illustrates how demand for a product differs from demand for European-made hydrogen. Ammonia remains necessary for fertilisers and industrial chemicals. The buyer’s real choice is where to produce it. In the central 2050 TFIE model, making qualifying green ammonia inside Europe can compete with imported green ammonia only when its hydrogen input costs roughly €2.62–€4.00/kg, depending on the origin and production route. The €5.70/kg onsite supply case misses those thresholds. Europe can keep consuming ammonia without building every electrolyser locally.

Ironmaking has a similar sourcing decision. The model’s hydrogen input-price ceiling versus qualifying imported hydrogen-reduced or hot-briquetted iron ranges from €2.28 to €4.45/kg. Against a European electrochemical iron process, the central ceiling is approximately €1.43/kg. Where enough suitable scrap can deliver the required steel grade, the hydrogen-based route can lose even at a zero price for hydrogen. Steel quality, industrial integration and the commercial maturity of electrochemical iron matter to those comparisons. They do not entitle a hydrogen supplier to ignore the alternatives.

Hydrogen used as a chemical reagent deserves a different assessment from hydrogen burned for heat. Chemical production may need the molecule. Industrial heating needs temperature, pressure, reliability and useful energy, all of which can be delivered directly from electricity for many applications. Manufacturing hydrogen from electricity and then burning it adds conversion losses and fuel-system costs before the plant receives the heat it needs.

The supply cases have defined boundaries. The central onsite cost is €5.70/kg. A generic delivery allowance takes that case to €6.95/kg. The model’s separately configured hub-and-pipeline case is €5.81/kg. Those are different cost structures, not interchangeable price quotes for the same customer. Even the favourable 2050 case, at €3.46/kg with its specified delivery allowance and €28/MWh electricity, clears some industrial thresholds but still misses others.

Policy can create demand that market prices do not support. Carbon pricing, procurement mandates, subsidies and carbon contracts for difference can raise willingness or obligation to pay. That may be a deliberate industrial or climate choice, but governments should disclose the premium, who will finance it and the contract duration. Describing a regulated purchase as competitive demand hides the cost rather than eliminating it.

The EU energy regulators’ market monitoring points in the same direction. ACER reported 4.2 GW of committed electrolyser capacity in November 2026, including operating plants, projects under construction and those with final investment decisions. Roughly 49% was associated with refining, where renewable-fuel mandates provide a strong demand signal. The remaining industrial sectors face a harder test when policy does not compel the same purchases.

For lenders, the consequence is immediate. A proposed hydrogen plant costing €5/kg has no viable commercial case when its intended industrial buyer can afford €3/kg. A memorandum of understanding cannot close that €2/kg gap. Developers need buyers with enforceable contracts at prices that cover supply costs, lower production costs, or identified support durable enough to finance the difference.

Industrial and public procurement should start with the product the customer must deliver, calculate the best eligible competing route, and determine the maximum hydrogen price that route permits. Only then should investors consider electrolysers, pipelines and capacity targets. Suppliers do not set the market by drawing cheaper future cost curves. Industrial customers set the ceiling.

The full TFIE Briefing and open European hydrogen assessment contain the industrial route comparisons, scenario assumptions and research submitted to the European Commission. The next Briefing examines the competing routes for sourcing green ammonia and iron.

#5637. Insulin Resistance by Age 30 Quite Telling of Future Heart Health

— Metabolic syndrome by age 50 marks next stage of a bad trajectory

Insulin resistance in young adulthood was a predictor of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) years down the line in middle age, according to a CARDIA cohort analysis.

There were more than 3,000 CARDIA participants who remained under observation and free of ASCVD through year 20 (when they were 38-50 years old), with one in four having shown insulin resistance at baseline (at age 18-30), reported a group led by Chuyue Wu, MD, PhD, of the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health in Los Angeles.

With repeated clinical assessments and long-term follow-up, these individuals with insulin resistance in early adulthood had a significantly higher risk of ASCVD events through year 35 of the study, when they were 53-65 years old (risk ratio [RR] 1.50, 95% CI 1.13-2.01).

"These findings have potential implications for early cardiovascular prevention by suggesting that IR [insulin resistance] in young adulthood may signal an adverse CKM [cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic] trajectory before conventional cardiometabolic risk factors become fully established," Wu and colleagues wrote in JACC: Advances.

Of note, fasting insulin is not routinely measured in clinical practice. In the study, insulin resistance was indirectly measured as a Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR) value at or above the 75th percentile (≥2.67) after a 12-hour fast -- which may not exactly correspond to the gold-standard method of using the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp.

The researchers also found that 63.4% of the insulin resistance-later ASCVD relationship was mediated by midlife metabolic syndrome at the year-20 mark (indirect RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.13-1.48).

"The substantial mediation through midlife MetS [metabolic syndrome] further identifies the clustering of abnormalities in adiposity, blood pressure, glucose, and lipids as a potentially important intermediate stage linking early IR to later ASCVD," Wu's group suggested. "These findings highlight midlife MetS as an important marker of adverse CKM progression among individuals with IR earlier in adulthood."

Study authors acknowledged that they had not tried to account for changes in metabolic syndrome status and its individual components before or after year 20. Residual confounding is also possible given the study's observational nature.

"Although the findings support closer cardiometabolic surveillance among young adults with IR, further research is needed to determine whether HOMA-IR improves risk prediction beyond routinely measured clinical factors, develop practical approaches for identifying IR when fasting insulin is unavailable, and test whether preventing or delaying progression to MetS reduces subsequent ASCVD risk," Wu and colleagues urged.

One interpretation of the results is that "insulin resistance may represent an early signal of an adverse cardiometabolic trajectory, whereas MetS may mark a subsequent stage of risk-factor clustering," according to an accompanying editorial by Amier Haidar, MD, MPH, of McGovern Medical School, University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, and Leonardo Roever, MHS, PhD, of the Brazilian Evidence-Based Health Network in Uberlândia, Brazil.

"For current practice, the most important implication is therefore not a new laboratory test. It is a new sense of urgency," the duo stressed. "A young adult with progressively increasing abdominal adiposity, worsening blood pressure, rising triglycerides, and deteriorating glycemic measures should not need to accumulate multiple abnormalities before clinicians recognize the direction of travel."

"Young adulthood represents a particularly important and underused window for prevention," the duo asserted. "Young adulthood is therefore not a cardiovascular waiting room; it is a period when cardiometabolic trajectories are being established."

The study included 3,622 participants in CARDIA, a multicenter, population-based, prospective cohort study. Included in this analysis were those who were enrolled in 1985-1986 as young adults (mean age at baseline 25.0 years, 45% men, 47% Black) who remained free of ASCVD through year 20.

A person was deemed to have metabolic syndrome if they met three of these criteria: waist circumference ≥102 cm in men or ≥88 cm in women; triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL; HDL cholesterol <40 mg/dL in men or <50 mg/dL in women; systolic blood pressure ≥130 mm Hg, diastolic blood pressure ≥85 mm Hg, or the use of antihypertensive medication; and fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL or the use of glucose-lowering medication.

Over a median follow-up of 14 years after year 20, 3.9% of participants logged ASCVD events.

#5635. Courts Are Undecided As To Whether Police Need Warrants For Flock Camera Data

The operative word in this story's headline is "undecided." Because whether a police officer needs a warrant to use data obtained via Flock cameras seems to fall across multiple legalistic gray areas that aren't settled law. Funny that our nation's founders didn't anticipate technology that surveils every driver (of course, they didn't anticipate cars, either).

Just for background (if you've been living in some paradise lacking this technology), Flock is a brand of device known as an automated license plate reader, or ALPR. And Flock contracts with law enforcement agencies across the country. Those agencies can opt to share their data with other police departments across a region, state, or the entire United States. In turn, that means police in many jurisdictions can use Flock to track anyone's movements nationally.

In the past we've reported on Flock cameras violating highway safety standards as well as the Fourth Amendment. But the meat of that latter nugget, of cops needing a warrant to obtain Flock camera data — or not needing a warrant — and whether that violates the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, is still up in the air.

In case you're fuzzy on the law, the Fourth Amendment protects all of us against unreasonable searches and seizures. It requires law enforcement to have probable cause (i.e., reason to suspect a crime) in order to pull us over, search our cars, and fine or arrest us. The nub of this debate has  been addressed recently by judges in two states, and they've issued contradictory rulings about this very question: Do police need a warrant or don't they?

Last month, at a federal district court in northern Oklahoma, Judge Sara Hill ruled that a Tulsa sheriff's deputy violated a defendant's Fourth Amendment rights when he used Flock's database to conduct a nationwide search on a Mazda SUV's previous location. The result: Pulling over 50 sightings from ALPRs across the U.S., he could see everywhere the car had been for the past 30 days.

But according to the ruling, the only reason for the officer's initial suspicion was that the Mazda SUV was from California. The officer followed the Mazda, noted a few driving infractions including following another car on the highway too closely, and pulled over the driver, Melissa Kyle. The traffic stop resulted in a search of Kyle's car, which led to Kyle's arrest on a charge of possession of marijuana. However, the charge was thrown out when Hill ruled that the officer's search of Flock data was unlawful and required a warrant. And so any evidence found subsequently was inadmissible.

Just to be clear, the federal court ruling is far more likely to lead to constitutional debate than a lower-level county case in Ohio. Court watchers say Hill's ruling is consistent with how the Supreme Court has declared certain mass-surveillance tech unconstitutional. And it's worth unpacking what happened in Oklahoma, because it illustrates how a police officer — with access to data via Flock — jumped to a conclusion that the judge in that case says violates the Fourth Amendment.

In 2022, we reported that Flock cameras could be used to track people traveling across state lines for abortion services. Then earlier this year 404 Media reported that cops in Texas did exactly that, tracking a woman via ALPR for seeking a legal abortion in another state.

The point of raising that matter is that the police didn't have a warrant for that ALPR search. The officer in Oklahoma also didn't have a warrant to search the movement of a car with California plates. The officer told Kyle that her long trip to and from California, spending only a little time there, had made him dubious about her — something he only knew about via Flock. Judge Hill found that the officer's logic didn't pass the test of reasonable suspicion and that, crucially, he decided to detain Kyle before he discovered that she had marijuana (recreational pot is illegal in Oklahoma).

Judge Hill ruled that the ALPR "... search was not supported by probable cause, and it was done without a warrant in violation of Kyle's Fourth Amendment rights." Hill found that ALPRs constitute "dragnet-style surveillance," and that "it becomes constitutionally problematic when law enforcement can indiscriminately and passively catalog your whereabouts ... and then use that information for any purpose whenever convenient."

We don't know whether Hill's ruling will carry up to higher courts. But this feels like the Fourth Amendment wreaking its own kind of vengeance. Especially because police have used Flock technology to stalk ex-partners, retaliate against police critics, racially profile minorities, and surveil protestors. Not to mention looking stuff up on Flock using search terms like LMAO. We're just journalists, not judges, but LMAO doesn't seem like probable cause. Nor does pulling the travel records of any car with out-of-state plates.

#5634. EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October

High gas prices and a never-ending wave of new BEVs have allowed October to reach 68% EV market share, a new record!

This record achievement is thanks to a significant ICE (internal combustion engine) crash. The overall market dropped 27% year over year (YoY), to around 1.6 million sales. Plugins were down 14% YoY, but pure ICE sales were much worse off, crashing 44% YoY!

Adding 45% BEV share to PHEVs (23% share) meant that in October a record 68% of all cars sold in China had a plug! If this trend continues in the future, the Chinese market will be fully electrified by 2030, and will be 100% BEV before 2035!

This great result pulled the 2026 share up, to 59%, already 5% above the full year result of 2025. BEVs on their own were up to 40% (versus 33% in 2025).

At this pace, I expect the final number for 2026 EV share in China to be above 60%, with BEVs alone north of the 40% mark. And when the largest global automotive market gets this electrified … then the ICE industry is in serious trouble.

The ICE extinction is also visible in the overall ranking. The overall top 10 was fully made by EVs. Again.

Looking at the best sellers in several size categories, the ICE extinction is also quite visible. Although, once again, the C-segment/compact category is the exception, with the only ICE representative showing up there — the Toyota RAV4, in 2nd, behind the leader Nevo Q05 and just ahead of the BYD Dolphin.

Having a quick look at the five size categories, the highlight is the B-segment/subcompact category, which is the hottest segment right now, with three of the top four top sellers in October belonging to this category.

Considering that 56% of the new SUVs launched this year were bigger than 5 meters/197 inches, there is a clear disconnect between what people want (small hatchbacks/crossovers) and what OEMs offer (large SUVs).

Another highlight is the fact that Xiaomi had a gold plus silver win in the full size category, with the BYD Great Tang closing out the podium while the midsize category podium was 100% BYD Group.

Here’s more info and commentary on October’s top selling electric models:

A BYD Dolphin for BYD Seagull money ($10,000). This was Geely’s internal memo to describe the formula for the Geely Xingyuan when developing its star model. With an interesting name — Xingyuan translates as “wishing upon a star” — it seems that Geely had its wish granted. However, the Geely model will have a tough adversary soon, as the new generation Seagull will land with only one goal — to steal the Xingyuan’s best seller status. But while the new Seagull didn’t land, the small Geely scored a record performance in October, with its 50,190 registrations representing a 14% increase YoY. Besides the new BYD Seagull, Geely’s hatchback now has to deal with Leapmotor’s B-segment contenders, the A10 and A05; the new-generation Wuling Bingo; Chery’s new QQ3; and let’s not forget about BYD’s Yuan Up, too.

BYD’s midsize SUV continues to transition into the new generation. Thanks to the ramp-up of the new Ultra body, BYD’s star player was 2nd, scoring 30,772 registrations. Sales were up by 6% compared to the same month last year. The new Ultra generation features lidar and 1,500 kW DC charging, and these two features aren’t even the most impressive aspects of the model! That would be the price. It starts at 152,000 yuan (or $22,000) with the 76 kWh battery, and it goes up to 180,000 yuan (or $26,000) with the 83 kWh battery. For comparison, the Tesla Model Y starts in China at 259,000 yuan ($38,250)…. Expect the Song to experience a second youth from here onwards, and while it is impossible to displace the Tesla Model Y from the runner-up spot, the last place on the podium is doable this year. And maybe higher up in 2027?

BYD’s small crossover continues to surprise, thanks to recently improved specs. BYD’s team player rose to 3rd in October, scoring 28,514 registrations, which was a 44% increase YoY and a new record score. Despite not being the most exciting vehicle to look at, or drive, the truth is that it is surfing the wave of small, affordable EVs better than most, scoring high in value for money with prices starting at $11,000 and higher end versions having BYD’s driver-assistance system. With small vehicles currently having a moment in China, expect the small crossover to show up in the top 5 more regularly.

Things continue to go well for the startup brand, with its new baby A10 now established as the star player in an already strong lineup. Thanks to 27,247 registrations, the small crossover managed another top 5 presence. The model has the usual value-for-money focus of the brand, and a low, low price of 66,000 yuan ($10,000). On top of that, however, the A10 offers something close to a distinct personality, as the design eschews the white product standard design of Leapmotor for something more personal, mostly thanks to the front and back lights and a floating roof effect. With B-segment BEVs now being the hottest category in China, Leapmotor is well prepared to benefit from the subcompact rising tide, thanks to the recent arrival of the A10 small crossover and its sibling, the A05 small hatchback. Talk about perfect timing….

After the SU7 and YU7, Xiaomi has another success on its hands. This big fat SUV — or shall I say SUVs, as the lineup is broken down between the 7-seat N90 and the 5-seat N70 — scored 27,132 registrations in only its second month on the market, pulling it immediately into the overall top 5. Even with the number of competitors growing every passing day, Xiaomi’s new land yachts have been selling like hot cakes, while drying up sales of the competition. Proof of that, is the fact that there were only two full size models in October’s top 20, with the other being … the Xiaomi SU7.

Looking at the rest of the best seller table, there were a number of models hitting record scores, starting with the #8 Nevo Q05 (20,022 units) continuing its success story. The #10 Bestune Xiaoma (17,887 units) benefitted from a recent refresh to score a surprise record score. Could this mean that small city EVs are (finally) seeing the light at the end of the tunnel?

As for the second half of the table, the highlight is the ramp-up of the Xpeng L03, with the attractive looking crossover, which kind of reminds of a mini-Lotus or small Polestar, reaching 13th thanks to 15,653 sales. This EV looks to be the startup’s star model thanks to a competitive price (124,000 RMB) that is half the price of the Tesla Model Y!

Other models with record performances were the #14 MG 4 (15,503 units), with the new generation proving to be much more popular and adaptable to local tastes than the previous one, and the #17 Chery QQ3 EV, which continued its slow climb in the ranking thanks to 14,041 sales, which made it the 5th B-segment model in the top 20.

Still in the top 20, we should also highlight the best selling foreign model, the Tesla Model Y VW ID.Aura T6, the new China-made (and China-developed) German crossover that has allowed Volkswagen to beat the Texans for the first time in years (the Tesla Model Y was down 60% YoY, to 7,807 units, while the Model 3 was down 85%, to 1,010 units). The Aura T6, VW’s take on the Model Y formula, rose to the 20th position in its first full month on the market!

A promising sign, or just hype? Only time will tell, but at least for now, VW seems to be getting some traction on the EV side of the Chinese market, a point also highlighted by the fact that it wasn’t just the Aura T6 getting decent sales. The also new VW ID.Era 5S (think Chinese VW Jetta) got 7,100 registrations in October. Is there hope after all?

Outside the top 20, the main event was the ramp-up of Nevo’s new baby, the Q06, which is looking to replicate the Q05’s success in the category above. With some 10,000 registrations in only its second month, it looks like it could join the top 20 soon. The same can be said about the Geely Galaxy TT, the make’s answer to the Xiaomi SU7, which had around 10,500 deliveries in October. Then there’s also the BYD Yuan Plus, which, after a long cross through the desert, seems to be picking up steam again. It scored 11,658 registrations last month, a new year best.

Looking at the 2026 ranking, the podium remained the same, and unless something unexpected happens, it should stay as it is until the end of the year, with the small Geely repeating its 2025 win. That also means the Tesla Model Y will return to silver after getting bronze in 2025, and the BYD Song will get back onto the podium after a one-year absence.

Below the podium positions, though, there was some news. The BYD Yuan Up and Leapmotor A10 are surfing the B-segment wave and both climbed a position, to 5th and 6th, respectively.

If the BYD Yuan Up continues on its current record streak, then the small crossover could even aim to surpass the #4 FCB Ti7 before the year ends.

Still, with three subcompacts currently in the top 6 (Geely Xingyuan, BYD Yuan Up, and Leapmotor A10), small is hot right now, in China.

Elsewhere, the BYD Sealion 05 was up two positions, to 16th, while the Wuling Mini EV is hoping to bring tiny city cars back into the spotlight, and in October, it jumped two positions, ending the month in 13th….

Looking at the overall manufacturer ranking, it is a sea of red. Everyone is losing sales — big time. The exception is #5 Leapmotor (+31% YoY), while #8 Xiaomi (+3% YoY) and #10 Xpeng (+0%) are just hanging on.

So, now, not only are foreign OEMs suffering (Nissan was down 70% in October, Honda was down 51%), but even domestic ones are being affected by the EV shift.

Some may be asking, “But what about #9 Nevo and its 125% growth rate?” Well, it isn’t so much that they are winning sales, but they are effectively replacing the sales of their mother brand, Changan, which in October was only 19th after a 60% drop in sales YoY.

Looking at the auto brand ranking, BYD is firmly in the leadership position (17.2%), while runner-up Geely held to its 7.1% market share.

Rising 3rd placed Leapmotor (6.7%, up 0.2%) is fast approaching Geely. It wouldn’t be surprising if the startup brand became the new silver medalist in the final days of the year.

One thing is for certain though — Leapmotor will win its first medal this year. The only question is the material that it will be made of….

Speaking of position changes, Tesla had a horrible month (4.4%, down from 4.9% in September), which allowed Wuling (4.6%) to climb one position in October, into 4th. At the end of the year, expect Tesla to keep the #4 position, as its December peak should help it surpass Wuling.

Looking at OEMs/automotive groups/alliances, BYD is leading with 21.9% share of the market, up 0.1% in October.

Meanwhile, Geely remained in second with 11.8% share. The multinational conglomerate has the runner-up spot secured.

#3 SAIC was stable (8%) and remained firm in the last place on the podium, while #4 Leapmotor (6.7%, up 0.2%) remained on the rise. Will we see the startup challenge SAIC in 2027 for the 3rd spot?

Always interested in the auto industry, particularly in electric cars, Jose has pioneered on documenting the plug-in sales evolution through the EV Sales blog, allowing him to gain an expert view on where EVs are right now and where they are headed in the future. Extending that work and expertise, Jose was co-founder of EV-Volumes and currently works with the European Alternative Fuels Observatory on EV sales matters.

#5633. Optum Rx rolls out new pharmacy tools aimed at transparency

Optum Rx rolls out new pharmacy tools aimed at transparency" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Earlier this year, Optum Rx teased the rollout of new pharmacy tools designed to address medication cost and access.

Now, the company is offering a look at how those tools work.

The pharmacy benefit manager said Tuesday that the tools build on Optum's new and more transparent pharmacy model, which the company announced in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

The first platform, called Shop MyScript, allows members to compare prices for their medications as well as their options for pharmacies or delivery before the prescription is dispensed. The tool will notify members of potential cost savings shortly after a script is written.

In addition, Shop MyScript embeds in the prescribing workflow, Optum said, so that the member does not have to make comparisons after the fact. If they choose to keep the existing prescription, it will then be sent to the pharmacy.

Optum said that early adopters have averaged $28 in savings through the program.

"People should have clear information about their medication costs and options when they can actually use it, not after a decision has already been made," said Katte Carey, president of Optum Rx, in the announcement. "These tools give people more information earlier in their journey, so they can make choices that work for them and get the support they need along the way."

In addition, the pharmacy benefit manager announced Optum Assistant, a conversational AI guide that helps members complete routine tasks and track down key information. The tool can triage concerns on a range of topics, from questions about medication and benefits to pharmacy experience challenges.

If the AI guide can't address the individual's needs, they can choose to be connected to live support to find a solution. Optum said about 80% of conversations using the tool led to a resolution without needing a live advocate.

The final new launch aims to support cash-pay options, according to the announcement.

Optum Price Wise will offer members a complete cost breakdown, including the price of a drug and any fees. That total, all-in price allows members to fully understand what their options may be and make the choice that works best for them at the pharmacy counter.

The PBM said new tools like these build on Optum's new and more transparent pharmacy model, which the company announced in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

#5632. Who Needs Automatic Driving? You Love to Drive! However, for Many Handicapped, Tesla’s Full Self Driving Is the Only Option. It’s Use It, or Don’t Drive!

Editor’s note: In my opinion, a person should not be using Tesla FSD to drive somewhere if they aren’t capable of driving the trip fully themselves. Fritz makes the argument here that it is easier to supervise FSD and that is why someone with a handicap can use it when they don’t feel like they can drive fully on their own — they just have to pay attention and be ready to intervene if needed. However, my experience and opinion is that it can definitely be harder to intervene when needed than to just drive oneself, so if someone isn’t capable of driving fully themself, they shouldn’t be driving somewhere relying on FSD. As he is showing here, though, there are people — himself included — relying on FSD to drive when they feel they can’t drive a trip fully on their own for various physical reasons. Feel free to chime in below with your opinion on this matter. — Z.S.

Warning! Tesla’s Full Self Driving Supervised is an extremely capable automatic driving system. However, to use it you need to be an unimpaired legal driver who can intervene (Supervise) in a fraction of a second if needed. With that caveat, I will discuss in this article how FSD can take over driving for drivers with various kinds of handicaps.

I love to ride my ebike! I ride 15 to 20 miles every day. A few days ago, just after shoulder replacement, I remembered that Vasa Fitness has stationary bicycles. Just two days after surgery with my right arm in a sling, I knew that driving there would be difficult. I thought about asking my wife to drive me. But I got into my Tesla Model Y with Full Self Driving V 14 and said Hey Grok! Navigate me to Vasa Fitness. My car drove me out of my garage and without any intervention by me, touching the brake pedal, steering wheel or accelerator drove me to Vasa Fitness and parked me in the parking lot as you see in the lead photo.

Numerous situations have come to my attention where Tesla FSD can or could drive you safely, where the only other option would be to not drive.

For more on these matters, also read these pieces:

Elon Musk is a despicable person who no longer cares about clean energy. Also, he apparently no longer cares about his stockholders. His choice of supporting Donald Trump and spending almost half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates in the last election have greatly damaged Tesla and reduced its stock value.

Many of my readers have been very critical of my support for Musk’s company. Unfortunately, in this early stage of EV development, no other company has the hardware, software, and Superchargers that make an electric car a reasonable alternative to a gas car for both city and cross-country driving anywhere in the US.

For those of you who wouldn’t consider buying a car from Musk’s company, I will present the next best alternative: You can buy a Rivian! It is a more traditional non-aerodynamic type of vehicle — a pickup truck or SUV. But it also has its benefits.

Rivian has the best non-Tesla driving automation available for consumer cars in the US at this time. I had planned to drive 40 miles down to the Rivian Demo Center in Salt Lake City to give their automatic driving a test drive. However, my research tells me that Rivian’s automatic driving is not nearly as good as Tesla’s at this point. It won’t drive you point to point in the city and on the highway without intervention. However, Rivian’s sensor suite is more comprehensive than Tesla’s. Tesla has made the bet that since human drivers can drive using only optical sensors, their eyes, it should be possible to drive automatically with only cameras. Human drivers need to pull off the road when the visibility is very bad, but Rivian will eventually be able to continue driving during 0% visibility conditions.

Final comprehensive analysis: you may hate Musk, but if you want the latest technology in automatic driving and the freedom to drive electric on all the major highways in the US without careful planning, you’re going to have to choose a Tesla with Hardware V4. #5631. Ranking Today's 4 Main V12 Supercars By Horsepower As They Scream Into The Sunset

Since burning tons of fuel to move one, maybe two, people around isn't the greatest thing for the planet, massive V12 engines are a dying breed. Even among supercars, there are pretty much only four left that use what is arguably the most romantic engine layout possible. You can count 'em on one hand: there's a Ferrari, a Lamborghini, an Aston Martin, and a Pagani. If you're curious as to how they rank purely in terms of horsepower, you've come to the right place.

And for the supercar geeks about to run to the comments to point out that one McLaren F1-shaped omission, Gordon Murray's T.50 did indeed use a V12 — a naturally aspirated 3.9-liter developed by Cosworth, no less — but that car actually ended production back in the summer of 2025, so it's out of the running. In a similar vein, the Aston Martin Valkyrie indeed made enough power to sit atop this list, but production stopped back in 2024. Without further ado, then, here are today's four main V12 supercars, ranked by horsepower.

Despite ranking at the bottom in terms of power, the Ferrari 12Cilindri is arguably, for one obvious reason, the car most overtly proud of the fact that it still uses a V12 — that name, by the way, is pronounced "dodici cilindri," where the first c is a "ch" sound. The cilindris in question are inside a 6.5-liter naturally aspirated V12 making 819 hp. The 12Cilindri can go from zero to 62 mph in 2.9 seconds and has a top speed exceeding 211 mph. While mighty by any standard, forward thrust plays second fiddle to this engine's real allure: a sky-high redline of 9,500 rpm.

In regular form, those revs generate power going to the rear axle through an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission. The recent big news about this car, however, is the introduction of a Manuale variant that pairs that V12 with a gated "manual" transmission that is, in reality, a meticulously programmed simulation of a three-pedal gearbox. There's been much debate over whether the Manuale's authenticity matters, but I'm just glad its screaming V12 remains a genuine article.

Besting its Ferrari rival by precisely 5 hp is the Aston Martin Vanquish. Where the 12Cilindri is staunchly naturally aspirated, the Aston makes its power with forced induction, adding two turbos to its 5.2-liter V12 to make 824 horses. Zero to 60 mph is achieved in 3.2 seconds, and it'll hit a top speed of 214 mph.

It's a real Aston engine, too, because unlike the Mercedes V8s you find in the brand's modern Vantage and DBX, this V12 is a continuation of the in-house motor that powered the old DB11 and DBS Superleggera. In addition to stronger connecting rods, higher flow-rate fuel injectors, and quicker turbos, this motor gets a new Boost Reserve function that builds boost in the background during partial throttle so it's ready to go when you do floor it. I've driven it, and in practice, the Vanquish pulls off the Aston Martin thing of being just as exciting as a sporting machine as it is livable and comfortable as a GT car.

Like any good exotic automaker, Aston loves a good limited-run special model, and, for posterity, the Vanquish-based Valen takes this engine and makes a slightly nuttier 838 hp. There's also a 705-hp, manual-transmission Valour, plus a more track-focused, 735-hp variant called the Valiant. As if being a manual V12 Aston made for the track wasn't cool enough, that last one happened to come about as a personal commission from two-time world champ and Aston Martin Formula 1 driver, Fernando Alonso.

When it comes to pure horsepower, none of Aston's current V12 fare beats the Pagani Utopia. An exotic among exotics, the Utopia is powered by a twin-turbocharged 6.0-liter V12, made just for this car by Mercedes-AMG, pumping out a mighty 864 hp.

You can get the Utopia with a seven-speed automated manual gearbox, but I'm not sure why you would when the seven-speed actual manual is right there. In true Pagani fashion, it has a gated gearbox where the entire shift linkage is exposed and shiny and glorious. Zero to 60 mph is said to take around 3.0 seconds, and the Roadster is electronically limited to 217 mph, but tellingly, a lot of Pagani's own literature shies away from discussing such specs.

This is not a car that seems to concern itself much with instrumented testing — you wouldn't strap a stopwatch to the Mona Lisa, now would you? To put it another way: the Pagani Utopia is arguably the car on this list I'd be in the most awe of coming across in the wild, and that insane 864-hp V12 somehow isn't even in the top three reasons that's the case.

If technical dominance is what you're after, the most powerful V12 supercar on the market today is the Lamborghini Revuelto SV, which makes 1,050 horsepower. Mind you, that doesn't come solely from its naturally aspirated 6.5-liter V12. Instead, it's a culmination of that engine plus three hybrid electric motors — yep, in case you missed the memo, both of Lamborghini's supercars are now plug-in hybrids.

In a parallel universe where the Revuelto wasn't a hybrid, however, it'd come last on this list because its V12 alone produces "just" 814 hp, six fewer ponies than that equally large Ferrari motor. But that's not how the game is played.

Taken as a whole, the electrified Lambo gets from zero to 62 mph in just 2.4 seconds, notably quicker than every other car here, and it reaches a top speed of 216 mph. The fastest and most powerful production Lamborghini ever dominates on a dragstrip not just on the back of its immense horsepower but also because it's the only car on this list with all-wheel-drive. Each front wheel is powered by a dedicated electric motor (the remaining e-motor is at the back, helping out that V12).

As it happens, I was fortunate enough to drive a "regular," non-SV Revuelto last year, which made a relatively paltry 1,001 hp. The speed was, in a word, ridiculous, and that V12 soundtrack remains an absolute treat. In the admittedly small pantheon of V12 supercars that remain, the Ferrari may be more pure, the Aston more refined, and the Pagani more special, but in the contest of pure horsepower and speed, the Lamborghini Revuelto, for now at least, sits at the peak.

#5630. Court Approves $7.25B Settlement With Bayer Over Claims Roundup Caused Cancer

— Some attorneys for patients contend the settlement payouts are too small

Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weedkiller Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge.

The nationwide settlement applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years. Participants could get an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed, and the severity of their illness.

For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from U.S. agricultural markets.

Litigants also faced uncertainty. While the settlement was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits. The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations don't require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labeling requirements.

Though some attorneys for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing -- which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling.

In a written judgment granting approval, St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are "fair and adequate" and the total dollar amount is "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."

Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement that the court-approved settlement is "a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation."

Roundup Has Been Used on Weeds for Over 50 Years

Missouri-based Monsanto debuted Roundup weedkiller in 1974 with the chemical glyphosate as its active ingredient. The product quickly became one of the most widely used herbicides in agriculture. Roundup is designed to be used with genetically modified seeds that can resist the weedkiller's deadly effect, thus allowing farmers to produce more while conserving the soil by tilling it less.

The product also is commonly applied on lawns and gardens.

Bayer added Roundup to its portfolio when it acquired Monsanto in 2018. With it came a growing number of lawsuits alleging glyphosate causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But that remains in dispute. The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer classified the chemical as "probably carcinogenic" in 2015. The Environmental Protection Agency has determined that it's not likely to cause cancer in humans when used as directed.

About 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens. As a result, Bayer has removed glyphosate from its new versions of Roundup sold for residential markets.

The lawsuits have produced mixed results. Only a couple dozen cases have gone to jurors, some siding with Bayer and others with plaintiffs. In one case, a Georgia jury awarded plaintiffs $2.1 billion.

In the first Roundup verdict since the Supreme Court's precedent-setting ruling, a Missouri jury in October sided with Bayer in a case alleging design defects, negligence, and fraud. The verdict "should send a strong signal" that plaintiffs "will face significant challenges" pursuing Roundup-related cancer claims in the future, said Bill Dodero, Bayer's U.S. general counsel and global litigation leader.

Medicare Shared Savings Program saved $2.5B last year: CMS" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Medicare Shared Savings Program has reached the highest savings number in its history, according to new federal data.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said Tuesday that the program generated more than $2.5 billion in net savings for Medicare in 2025, making for the ninth year in a row that it led to cost savings. The agency added that every accountable care organization met or exceeded quality reporting requirements.

As of 2026, 511 ACOs representing more than 700,000 providers are participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, which represents 12.6 million people enrolled in traditional Medicare, another record.

"These record savings show the power of rewarding providers for quality and coordination. CMS said that it wants to make it easier for providers to participate in MSSP if they choose, especially given the program's results to date. It included changes in the latest Physician Fee Schedule to encourage participation, including increased opportunity for certain ACOs to earn shared savings and new financial incentives to draw in first-time participants.

In addition, CMS said that would create more predictable spending targets that make planning and participation straightforward. The agency is also aiming to streamline patient notices and simplify required technology.

“We are excited to see continued progress on both savings and enrollment for Medicare beneficiaries. Beneficiaries are best served when a provider is watching out for them and coordinating their care,” said Center for Medicare Director John Brooks in the announcement.

"NAACOS looks forward to partnering with CMS to build on this momentum," said Brower. "Policies that unleash innovation, reduce burden, and create sustainability through fair and predictable budgets will allow ACOs to deliver even greater value for patients and the Medicare program."

#5628. Ford Begins Producing Its Own LFP Batteries

Ford is now a battery producer. Yes, it’s using battery technology licensed from CATL, but it is now producing EV batteries it is going to be using in its own vehicles. In fact, it is reportedly doing so in a really fast, advanced way. “The BlueOval Battery Park Michigan assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it among the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside of China.2 That pace helps drive down battery costs, and the facility has capacity for more. But speed must go hand in hand with quality,” Charles Poon, vice president of hardware engineering at Ford, writes.

“The first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells are rolling off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan and headed to Louisville Assembly Plant to power Ford Fathom prototypes. With this milestone, Ford is now in the battery business and will be the first to deliver LFP batteries in the U.S. for mainstream consumer automotive use,” Poon writes. He goes on to explain further in a recent article why Ford chose to produce LFP battery cells and a bit on how it is doing so. Here’s a bit more from that article:

“The shipment caps years of work by the team that designed, built, and launched the plant on schedule. Ford now delivers cells at a plant it owns and operates, building expertise to support more affordable electric vehicles (EVs) and Ford Energy’s battery energy storage business in Kentucky.

“Why Start with LFP Prismatic for Fathom?

“When Alan Clarke, vice president, Advanced Development Projects, first joined the development team that created the Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, he issued a clear challenge: find an efficient LFP prismatic battery. The goal was to make EVs significantly more affordable.

“We talked to battery companies around the world. We wanted a technology that was proven in the field, ready to manufacture at scale, and suited to what we were building. That led us to the world’s leading battery manufacturer, CATL, whose batteries power 30 million vehicles across the globe.

“A battery is one of the biggest contributors to an EV’s cost and weight. So, we asked: How do we get more out of the battery without simply adding more cells? Our answer was efficiency over excess.

“LFP chemistry uses no nickel or cobalt, which helps hold down costs. It also holds up over years of charging and use. That durability is valuable as we give customers ways to use their battery beyond driving. For example, AC bidirectional power lets a vehicle receive electricity from a properly equipped home and supply power back to it.1

“This milestone is about more than shipping our first cells. We’re building the expertise to produce high-quality batteries at scale — for more affordable EVs and a new energy storage business.”

It looks like a serious effort and serious progress toward making more affordable, more competitive electric cars at Ford. The aim has been to get as good as making electric cars as Chinese companies are. How effective and successful will this new path be for Ford? We’ll see.

#5627. Maybe Don't Paint Your Car With House Paint

The mates at Australia's creative Garbage Time have done it again. Last year they painted a Toyota Corolla entirely with house paint, more or less color matched to the car's existing paint by a local hardware store chain. This turned out to be a bad idea, as house paint is fundamentally very different from your favorite automotive paints, but then the geniuses behind the channel had a brain blast: Leave the car outside, parked under a tree, for a year. Surely that would make things better, right?

You may be surprised to hear this, but no — covering a house-painted car in dust, dirt, pollen, and bird droppings does not, in fact, improve the quality of the paint. Washing it afterward doesn't help, either, because a touchless wash can't really get anything out of that soft, ductile paint. No, once you've covered your car in hardware-store house paint — without any preparation, primer, or clear coat — you're pretty much screwed.

After a year of dealing with outdoor conditions, the Corolla's paint is pretty thoroughly wrecked, which is saying something for a carmaker noted for its terrible colors. A touchless wash did absolutely nothing to fix that, and even a hand wash was only a marginal improvement. The house paint, constantly referred to as "gummy" throughout the video, is just too good at grabbing onto dirt and holding onto it. It's also pretty great at peeling off the car when aggressively cleaned.

From a distance, the house-painted Corolla actually doesn't look terrible — a bit wet, like the paint isn't fully dry, but not uncannily so. It's clearly not a factory paint job, but from 20 feet away you'd be hard-pressed to tell this automotive travesty from a poor rattlecan job that combined proper materials with improper technique. This Corolla got neither the right stuff nor the right methods. But hey, at least it was cheap.

#5626. Alzheimer's Test Results Delivered Digitally Didn't Increase Distress

— Anxiety and knowledge scores also met noninferiority versus telehealth in randomized trial

Getting Alzheimer's genetic and biomarker results through a digital tool was noninferior to receiving the information during a telehealth appointment, the randomized eSMARTER trial showed.

One to 7 days after APOE results were disclosed, scores on measures of anxiety, disease-specific distress, and disease-related knowledge met noninferiority whether patients were randomized to a digital platform or to a clinician-mediated telehealth session, said Jessica Langbaum, PhD, of the Banner Alzheimer's Institute in Phoenix, at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in Boston.

Similar results emerged for phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) disclosure, Langbaum reported. These findings were also published in JAMA Neurology.

"We found that learning Alzheimer's genetic and biomarker information from a digital platform is no less effective -- in other words, no worse than -- receiving this information from a clinician telehealth visit," Langbaum said.

"This is important given that most patients learn their test results from a report in their patient portal -- often a static report or PDF, with limited to no additional information or context about their results and what they mean -- and have to wait until their scheduled follow-up appointment to speak with their clinician," she pointed out.

Under the 21st Century Cures Act, most medical test results, including Alzheimer's genetic and biomarker findings, must be made available to patients immediately. Previous research has shown that disclosing Alzheimer's biomarker data is safe and generally well tolerated, but in those studies clinicians led the disclosure, either in person or by telehealth.

"eSMARTER is the first randomized trial to examine whether learning Alzheimer's genetic results via a patient-centered digital platform is noninferior to a telehealth visit with a study clinician," Langbaum said. "The study then offered participants the option to learn their plasma p-tau217 results via the same method -- digital platform or telehealth visit -- again examining differences in anxiety, distress, and knowledge."

The eSMARTER trial included participants ages 60 to 80 who had previously had APOE genotyping (without disclosure) through the GeneMatch research enrollment program, passed psychological screening, and had internet access. Participants had a mean age of 68 and a mean Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score of 19. Approximately 36% had MoCA scores below 19, a cutoff commonly used for cognitive impairment, and most participants were women (67%).

The study randomized 216 participants to clinician-mediated APOE disclosure and 435 to digital disclosure. Genetic test results were revealed first, and after 6 months, participants could choose p-tau217 disclosure. All participants were offered optional digital educational materials about APOE and p-tau217 to review before the disclosure sessions.

Of 651 participants who received APOE disclosure, most were APOE4 carriers (58% heterozygotes, 10% homozygotes, and 32% noncarriers).

There were no overall differences in Alzheimer's-related knowledge, symptoms of anxiety, or disease-specific distress between the digital and telehealth arms after APOE results were received.

Among APOE4 carriers, three differences emerged:

The eSMARTER study shows that digital disclosure is an acceptable alternative to telehealth, Langbaum observed. The results suggest that a scalable platform could be developed "to plug into patient portals to help patients understand and contextualize their test results," she said. "We envision that these platforms can be used by clinicians and health systems to better support patients to navigate complex health information."

#5625. Memo To Musk: Denial Is Just The First Step On The Long Road To Recovery

Tesla CEO Elon Musk made headlines yet again last week, when he publicly denied any affiliation with US President Donald Trump’s “MAGA” movement. If Musk intends to stage a sort of political recovery, he still has a long way to go. Denial is just a precursor to recovery, which begins in earnest when you stop denying the reality of your situation and start admitting you need help from a higher power or some such. And in fact, a higher power is coming for Musk —  if not in spiritual form, then in the form of Congress, where the incoming Democratic majority plans to exercise its authority, and call Musk to account for manipulating SpaceX satellite services in Ukraine.

During an interview for the New York Times DealBook Summit last week, Elon Musk claimed that he was not affiliated with MAGA, though he did not apologize for supporting MAGA candidates this year, or for supporting Donald Trump in 2024. Musk simply said he “felt foolish” for wasting his money on losers.

In the same interview, Musk insisted — falsely — that Russia was the aggrieved party when Russian President Vladimir Putin invaded the Donbas region of Ukraine back in 2014. Justin sayin’…

For those of you wondering why Elon Musk’s politics should be a matter of concern to CleanTechnica, that’s a good question, and here’s the answer: Elon Musk sailed into clean tech history on the coattails of the EV startup Tesla Motors (soon to become simply Tesla) in the early 2000’s, only to emerge in more recent years as a champion of the far right alongside President Donald Trump’s notoriously racist, fossil fuel-supporting “Make America Great Again” movement, thereby setting back the US decarbonization movement by years if not decades.

Musk has also made his own contribution to the resurgence of fossil fuels in the US. His new xAI data centers are well known for deploying loosely regulated (or illegal) on-site gas generators, and his SpaceX venture has been gobbling up natural gas for rocket fuel while laying plans for future expansion.

So much for Elon Musk’s footprint on the US energy profile. Let’s move over to Ukraine, where rich fossil energy and mineral resources in the nation’s Donbas region prompted Russian President Putin to send unmarked soldiers — aka the “little green men” — to annex that portion of Ukraine in 2014 (see clarification/correction below). A ceasefire temporarily calmed the situation until February of 2022, when Putin sent a fully equipped convoy to the Ukrainian capital city Kyiv, aiming to take over the entire seat of government in one fell swoop — literally, in one day.

The effort failed, both militarily and in terms of Putin’s energy goals. Ukraine promptly cut Russia off from its electricity grid and hooked up with the European grid, a complex effort assisted by the Biden administration. Ukraine also set the wheels in motion to join the European Union as a significant source of clean energy, including green hydrogen gas alongside its copious potential for clean power including biomass, wind, and solar power.

To put that into perspective, consider that Ukraine is almost 90% as large as Texas, which has staked out a leadership position in wind and solar power among the 50 US states.

With Ukraine as a leading renewable energy supplier, the EU would have a fresh opportunity to meets its decarbonization goals on schedule while also reducing imports of fossil energy from Russia… And… Well… That’s where Elon Musk enters the picture.

Musk first emerged as a full blown MAGA supporter in 2020, when he helped Trump stir up conspiracy theories and confusion over the federal response to the COVID-19 crisis, in a failed effort to support the President’s bid for re-election that year. Had Trump won, he would have continued to implement a key part of his foreign policy agenda, namely, withdrawing the US from NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Alliance. NATO formed in 1949 as an effort to curb Russian expansion in Europe, an effort Trump has upended on account of his longstanding friendship with Putin.

The election of Joe Biden in 2020 did not prevent Musk from providing additional aid and comfort to Trump. Musk used his media-grabbing public profile to undercut the authority of President Biden at every opportunity, including on the world stage as well as here at home. The stream of insults extended into January of 2022, even as the reality of a fresh round of Russian expansion into Europe began to materialize.

Musk had an additional opportunity to challenge Biden’s authority in January of 2022, when the so-called “Freedom Convoy” of truckers barricaded government offices in Canada, ostensibly in protest of a vaccine mandate. Musk gleefully cheered the effort, which disrupted transportation systems and distracted public attention in two key NATO allies — Canada and the US — even as Russia began ratcheting up its plans to take over Kyiv.

However, once it became clear that Putin’s one-day takeover of Ukraine was a failure, Musk about-faced. He took credit for providing “free” communications aid to Ukraine in the form of satellite services through the Starlink branch of SpaceX.

JK! A later assessment revealed that other sources shouldered about 85% of the cost of Starlink terminals initially supplied to Ukraine, including USAID here in the US (not a typo — that’s the US Administration for International Development, the same agency that Musk later destroyed in 2025).

Poland and other groups also contributed initial assistance to purchase  the terminals alongside an estimated 30% of connectivity costs. In addition, by September of 2022 Musk was making the case for US taxpayers to foot the bill.

Don’t just take my word for it. In 2023, the Belfer Center for International Affairs at Harvard recapped SpaceX’s negotiations over payment for its services to Ukraine during the previous year, concluding that “we can assume the U.S. government agreed to pay some, if not all, of the costs for continued operation of the technology.”

“SpaceX, and particularly Musk, was able to play the role of wartime hero, showcasing the power and value of the technology products the company developed, while simultaneously avoiding sustained and hefty bills,” Belfer Center observed.

US Department of Defense contract or not, by 2023 SpaceX was already making unilateral decisions that restricted Ukraine’s ability to deploy the technology, with SpaceX CEO Gwynne Shotwell publicly insisting that the company never intended for Ukraine to use it “for offensive purposes.”

Of course, “offensive” is in the eye of the beholder. Since Ukraine is the invaded party seeking to assert its rights over internationally recognized borders against Russia, one could argue that every action Ukraine takes is a defensive one until Putin agrees to concede defeat and cede back his illegal claims over Ukrainian lands.

Of course, that’s not how Musk portrayed the situation in his DealBook interview last week. Nevertheless, one also could argue that the US government, not the vendor, controls the use of contractually obligated resources. Be that as it may, Musk raised the bar considerably in October, when he — or Trump — or both — once again dialed down satellite service in Ukraine, exposing that country to further attacks.

Musk attempted to mollify bipartisan outrage over the debacle with yet another publicity stunt for SpaceX. However, service interruptions have continued into this week. Meanwhile, Trump has spent the same week cozying up to both Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, aided and abetted by an obedient Republican majority in Congress.

That majority will evaporate, though, in January 3, which is just around the corner. The incoming Democratic majority is already gearing up for a fight. In a letter dated November 20, the incoming Chair of the House Intelligence Committee, Jim Himes (D-CT), demanded an in-person briefing from senior SpaceX officers, seeking an explanation for the disruption of military-grade Starshield service in Ukraine. As leverage, Himes warned Musk that a Democratic majority in Congress will do what the Republican majority failed to do, namely, exercise its constitutional authority over federal contracts.

Referring specifically to SpaceX’s military-grade Starshield satellite services in Ukraine, Himes warned Musk that his entire suite of present and future SpaceX security contracts with the US government is at risk. “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes explained.

“For that reason, it is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX- developed, government-owned systems until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes continued.

Will Musk simply ignore the request for a briefing? After all, as Himes notes, Musk failed to respond to earlier requests. Stay tuned…

#5624. Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination pulled by White House

Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination pulled by White House" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The White House pulled the nomination for Heidi Overton, M.D., Ph.D., to lead the FDA just hours before the Senate was scheduled to vote on her confirmation.

The move hardly comes as a surprise after Overton’s confirmation hearing before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee drew contention.

The news was first reported by Axios on Tuesday evening. The White House confirmed the news to Fierce the following morning.

In September, the HELP committee questioned Overton in a hearing marked by tightrope-walking on issues like vaccines, abortions, flavored vapes and whether or not President Donald Trump is capable of being wrong.

Overton conceded multiple times during the hearing that vaccines approved by the FDA, as well as the “abortion pill” mifepristone, are safe and effective. But she stopped short of admitting that Trump has been wrong when dispensing medical information out of line with what scientific evidence shows.

Overton’s nomination faced mounting pushback and uncertainty from senators ahead of a planned HELP Committee vote on Nov. 18. Fierce reached out to Sen. Ed Markey, the veteran Democratic lawmaker from Massachusetts, ahead of the vote, and he told Fierce that he would “vote against her nomination, and I urge my colleagues to do the same.”

“The FDA needs a leader who will stand up for science and for our kids’ safety, not one who stood by while both were undermined,” he added.

Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who chairs the Senate health committee, and other Republicans had also raised questions about Overton's nomination.

As support for Overton looked thin, Republicans were discussing Sen. Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, as a potential replacement, Semafor reported today. Health Secretary Kennedy reportedly met with Marshall in recent days to discuss filling the role, according to Politico, but the White House told the publication that it is not considering him.

Robert Steinbrook, M.D., health research group director for Public Citizen, commented today urging the HELP committee to reject Overton’s nomination: “The FDA needs a strong commissioner who stands for science and the integrity of the agency,” Steinbrook said. “Overton is the wrong choice for FDA Commissioner and has done nothing to dispel the well-founded reasons to oppose her candidacy.”

Analysts from Citi shared that the White House’s decision to pull the nomination has a negative impact on biopharma, “extending uncertainty around permanent agency leadership.”

“We view the withdrawal as a modest sentiment negative, but not a material near-term change to the regulatory environment facing most drug and biologics sponsors,” the analysts said in the note.

The withdrawal of Overton's nomination leaves a gap at an FDA that has already faced significant upheaval. The White House only shifted its focus to Overton in August, after the agency had spent three months without a permanent leader.

Since former FDA commissioner Marty Makary, M.D., departed the agency in May, Kyle Diamantas, who hails from the agency’s food regulation division, has been at the helm in an interim capacity.
