#5623. 8 Things Your iPhone Does As You Flip Your Car Down An Embankment

A phone puts in a lot of work while we're driving around, especially if your car's infotainment system is painfully old and it's doing double duty there. And while plenty has been said about how our phones can help cause a crash – texting-while-driving bans exist in every state but one – we don't talk as much about how they can be downright heroic when one actually occurs.

Apple introduced Crash Detection with the iPhone 14 in 2022 (it works on iPhone 14 or later running iOS 16 or later). The underlying technology unlocks a number of possibilities, some of which could literally save a user's life. That's because once your phone knows you've been in a crash, it can do a number of phone-based tasks that you might no longer be in a position to do yourself, from calling 911 and letting them know where to find you to alerting your emergency contacts that something has gone awry.

It's worth noting that nothing here is exclusive to Apple. In fact, Google Pixel phones have been doing crash detection since 2019. But since more Americans use iPhones than every other competing device combined, getting Crash Detection into iOS represented the first mainstream on-by-default introduction of the technology in the United States, even if many users were unaware it was even there. So if you have a different device, there's a chance it can do what's being discussed today. We're sharing the iPhone perspective for the sake of being relevant to the most users and letting us be specific about the details. So here's what your phone might get up to right after you overcorrect from hitting inexplicable gravel on that backroad sweeper.

Your iPhone starts determining that you're in a crash based on a bunch of real-time data that it's taking in all the time — think change in speed, impact force, and even changes in air pressure. But before it takes any action that could lead to a rescue helicopter being summoned to your location or scaring the daylights out of your emergency contact, it's going to evaluate whether you've actually been traveling along in a car versus, say, knocking your phone off a balcony or falling down a flight of stairs.

There are no exact criteria that answer this question. A crash detection algorithm notes things like whether you are connected to a vehicle via Bluetooth, how rapidly it is passing through the range of nearby Wi-Fi connections, and even analyzes ambient engine sounds or road noise. The goal is to cobble together a clear enough picture of what's going on to distinguish between a phone being dropped on a moving subway and one flying through the air in an auto accident. It's an approach that had to be dialed in. When the feature was first introduced, there was a tendency for crash detection to be triggered in non-crash events, such as violent jostling on a roller coaster. Subsequent updates refined the criteria, aiming to reduce false positives and emergency crews being dispatched to amusement parks.

Apple has done research with crash labs to effectively draw this line, both determining when someone is traveling in a car and also filtering out minor incidents like a small fender bender or a phone simply being knocked on the floor while a vehicle is in motion.

Once your iPhone has established that you're likely traveling in a vehicle and not bungee jumping or getting your clock cleaned playing football, it uses on-device hardware to get a handle on how much trauma the laws of physics are putting on the phone and, by extension, probably you.

New motion sensors introduced with the iPhone 14 include a three-axis gyroscope and high-g force accelerometer able to detect up to 256 Gs of force, which helps estimate if whatever is happening to you would land in a sufficiently severe place on something called the Maximum Abbreviated Injury Scale (MAIS). Apple says it has set the crash detection threshold in an effort to detect incidents with a MAIS level 3 and higher, at which point your injuries are likely to include "major lacerations, multiple fractures, crushed limbs, and bruised organs." Like we said: not a fender bender.

These sensors fire off more than 3,000 times per second, slowing your terrifying automotive mishap into a veritable eternity of data that captures the initial impact and every twist, turn, bump, and smash that follows. On the plus side, in this case your phone probably isn't spreading your information to advertisers, so there's that.

In addition to cutting-edge tech like the gyroscope and accelerometer, the iPhone also leans on pre-existing hardware to decide if the thing you're experiencing is indeed a crash that warrants an emergency response. One of those is the microphone, which can capture the acoustic data needed to identify crash sounds and help distinguish a real crash from false alarms G-force data might trigger.

Perhaps even more unexpected than your phone listening for tire-screeching and tree-hitting sounds is what's going on with its internal barometer, a sensor used primarily to measure elevation changes for activity tracking and support location services. Because airbags have a lot more going on than you might think and can temporarily alter the ambient air pressure inside the car when they go off, that barometer can often recognize the clue and relay the data point to the algorithm for consideration.

None of this is a sure thing. If your windows are down, the barometer might not be able to detect the change in pressure and the sounds of the accident may or may not align with what Apple's programming has decided a crash sounds like. Similar to the logic that determined you were in a car in the first place, it takes a number of differently-weighted data points to come up with an educated assessment of the situation. That assessment may be wrong, in either direction.

And because all these calculations can be wrong in either direction, the iPhone does provide a couple of clear opportunities for you to indicate there's been a wacky misunderstanding rather than a dangerous crash before it mobilizes a dramatic and potentially expensive emergency response on your behalf.

Before springing into action, it'll first sound an audible alarm and show an alert on the screen. This lasts 10 seconds. If you swipe where indicated it will call emergency services and if you dismiss the alert it'll cancel the whole thing. Of course, emergencies being emergencies, you might not be able to do either, in which case a 30-second countdown will occur before it moves forward.

During this time your phone will be making loud noises you probably haven't heard before, vibrating in a way you didn't realize it was capable of, and activating an LED strobe. If you swipe to call emergency services, you'll be connected. If you take no action, presumably because you can't, not because you didn't notice the air raid warnings coming from your phone, the countdown reaches zero and the phone springs into action on your behalf.

If you didn't have the foresight to sail your car into a ravine someplace with respectable cell phone coverage, you might think that all of this would just result in you having to listen to your phone make awful noises while you try to get yourself out of a dangerous situation with a cheap seatbelt cutter tool followed by it realizing it doesn't have any service anyway.

Not so! Since 2022, iPhone users in the U.S. and Canada with iPhone 14 models and later have had access to Emergency SOS via satellite. Whether you swiped right during the scary countdown or allowed it to reach zero while unresponsive or otherwise indisposed, the phone can use a data connection via satellite to reach help if cell service isn't available. If you're in a position to operate the phone, this won't be a voice call. You start with an emergency text, which will connect to emergency services after you enter "Report Emergency" mode. This prompts you to describe your situation using multiple choice questions to narrow down your predicament and relay the appropriate information.

Depending on where you are, a satellite connection may or may not be readily available. Dense tree cover above or the fact that you're upside down under a car may limit your phone's ability to reach a satellite. If that turns out to be an issue, the screen will walk you through how to best get a connection, such as moving to a place with a clear view of the horizon, which hopefully you'll be in a position to do. Of course, having to get yourself to the top of a hill remains preferable to having to get yourself to the nearest town.

If you have cell service, none of that satellite business happens. After you don't respond in time and the countdown reaches zero, the iPhone calls emergency services. Because you're presumably unavailable at this point, once emergency dispatch answers the call, they will hear a repeating audio message indicating that a serious car crash has been detected with an unresponsive person in need of help. The message also includes a search radius based on your approximate latitude and longitude.

During this time, two-way audio is enabled and the repeating recording will play at a reduced volume, so if you become able to speak with emergency services or someone else arrives on the scene, the conversation can proceed like any other 911 call. The phone screen will be commandeered with a "Crash Detected" message and the available interface will include one button to stop replaying the recorded message and another to end the call.

By the way, this all works over Wi-Fi calling as well, so you've also got options if you happen to flip your car down an embankment and into a Starbucks or something.

After your phone is done contacting emergency services, it can also send a message to your designated emergency contacts, letting them know that a crash has been detected and that 911 has been called. It will include an approximate location. This will appear as a text message coming from you, and its content will make it immediately apparent that something significant is happening.

This only works if you've set your phone up for emergency contacts, which you do somewhat unintuitively through the Health app. Apple explains how to do it on its support page, and now is as good a time as any to get that taken care of if you haven't already. While you're in there, you can also enter any medical information that emergency responders might benefit from having, which they can access under your phone's Medical ID feature.

Don't assume that you've designated your emergency contact just because your phone seems to already know who your mom is and reminds you to call her on her birthday. You can add more than one — just make sure that whoever you put in there is someone you're willing to wake up in the middle of the night with a terrifying text message they can never unsee.

One of the most important takeaways here has nothing to do with satellite technology or crash identification algorithms. Car crashes are chaotic, and even as your phone is processing data with mind-bending speed and preparing to summon help if you need it, the device itself may also be flying somewhere you aren't going to be able to get it. This doesn't just matter because an unsecured phone can become a projectile that hurts you or someone else. It's also important because something simple like placing a call is trivial while you're driving along but can become impossible in an emergency. And the remarkable thing is that, provided your phone survives and detects the crash, it can still call for help without you ever laying a finger on it.

You might have no earthly idea where the phone went when you need it. The screen might be shattered and your pleas to Siri might be met with "Here's 'Help!' by The Beatles on Apple Music." Crash Detection isn't foolproof, it can't detect every wreck, and your phone might fall off your motorcycle and tell your family you crashed. On the other hand, it just might save the day.

#5622. The Insurance Affordability Crisis: Risks, Resilience, and Solutions

NRDC resources on insurance affordability, market availability, climate risk, resilience investments, and strategies to protect homeowners, businesses, and communities.

For property owners, insurance provides a critical financial safety net that protects homes, businesses, and other assets from unexpected losses, helping owners recover and rebuild when disasters occur. Beyond individual protection, insurance is fundamental to the resilience of communities and local economies, enabling faster recovery, supporting continued investment, and reducing the long-term financial impacts of shocks. As risks become more frequent, severe, and costly, access to affordable, available, and reliable insurance is increasingly essential, not only for safeguarding property owners but also for maintaining overall property affordability, economic stability, and the resilience and prosperity of the communities in which they live and operate.

The frequency and severity of losses are increasing faster than insurers can sustainably price and absorb them, leading to higher premiums, reduced coverage availability, and, in some cases, the withdrawal of insurers from certain markets. This trend is eroding the affordability and accessibility of insurance, increasing the total cost of property ownership, and placing additional pressure on housing and business affordability while leaving individuals, businesses, and communities more physically and financially exposed.

However, the insurance sector is increasingly recognized as a key component of resilience, incentivizing risk reduction through pricing and support for adaptation measures that can help moderate long-term insurance costs. When functioning effectively, insurance enables communities to not only recover from shocks but also to better prepare for future risks while preserving access to coverage.

Linked below are reports, expert blogs, and other resources that examine the insurability crisis and how insurance can play a key role in advancing housing resilience and adaptation.

NRDC’s director of insurance and financial risk, Alfonso Pating, breaks down how homeowner’s insurance works and why climate change is making it unaffordable.

More reports and resources on this topic here.

#5621. The Longest Stretch A Sports Car Has Gone Without A New Platform Is 84 Years

Sure, the 2027 Chevy Express is the same as the 2026 model, which was the same as the 2025, which was the same as the 2024, and so on. But all joking aside, the Bowtie brand's body-on-frame van has only been riding on the same platform for about three decades. That's nothing compared to what Morgan did with its sports cars. The company introduced a steel ladder-style chassis with its 1936 Morgan 4-4, and from that point through 2020 — a span of 84 years — nearly every four-wheeled Morgan featured the same basic setup.

Of course, Morgan cars have remained true to their original 1930s vibes in a lot of ways, right down to their appearance. Even the new Morgan Supersport 400, the company's most powerful vintage-look roadster yet, maintains its flowing pontoon-style fenders, ash-wood body frame, and disdain for most modern technologies. Despite being the first Morgan to come with hands-free calling, the Supersport doesn't have a touchscreen — just a small and simple driver display with a trip computer and a digital speedometer. As for advanced driver-assistance systems, well, the car doesn't even have a rearview camera. It's exempt from most federal safety regulations due to its highly limited production numbers. The company produced approximately 35,000 steel-chassis cars before switching to a new platform, representing an average of roughly 417 cars per year.

Morgan's long-running steel chassis was likewise fairly old-fashioned. Essentially just a pair of Z-shaped steel rails connected to each other by five cross-members, the chassis rode on a basic leaf-spring suspension at the back and a sliding-pillar configuration up front. And the roots of that front suspension go back even further, as it was developed by Henry Frederick Stanley (HFS) Morgan in 1910.

Just to be clear, Morgan actually started using aluminum chassis in 2000, when it introduced one for its relatively short-lived line of Aero cars — starting with the Aero 8, which also stands out as the first Morgan model with a BMW powertrain. However, other Morgans continued to ride on the steel setup through 2020.

Meanwhile, Morgan was ready to introduce its new CX platform made from bonded aluminum. It first underpinned the 2019 Morgan Plus Six, which was named for its BMW-sourced I6 turbo engine. The lightweight chassis weighed a mere 220 pounds, but it was so stiff that the Plus Six had twice the torsional rigidity of the car it replaced in the Morgan lineup.

Then, in 2025, Morgan premiered the new Supersport with a further evolution of the CX chassis. The Supersport's CXV setup stiffened the chassis by 10%, plus another 10% when the detachable hardtop was in place, and enabled Morgan to enhance the steering and suspension systems as well. As regards the former, the results included a 13% quicker steering speed backed by improved feedback for the driver. The new suspension, now with standard anti-roll bars and revised geometry, promises "a compliant ride, better body control, and enhanced handling."

And yes, the Morgan Supersport is available in the U.S. The one major catch, though, is that we only get the four-cylinder model — a 2.0-liter TwinPower turbo-four with 255 horses and 258 pound-feet of torque. It's plenty peppy for a car weighing around 2,500 pounds. But the European Supersport 400 can deliver up to 402 horsepower from its turbocharged 3.0-liter BMW straight-six, taking the Morgan experience to a whole new level.

#5620. HLTH 2026: How Whoop aims to play a bigger role in healthcare

HLTH 2026: How Whoop aims to play a bigger role in healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Whoop gained traction as a performance wearable used by elite athletes, professional teams and Olympians to track physiological strain and sleep.

The company has evolved into a broader clinical and digital health platform that layers medical-grade hardware, blood diagnostics, electronic health record (EHR) syncing, and physician care on top of its continuous biometric tracking. The company's FDA-cleared ECG detects signs of atrial fibrillation and allows members to share results with their healthcare provider.

Whoop is a screenless, wrist-worn device that measures strain, recovery and sleep 24/7, paired with Whoop Coach, an AI-powered, in-app health and fitness assistant. The company expanded its Advanced Labs testing—combining Quest blood testing, clinician reviews and AI insights—to non-members, alongside integrating Grail's multi-cancer early detection test. Whoop partners with health platform HealthEx to let users connect their medical records directly to the Whoop app, combining medical history with biometric data. A feature rolled out earlier this year lets Whoop members directly connect with clinicians through the app, including live, on-demand video consultations.

The company has raised over $900 million to date, including a $575 million series G round in March, pushing its valuation to $10 billion. Whoop told Bloomberg it plans to hire 600 people this year, a roughly 75% boost to its headcount, as it works to further integrate AI into its health and wellness monitoring tools and to expand internationally. The company is on track for an initial public offering in 18 months, executives told Bloomberg in August.

The company is positioning itself as a continuous health monitor that goes beyond fitness tracking. The device's 24/7 physiological data can function almost like an ongoing health check, becoming a bridge between everyday health and medical care, Will Ahmed, founder and CEO of Whoop, said during an on-stage interview at HLTH on Tuesday.

Ahmed argued that the conventional annual medical physical is "frozen in time."

"The reality is wearing a continuous health monitor like Whoop that should be a 24/7 annual checkup. That's how it should function from a data standpoint," he said during a fireside chat with Michael Phelps, U.S. former competitive swimmer, who is the most decorated Olympian in history with 23 gold medals, and also a Whoop customer since 2015.

"Then there will be alerts when something is really wrong, and particularly as we combine these different data sources together, again, 24/7 physiological data, blood tests, medical records, how you're feeling and contextual cues. When we have all this information in one place, and now we've got 3.5 million members, about to be 4 million members, it's just amazing the insights that you can pull together from that. And so you can start to predict that someone may need to get a cancer screening, or may actually have a real heart problem," he said.

Whoop can pull together biometric data, labs, medical records and information to establish a baseline for an individual, recognize meaningful changes and recommend an action. By combining continuous monitoring with information such as blood tests, the company hopes to help users piece together health signals and determine when they may need care, Ahmed said.

For Phelps, Whoop has shifted from being about maximizing elite athletic performance to helping him manage his health, energy and recovery around everyday life and longevity, he told the audience.

"For me, for 20-plus years, I've been trying to chase time, and now I'm just trying to be the healthiest person that I can be," Phelps said. "For me, the data that I get every single day, if my body isn't 100% or I'm not full go, then I take a step back and I tone down my workout. When I'm talking to my trainer, I'm taking it down a little bit, so I have enough energy and I have what I need to be a good dad, to be a good husband, to be a good worker, hard worker, whatever it is, just to be a good person."

Whoop sees opportunities to turn deviations from an individual's baseline into actionable signals. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Phelps said his Whoop device signaled that his temperature, respiratory rate and HRV changed, but he noted that the real benefit was that Whoop knew what normal looked like for him.

Using biometric data to recognize signals in a person's health can have broader implications, Ahmed noted, citing examples where members identified potentially serious health problems after noticing significant changes in their physiological data.

"We're just starting to see all of these different maps presenting themselves, and it's very empowering. We're excited about the role that we can play with the broader health ecosystem," Ahmed said.

Ahmed said Whoop's high user engagement and continuous monitoring can fill gaps between doctors' visits and provide clinically relevant information to care teams.

"I do believe that technology like Whoop can make the whole system much more efficient and also make a doctor's life easier if we do our jobs properly, which is again to say, how do you take all this information that's being collected about a patient or a consumer and how do you simplify it to the one, two, or three questions that a doctor might actually want to know the answer to before you show up to their office?" he said.

Ahmed sees the AI coach evolving into a personal health companion sitting on top of a longitudinal health record.

"That's another area that we're really excited about, where this idea that you can have a conversation with Whoop or what feels like this entity that sits on top of your data, and all of a sudden you feel like you have a health companion, and yes, you've got 24/7 physiological data from sensors, but you can also now have your medical records. You can also now have your blood tests. There are all sorts of conversational cues. 'How are you feeling today?' 'Did you drink alcohol last night?' Were you traveling?' You put all that information together, all that data in one place, and the insights are quite profound," he said.

Partnerships with other digital health companies and acquisitions help Whoop broaden the platform, he noted.

"We like to think about it from the consumer's vantage point first, which is to say, if you're an individual, if you're a consumer, what is data that you want on your body or you need on your body, and that may be data that's being collected somewhere else, in which case, we feel like there could be an opportunity for a partnership," Ahmed said, adding, "We're also comfortable now acquiring technology and acquiring different innovations, which has become more of a muscle that we've built over the last 12 months."

Whoop believes its biggest strategic advantage is the consumer relationship.

Members open the app roughly eight times a day and wear the device nearly 23 hours a day.

"There are so many of us who have been in health tech where we would die for that kind of engagement, and I think that's something we're always striving for because we're an industry that was never built with the consumer in the center," said Lynne O'Keefe, founder and manager partner of Define Ventures, who moderated the on-stage interview.

The company is strategically expanding into an older, more medical population. Whoop is a participant in the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' ACCESS model. Ahmed said members 65 and older are actually Whoop's most highly engaged demographic, challenging the assumption that consumer health technology primarily appeals to younger people.

"It's clearly a population that cares a lot about their health. They want to focus on what's going on with their blood pressure, their ECG, or whether they need to send data to their doctors," he said.

Ahmed framed CMS' ACCESS model as a move from consumers simply paying for a wearable toward government reimbursement tied to measurable health outcomes, such as improvements in blood pressure or weight.

"I think as a model of innovation for a government and its citizens, it's pretty interesting because it incentivizes companies to actually create technology or programs that are making people healthier. It should change the cost curve because you're paying if that outcome is delivered, and then to the consumer, you're both hopefully being healthier and not paying for a product that otherwise would have had to," he said.

Whoop also positions itself as a platform that can wrap around drugs and other healthcare interventions. The company announced this week a partnership with Novo Nordisk as part of the pharma company's redesign of its direct-to-consumer NovoCare program. Novo Nordisk relaunched its NovoCare direct-to-consumer program. Patients taking a GLP-1 can integrate wearable data from Whoop as part of their program.

Whoop can function as a potential companion for GLP-1 users, monitoring exercise, sleep, resting heart rate, HRV and other signals while helping users preserve health and fitness during treatment, Ahmed said.

When asked about the future vision for Whoop, he said, "I think in simple terms, it's our responsibility to build technology that either makes you healthier or one day saves your life. You're going to have all of this health data on your body. I think organizing that information in one place, alongside 24/7 wearable data, and alongside a powerful AI that can sit on top of that data and go off on your behalf and take actions and schedule appointments with the doctor, or go speak to your doctor on your behalf, or alert you when something's wrong," he said.

He added, "God forbid this day comes, but you should wake up and be told from Whoop you need to go to the doctor in the next 30 minutes, and it's been scheduled, and you show up, and all of a sudden you find out that you're having a heart attack, or you're having some serious life event. To me, that feels like an inevitable future, and I do predict that a large percentage of humanity in the future will be wearing a continuous health monitor."

#5619. RMI’s Hydrogen Research Is Getting Better. Its Investment Advice Still Falls Short.

RMI has become much more realistic about hydrogen demand and competing technologies. That makes the gaps between its findings and its recommendations harder to excuse. Its latest work acknowledges that battery trucks generally have better economics than hydrogen fuel-cell trucks, that Europe needs far less hydrogen in 2030 than it originally targeted, and that low-emissions ammonia still costs substantially more than conventional ammonia. Several recommendations still seek public money to develop the very hydrogen markets the research has found difficult to justify.

I have been challenging this tension since January 2024. RMI matters because governments, investors and industrial companies use its research when deciding where to spend money. Its hydrogen program has made genuine analytical corrections. It has not made all of the accompanying strategic decisions.

Consider RMI’s February 2026 report on hydrogen trucking in India. The baseline comparisons find that fuel-cell trucks do not reach battery-electric truck ownership-cost parity through 2040, including the long-haul use case. The report also explores a much more favourable hydrogen price in an alternative sensitivity, which brings fuel-cell trucks closer to parity. Those are different findings, and the baseline matters to investment decisions today.

The report nevertheless recommends hydrogen vehicle subsidies, support for refuelling stations, production incentives and tax relief. It treats a parallel hydrogen-truck market as something to build. The case for spending public money on that market should start with evidence that a particular freight service cannot be served as well or better by batteries. The reported cost advantage of batteries does not disappear when the policy section begins.

The problem reaches beyond India. RMI’s 2025 US hydrogen report says battery trucks have greater market readiness and lower total cost of ownership, especially in the near term, yet calls for hydrogen distribution and refuelling infrastructure along freight corridors. The independent NACFE Run on Less ownership-cost work, developed within RMI’s freight research ecosystem, projects batteries becoming the lowest-cost option across its modelled duty cycles by 2035 without incentives. Hydrogen remains the most expensive option across nearly all of them. These findings support battery infrastructure as the default and a high evidentiary bar for hydrogen exceptions.

RMI already knows how to make appropriate distinctions elsewhere. Its 2026 steel research separates hydrogen used to reduce iron ore from hydrogen burned merely to supply process heat. In the illustrative plant, electric heat requires about 850 GWh a year, compared with 1,300 GWh of electricity to produce enough additional hydrogen for heating. That is the kind of direct service comparison that ought to govern recommendations throughout the organization.

Its new Green Ammonia Buyers Alliance also has a coherent industrial purpose. Fertiliser production already requires ammonia, commonly made with fossil-derived hydrogen. Purchasing lower-emissions ammonia to replace that supply addresses an existing industrial input. It does not require inventing a new energy market for ammonia combustion.

Europe shows how improved diagnosis can coexist with excessive policy ambition. RMI’s March 2025 recalibration reduced expected mandate-driven renewable hydrogen demand in 2030 to 2.2–2.8 million tons, far below the EU’s original 20-million-ton supply-and-import ambition. Its analysis identifies €13.9 billion in public support under existing mandates, plus €31.7 billion for an accelerated scenario. The combined €45.6 billion deserves a comparison with the other ways industry could obtain the same low-carbon products and services, including direct electrification and imported green materials.

That comparison changes the question for ammonia, steel and refining. A European fertiliser or chemical manufacturer needs ammonia, not necessarily hydrogen manufactured inside Europe. A steelmaker needs iron meeting its grade and emissions requirements. A mill needs process heat at specified temperatures. Governments can pay a premium to preserve domestic capacity for security or resilience, but the benefit must be valued and the public cost made explicit.

My November 2026 European hydrogen assessment applies that approach. In its central 2050 scenario, ammonia produced in Europe with on-site green hydrogen costs approximately €1,222 per ton. Qualifying imported green ammonia costs €745–755 per ton under the model’s assumptions. These are modelled values, not supplier bids. They demonstrate why an analysis that starts with hydrogen production targets can produce the wrong infrastructure plan.

RMI’s 2026 China green ammonia and methanol report acknowledges that green production costs remain two to three times conventional costs and that demand development lags supply ambitions. The report nevertheless discusses expanding ammonia and methanol as energy carriers, including ammonia for electricity. The relevant comparison for electricity is renewable generation with storage and other flexibility, not fossil-derived ammonia alone. RMI has not demonstrated that adding an ammonia combustion pathway wins that comparison.

This is a strategy problem as much as a modelling problem. Using Richard Rumelt’s framework, RMI’s diagnosis has improved, its guiding policy remains too committed to expanding hydrogen markets, and some coherent actions are missing. An economically unfavourable comparison should be able to end an infrastructure recommendation. Instead, it too often generates proposals for subsidies that would make the hydrogen route easier to sell.

RMI has the expertise to correct this. Its hydrogen recommendations should carry explicit alternative-technology comparisons, investment thresholds and exit criteria. Cross-program review should include the researchers measuring battery costs, industrial electrification, freight operations and grid flexibility. Where hydrogen is an essential chemical input or demonstrably the best means of delivering a service, support it. Where competing technologies win on cost and deployment readiness, stop trying to create demand through policy.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines RMI’s US, India, Europe and China reports side by side, including the differences between its findings and recommendations. It also links the original sources and the 2024 critique.

#5618. Plastic Surgeon Convicted of Killing Lawyer Is Sentenced to Death

— Tomasz Kosowski killed attorney Steven Cozzi in the bathroom of a law office

A judge in Florida this week sentenced a plastic surgeon to death for killing an attorney in a law office bathroom and then dumping his body in a trash bin in the Everglades, where it was never found.

Tomasz Kosowski, MD, killed attorney Steven Cozzi in the bathroom of Cozzi's law office in March 2023, moments after both participated in a conference call about a lengthy, acrimonious legal battle over medical billing, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors said Kosowski took the call from a Toyota pickup truck outside the office and that he had supplies to commit the killing, including trash bags, a syringe containing a paralyzing drug, and a wagon to haul the corpse out.

Investigators used cellphone records and surveillance video to track Kosowski to a remote area west of Miami on the Tamiami Trail, also known as U.S. Highway 41. That's where they believe Kosowski tossed the body into a dumpster that was eventually emptied by a garbage truck. The driver noticed an unusually "vile" smell at the stop, authorities said.

Trash from the route is typically hauled to a Collier County landfill, but authorities who searched the property for Cozzi's body said the facility routinely compacts its trash, making recovery efforts nearly impossible. In addition, investigators said, Cozzi's blood and DNA were found in the law office bathroom and in the garage at Kosowski's home.

Kosowski was convicted in September, following a trial in which he represented himself and presented no defense beyond making a closing argument in which he said prosecutors had not proved their case.

Pinellas Circuit Judge Joseph Bulone was tasked with deciding whether to sentence Kosowski to death or to life in prison without the possibility of release.

Kosowski declined to present any mitigating evidence on his own behalf, but a special counsel appointed by the court highlighted his lack of criminal history and his medical work. A graduate of Dartmouth College medical school, Kosowski specialized in reconstructive breast surgery.

The judge acknowledged in court that there were several mitigating factors, but said none outweighed the aggravating factors -- most importantly, that the crime was committed in a "cold, calculating, and premeditated manner, without any pretense of moral or legal justification."

"The court concludes that the defendant, under the laws of the State of Florida, has forfeited his right to live," Bulone said.

Investigators said that when they arrested Kosowski, he had $280,000 in cash, masks, duct tape, firearms, a ballistic vest with "EMS" written on it, law enforcement patches, and a vial of succinylcholine, which is a paralyzing drug. A search of his home turned up about 200 guns, according to court documents.

Cozzi, meanwhile, seemingly disappeared without a trace. His keys, wallet, and cellphone remained on his law office desk and a work file was open on his computer. His husband never heard from him.

The missing lawyer represented a Dunedin, Florida-based medical practice that Kosowski alleged had shorted him thousands of dollars in billings and damaged his reputation as a doctor.

Bulone appointed the public defender's office to represent Kosowski in his appeals.

#5617. Are End-Of-Year Car Sales Actually A Good Time To Buy?

Maybe you don't pay close attention to local car commercials. That's understandable, especially when it comes to the ads where the owner drags out their dog and grandkids. But if you do notice them, you'll see that in December or a little earlier, dealers start touting their deep year-end discounts and special pricing. Maybe you've even heard your friends say that the end of the year is a good time to buy a car — but is that true?

It can be. Dealers do, in fact, run special year-end deals in order to move inventory. They have to make room on their lots and meet annual sales quotas. In addition to discounts, they'll add incentives to sweeten the deal. It's a good time to buy used cars, as well. We say this because the availability of deals has been seen statistically to increase during December. But it shouldn't be seen as a hard-and-fast rule for every year, since there could be factors like supply-chain shortages that affect the price of cars.

Of course, the prevalence of deals is not a substitute for thorough research. Nor does it mean you don't need to try to negotiate. Don't assume just because you're car shopping in December that you're going to automatically walk into a great clearance deal on the car of your dreams. After all, end-of-year deals don't apply to every model. But as times to buy, the end of the year is a good one.

December is typically the month a dealership will offer its highest discounts. How much those discounts are higher than other months can vary year by year. Edmunds did a month-over-month comparison of discount percentages dating back to the beginning of 2023. December held the highest months in all three complete years in the report.

The discounts in December of 2023, at 3.1% of manufacturer's suggested retail price, were much higher than the lowest discount of that year, which was 0.6% in January. The differences between December's discounts and the lowest of the year were less drastic in 2024 and 2025, however. In 2024, they were 4.2% in December and 3% in January. In 2025, they were 4.7% in December and 3.9% in April (the month with the lowest discounts that year). This year, we've already found you five new cars with deep, deep discounts.

Why all the discounts in December? New cars from the latest model year gradually start arriving at the dealership as they are released during the previous calendar year. In other words, 2027 models have been arriving at many dealerships for a few months now. That means the dealer has to get rid of last year's models to make room for the new model year. The biggest push generally happens in December. According to Consumer Reports, customers who bought 2024 models as 2025 models were rolling out could have saved over $2,000.

Discounts aren't the only trick dealerships have up their sleeves to entice you to buy a new car. There are other incentives, like rebates and finance deals. These incentives are typically more generous in December, as well. Some incentives are tied to holidays and, as you may be aware, there happens to be a holiday in December, and it's kind of a big deal.

Cox Automotive looked at the statistics and noted that in 2025, incentives were at their highest in December, rising to 7.5% of the average transaction price (ATP). That's an 11% increase over the previous month, which saw incentives at 6.7% of ATP. The average price paid for a vehicle also went up that month, so it may seem that discounts and other incentives weren't that big a deal. However, that factor is skewed by the fact that more luxury cars are sold at the end of the year, raising the average price paid.

The fact is, dealerships are motivated to offer year-end discounts, rebates, and other incentives by more than just the need to move inventory. They often have annual quotas that need to be met. December offers the opportunity for a final push before that deadline. Automakers also want to clear the way for their newest models, which is why they often offer their own incentives at the end of the year.

Taking advantages of discounts and incentives at the end of the year often means you're buying a car from the outgoing model year. But maybe you buy new because you want the latest model, especially if there's an updated design or new generation. Buying the outgoing model might mean you'll be driving off the lot in a car that already looks dated. How embarrassing! Seriously, though, if the new generation offers new features, you might be missing out on them. And then there's the fact that a car from the outgoing model year will likely depreciate faster than one from the incoming year.

Remember, however, that buying a model as soon as it comes out means you're probably going to be paying the highest price it will ever be offered for. Eventually, it's going to be discounted to make way for the next year's model. And the first model year is typically the worst year of any generation in terms of flaws, bugs, and defects that need to be worked out. Expect a few trips to the dealership for some warranty repairs, possibly along with some recalls.

A generation's last model, on the other hand, is often its most reliable. And considering how much you could save buying the outgoing model year, it seems like a much better deal to us.

December isn't just the best month to buy a new car. It's a great time to buy used, too. In fact, it might be even better for buying used. The folks at iSeeCars did a detailed comparison of different times of the year for finding deals on used cars, defining a "deal" as a car offered for at least 10% less than market value.

On an average day throughout the year, the site found, a car shopper has an 11.5% chance of landing a deal. In December, however, the possibility increased to 46.2% more deals than average. The good news is that you have some flexibility if you miss the December deals. January isn't far behind December with a 44.1% chance above average of finding a deal on a used car. In fact, the best months are November through February, though December and January are the clear winners.

Their report also broke the numbers down by holidays. Martin Luther King Jr. Day is the best day to shop for used cars, as shoppers are 52.7% more likely than average to find a deal on that day. Right behind are New Year's Eve/New Year's Day and Christmas Eve. And it turns out Black Friday is a good day to find a deal on a used car, not just the next PlayStation.

So now you know December is a good time to buy a car. The problem is that dealers know you know this, and the smart ones lean into it. They'll advertise about how they're slashing prices because they're desperate to make room for new inventory. You believe them, and walk onto the lot believing you're taking advantage of their plight by exploiting their year-end deals. But thanks to hidden fees, unwanted add-ons, bait-and-switch tactics, and high-interest financing, you may end up paying as much for your new car as you would have in mid-July. You can't drop your guard just because it's the end of the year.

Did you see an ad promoting a really good deal? Great. Before you drive to the dealer, verify over the phone that the car is actually on its lot and available at the advertised price. Compare prices for that same car to be sure it really is a good deal. Call multiple dealerships and get their out-the-door price in writing. Take the lowest one into another dealership and get an even lower out-the-door price.

Get pre-approved for financing. If the dealer can beat your interest rate, cool. If not, you know you have options. Don't even talk about your trade-in until you have that out-the-door price. And check out our guide on other things not to say at a dealership. December is a good time to buy a car — just be smart about it.

Longevity platform Hone Health nabs $228M to build out offerings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hone Health, a physician-led virtual longevity care platform, has raised $228 million.

The investment is structured as a combination of equity and growth financing. The $28 million series A extension was led by MarcyPen Capital Partners, with participation from Pentland Ventures, Kinship Ventures, Hanwha, Gannet Capital, humbition and Comma Capital. Other angel investors also participated, including the Jonas brothers. The $200 million in growth financing came from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund.

Hone will use the investment to support a number of expansions. It plans to launch more programming for metabolic health, PMOS, inflammation and immunity, and to launch a physician-supervised peptide program. It will add more diagnostics, including coronary CT angiography and gut microbiome analysis.

Hone also plans to continue building out its AI operating system that brings data together to help personalize care. And it plans to build out clinical trial infrastructure to support pharma partners.

“Longevity is thought of as this super exotic thing. […] I actually think longevity is now becoming primary care,” Saad Alam, co-founder and CEO of Hone, told Fierce Healthcare.

It costs $65 to test for 70 biomarkers with Hone, followed by a clinician consult with the option to add more diagnostics. Labs, health history, symptoms and medications are run through its AI, which then gives providers treatment recommendations. Hone can keep adding additional diagnostics and medications, per Alam, “and the AI gets smarter as we get more patients into that system.”

Additionally, Hone is publicly announcing Hone Black, a new concierge longevity membership that has operated in stealth for a select group of patients for the past year. It combines diagnostics on over 1,600 health markers with ongoing medical care from physicians. Offerings include prescriptions, supplements, peptides and lifestyle guidance, plus exosome and stem cell therapies.

Alam founded the company after experiencing a shift in his health at 35 years old, including mental health issues, depression and weight gain. His doctor was initially of little help. It took Alam a year to find out he had low testosterone, and after treatment, he finally felt back on track. That experience, along with his father dying from kidney disease and his mother going through early menopause, opened his eyes to the longevity space.

“This whole concept of longevity is going to be one of the single greatest problems I can dedicate my life to solving,” Alam realized at the time. He experimented with everything, from peptides to cold plunges to meditation.

Hone is a subsidiary of Time Therapeutics, which aims to support production of drugs that help people live longer. Alam, who started his career doing market research at Eli Lilly, knew clinical trials are expensive and inaccessible. He wanted to create a company that could help commercialize drugs. The first step to that is Hone, or a DTC virtual care company that can capture longitudinal data on patients. The next phase will be publishing research. Finally, Hone will look to partner with pharma to get drugs to market faster.

The company has been providing care for five years, treating about 200,000 patients to date. It requires patients to have a physician and get bloodwork every 90 days in order to get medication refills. Members can contact their clinician between sessions as needed.

“We make sure, for the most part, that you are doing bloodwork and talking to a physician, a real conversation with a physician, in order to get prescribed medication,” Alam said.

It isn’t about overprescribing medications. It’s about finding the most personalized protocol for each patient. “The companies that have—no pun intended—longevity are the ones that are going to figure out how to reduce the number of medications somebody might need,” Alam said.

Hone began with hormone therapy, then moved into longevity care with biomarker analysis and women’s health. Two months ago, Hone’s offerings for women surpassed offerings for men in terms of net new members. It soon plans to run clinical trials on poly-chronic patients as well to help determine the right drug at the right time. Hone crossed $100 million in revenue in 2025, per Alam, and is on track to double this year.

“When I started goop, wellness was a niche conversation,” Gwyneth Paltrow, founder and CEO of goop and co-founder of Kinship Ventures, said in a press release. “Today, it’s one of the biggest categories in the world, and the next step is bringing real health and wellness to the masses, not just the few. Saad has built Hone to do exactly that, with serious science and at real scale. That’s why Kinship invested, and we could not be more excited about what’s ahead.”

Hone will soon offer 14 longevity care categories, which Alam argues is akin to primary care. He estimates that Hone only refers to in-person care about 10% of the time, usually for higher-acuity conditions. Some Hone patients are already healthy; most are sick and willing to pay out of pocket because the current system has been inadequate in solving their health needs, per Alam.

“This is just the beginning of not only a way but a complete change in the way that medicine is practiced,” Alam said. “A lot of other companies are what I’ll call pill mills, and where we’ve really focused—our energy is making sure that we go through the more difficult work of managing the long-term health of our patients.”

#5615. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. New research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline

To investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

"This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy said. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect."

This effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

"I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed."

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

The research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

This increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

"There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy said. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well."

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

Murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

The researchers then plan to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce important features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

Materials provided by University of Chicago Medical Center. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5614. An Insurer Paid Me $6.73 to Save a Teen's Life

— The No Surprises Act allows me to keep saving others

In October 2023, a 19-year-old came into the emergency department with a perforated appendix. By the time I got him to the operating room, his abdomen was full of pus. A surgery that normally takes me 15 minutes took an hour and a half due to the amount of inflammation distorting his anatomy. I rounded on him in the hospital every day for a week until he was stable for discharge, then followed him for another 2 months until he had fully recovered.

For that surgery, the week of inpatient care, and 2 months of post-op follow-up, the insurance company sent me a check for $6.73.

This wasn't a clerical error -- it was the contracted rate the insurance company had set for the procedure. Laparoscopic appendectomy, like most operations, falls under a 90-day global period, which meant I couldn't bill separately for any care delivered in the 90 days after surgery. As far as the insurer was concerned, $6.73 was full and final payment for treating a teenager with sepsis from a ruptured appendix.

This is precisely this kind of payment that makes the federal No Surprises Act's (NSA) independent arbitration process so important to physicians like me. The law gives us a way to challenge inadequate insurer payments through a neutral process, helping independent physicians keep our practices open so we can continue caring for patients and saving lives.

I opened my own practice in 2023 after several years in academic medicine, where I had learned exactly how little say a physician can have over her own patients, her own schedule, and her own worth. I wanted to make medical decisions based on what my patients needed, not on what a hospital system's spreadsheet required. I did not expect that the fight for that independence would move from the hospital administration to the insurance companies.

When I first opened my doors, I kept a part-time position at a county hospital to make ends meet while I built a patient base. When that wasn't enough, I added emergency general surgery call at another hospital for $40 an hour. For about 6 months I was working four jobs. My savings dwindled. I started drawing from my 401k. As a single mother and the sole provider for my two daughters, I was doing the math every month to make sure I could pay my staff, office rent, medical malpractice insurance, and my mortgage. For 2 years I did not pay myself, and I wondered whether staying in medicine was still something I could afford to do.

Lately, I find myself wondering whether I can keep practicing independently, because that $6.73 check was not an outlier; it is part of the pattern. A few months after the teen with the perforated appendix, another patient came in with severe anemia and a bowel obstruction due to a large colon tumor. I performed a robotic colectomy to remove the cancer, relieve the blockage, and stop the bleeding. The insurer denied the claim, stating the operation was "not medically necessary."

This is where the NSA arbitration process became critical to my practice. When an insurer and a physician can't agree on payment, each side submits an offer to a neutral arbitrator, who picks one. It isn't a settlement. It's one of the only checks that exists on an insurer's ability to set whatever price it wants for care the patient has already received.

Physicians win these disputes more than 80% of the time, and some critics have pointed to that number as evidence the system is broken. It isn't. It's evidence of how low insurers' offers actually are. An analysis of nearly 160,000 arbitration cases found insurers offered $0 to the physician in more than 20,000 cases. In the fourth quarter of 2024, roughly a quarter of all disputes were resolved by default, seemingly because the insurance company provided incomplete information or failed to make an offer at all. When one side offers nothing, or next to nothing, an arbitrator does not need to search hard for the fair number.

I did not go into medicine and open a solo practice in a saturated Houston market because I thought I could get rich. Sixteen years of education and training to be paid $6.73 for emergency surgery is a terrible way to build wealth, it turns out. I built my practice so that I could provide accessible surgical care while maintaining autonomy and agency over my life and professional choices. Every solo and small-practice physician I know who now uses this process was doing the same math I was doing at my kitchen table over the last 3 years, wondering if it was truly possible to practice medicine independently, outside of large institutions and private-equity-owned medical practices.

Arbitration is one of the only tools we have that puts a solo surgeon and a multibillion-dollar insurer on anything resembling equal footing.

The numbers show what happens when that tool disappears or is weakened by suggestions that doctors are the ones driving up costs. The share of physicians in independent practice fell from 37.8% in 2019 to 22.4% in 2024, with more than 75% of physicians now employed by hospitals or corporate entities. Every one of those doctors who left independent practice took something with them: continuity with patients they'd known for years and the ability to make a clinical decision without checking it against a corporate metric.

No physician is asking for sympathy. We are asking that the next time someone suggests that physicians are "gaming" the NSA, she instead asks why an insurer's opening offer for a week of care after a ruptured appendix was $6.73, and why it took a federal arbitrator and an 8-month process to make that number make sense.

The law was written to protect patients from surprise bills. What's often left out is that it also protects physicians who are trying to practice independently, because we are not interested in 5-minute visits and being told to double-book patients. Take this protection away and let end-stage corporatization and consolidation of healthcare finish the job, and we will witness the end of the independent practice of medicine in America.

#5612. HLTH 2026: Noom, Hims & Hers roll out peptide offerings

HLTH 2026: Noom, Hims & Hers roll out peptide offerings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Direct-to-consumer health companies Noom and Hims & Hers are making a play for the peptide market as the federal government loosens restrictions on compounded treatments.

The companies are betting that peptides could be the next big thing in consumer health. For Noom, the new peptide offering extends the company's business beyond weight loss into the broader longevity and wellness market. Hims & Hers signaled months ago that it was ready to tap into the multi-billion-dollar peptide market.

Federal policy shifts and U.S. Food and Drug Administration enforcement discretion around compounded peptides have opened new pathways for telehealth and compounding pharmacies.

On Tuesday, Noom launched OpenRx as a separate peptide and preventive health brand. At launch, OpenRx offers two injectable options: sermorelin, a peptide frequently prescribed for muscle support, and NAD+, a coenzyme frequently prescribed for energy. OpenRx also offers two oral dissolvable tablet options: the first formulation combines the peptides PT-141 and oxytocin with tadalafil to support sexual health. The second ODT formulation is the peptide oxytocin to support intimacy.

Noom says it plans to expand into other areas including recovery, muscle health, skin, gut health and sleep. Peptides are small pieces of protein that occur naturally in the body and help control functions such as growth, healing and appetite.

“Peptides are an important portion of the formulary of healthy aging,” Geoff Cook, CEO of Noom, said in a statement. “OpenRx enables our flagship Noom brand to deepen into cardiometabolic health while the new brand OpenRx supports patients with conditions too often neglected by traditional care models, like energy, muscle composition, skin health, sexual health, sleep, and recovery. Together, both brands support the same mission: to empower everyone, everywhere to live better longer – every day.”

Noom says every OpenRx prescription is written by a licensed clinician following an evaluation of the patient’s health history, goals and clinical appropriateness. Treatments are fulfilled through Noom’s U.S.-based pharmacy network, which operates under state boards of pharmacy oversight and adheres to USP compounding standards, the company said.

Noom is currently reviewing BPC-157 and TB-500 as part of its ongoing process of evaluating emerging treatments for inclusion in our formulary, Jeffrey Egler, M.D., Noom's chief medical officer, said in a statement. "Each therapy offered by OpenRx is selected because our clinical team and I believe it is appropriate for improving patient health. The process involves continuous monitoring of safety-related signals, gathering the judgment of our medical directors and the medical directors of affiliated clinical networks based on years of prescribing experience with the compounds in question, ensuring a compliant and stable supply chain, sourcing of active pharmaceutical ingredients, and setting up processes for compliance with state and federal adverse event reporting guidelines," Egler said.

Online health and wellness brand Hims & Hers announced earlier this month it planned to roll out a peptides business. As part of the company's new Peptides+ specialty, launched today, it plans to initially sell five U.S.-compounded peptide and longevity treatments—Sermorelin, NAD+, Glutathione, Vitamin B12 and L-Carnitine, with plans to add more peptides and therapies over time.

The company also plans to offer U.S.-made BPC-157 and TB-500 "consistent with regulatory requirements," the company said.

A survey the company conducted in October of 2,000 adults found that more than half (55%) said they were interested in or curious about peptide therapies, and 40% of U.S. adults say they are interested or very interested in a telehealth offering of injectable prescription treatments, including peptides and other compounded treatments. Nearly 1 in 10 U.S. adults (9%) say they currently use peptides, not including FDA-approved peptides such as Ozempic, Wegovy and insulin, the survey found.

Peptides are in the spotlight due to the massive success of FDA-approved GLP-1 weight loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which are peptide drugs. Wellness influencers and biohackers on social media are promoting other lab-made peptides for fast-tracked healing, anti-aging and muscle growth.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has championed looser federal rules on trendy, unapproved peptide injections. In July, an FDA advisory committee recommended broader access to six unapproved peptides. The panel recommended adding these six substances to the Section 503A Bulks List, which would remove the restrictions on how they are produced by compounders, Fierce Pharma reported.

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, Kennedy has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides, Fierce Pharma reported. Under Kennedy’s "enforcement discretion policy" issued in late October, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

But medical experts have raised safety and clinical evidence questions around unapproved or experimental compounds. The American Medical Association (AMA) publicly opposes the Trump administration’s plan to make certain unapproved peptides more widely available for human use.

In a letter (PDF) to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the AMA pushed back what it called a "rushed" decision to permit the compounding of certain peptides because they have not been approved for safe use by the FDA.

Unproven peptides may pose serious health risks, including allergic reactions, infections, hormonal imbalances and other unexpected side effects, according to the FDA website.

"We should not bypass the science and put patients at risk by making them guinea pigs for unapproved drugs," AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., said in a statement. "If these substances are safe and effective, the evidence should demonstrate that through the FDA’s rigorous review process."

Hims & Hers' peptide therapy program provides a "clinically guided, personalized plan" for consumers "backed by a licensed provider who understands these therapies," according to Anant Vinjamoori, M.D., chief medical officer of the Hims brand.

Hims & Hers wants to "set the standard" for peptide therapy and offer consistency in the quality of the products, Vinjamoori said in an interview on the sidelines of the HLTH conference this week.

"If you think about what we have to bring to the table with our scale and resources, I would argue there's no one better equipped to do it than us," Vinjamoori said.

Hims & Hers has invested in its supply chain and expanded its domestic manufacturing facilities. In 2025, the company acquired a Menlo Park peptide facility to run API validation and stability testing to support its specialized peptide offerings.

"That's why we're investing in our supply chain and doing a lot of the hard work that, frankly, is not the fastest path to making these available. There are pharmacies that are already out there that are making these available, and there are companies out there that will simply just plug into those pharmacies and service patients. But there are inconsistencies," he noted.

Until now, getting these types of medications has often meant relying on unreliable and unregulated online sellers, or a high-cost longevity clinic, Hims & Hers executives said. Hims & Hers' peptides offering gives consumers more accessible care, "backed by real medical leadership and with consistent clinical oversight," the company said in a press release.

Hims & Hers believes its scale gives it an opportunity and responsibility to help build the evidence base around peptides, using growing patient interest not just to expand access but to better understand how the treatments can be used safely and effectively, Vinjamoori said.

Expanding into peptides fits with Hims & Hers' ongoing focus on personalized health, he noted. "We started with sexual health, moved on to hair loss, and then we've continued to broaden into other categories such as hormone replacement, GLP-1s, and now peptides, and many others to come. And the common theme in all of this is that we're talking about helping people accomplish a specific goal that they have. We're not talking about curing a disease or treating a disease per se," he said. "We're talking about, 'Hey, there's something you want to do in your life that you're not able to do right now. Let's help you figure out how we can put together a plan to help you accomplish that."

"This is a big part of the future of medicine itself," Vinjamoori added. "It's been the missing part of the equation, where we've been very focused on treating and responding to disease, but not as much, not just on prevention, but really on helping people use their health as an asset and as a tool to help them accomplish what they want in life."

With Hims & Hers' peptide therapy offering, consumers start with a clinical visit with a licensed provider that includes a comprehensive intake of health history and goals. The company said a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies assesses each individual and, if appropriate, tailors a personalized protocol to their needs.

Hims & Hers treatments are compounded in the U.S. and dispensed directly by licensed, U.S. pharmacies regulated by state boards of pharmacy and "held to rigorous quality and safety standards," the company said.

The buzz around peptides ties into consumers' growing interest in taking control of their health "driven by the cultural zeitgeist moment," Vinjamoori told Fierce Healthcare.

"There's a variety of different factors that catalyze that. I think the COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed a lot of it for a variety of reasons. I think you see accelerations in biotechnology where people now see something like GLP-1s that can help with a problem that seemed intractable before. I think people are now interested in figuring out what is the range of solutions that could help me. I also think peptides represent something that has a lot of promise, a lot of excitement," he said.

"But there are also some cautions that we need to take as well. Something we think a lot about is how do we meet this moment of excitement and enthusiasm with some degree of rigor and guardrails," Vinjamoori said.

"It starts with the product itself. How do we ensure the quality? The compounds are of the highest quality and are compounded in the most rigorous way, made available in the most rigorous way. That's why we are trying to have as much oversight as we can into the full process of making these available," he said.

He asserted that informed consent and transparency with consumers are critical. "I've spent a lot of time with the team to make sure that we understand that people have this enthusiasm, but we need to make sure that they understand what they're getting into. There is a difference between this and FDA-approved therapies," he said.

"Sometimes people should try the standard of care before they engage with some of these things, and so we want to make sure we have these conversations with people openly and honestly. But at the same time, we also want to respect their choice," he added.

Hims & Hers Peptides+ is available with its Care+ program that gives customers access to twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress, unlimited support and ongoing check-ins from a dedicated care team. Customers can also message providers trained in peptide therapy 24/7 with any questions. The Hims Men’s panel includes at-home blood collection and access to lab tests that provide insights across 22 biomarkers, including testosterone, vitamin D, and cholesterol. The Hers Women’s panel tests 22 biomarkers across hormones, vitamins, and heart health.
